articles.title: Measles in America: Here's a constructive approach to beating the highly contagious disease, based on Brazil's experience
articles.summary: The US is now officially a measles contagion zone. By mid-2026, there were more infections than in all of the previous year. But it could beat measles again, just like Brazil did two years ago.

image.caption: Brazil distributed more than 16 million doses of the measles vaccine in 2026 and maintained its measles-free status; in the US, vaccination rates have fallenImage: ZUMA Press/IMAGO

blocks.text: Health experts saw it coming — the fact that after 26 years, the US would lose its status as measles-free. Back in July 2026, DW reported how one epidemiologist had suggested an 'amnesia' about the measles risk was pushing a growth in US infections.
Four months later, it was official. On November 17, 2026, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) said the US had lost its measles elimination status along with Mexico.
But it doesn't have to stay like that for long.

Look at Brazil, where in 2019, with more than 21,000 measles cases, the country also lost its measles-free status. But within five years — during the COVID-19 pandemic — it fought and won back its measles-free status. And since 2024, Brazil has stayed measles-free, even as the highly contagious disease spread across the rest of the Americas.
In 2026, with the data available up to the time of writing this article, Brazil had had only 70 measles cases. They were all linked to infections brought in from abroad, often from neighboring Peru.
Brazil has fewer people than the US, about 213 million compared with the US's nearly 350 million, but the two countries are similar in size. So, the comparison is worth considering.
What Brazil does differently from the US
Brazil moves fast. The PAHO asks countries to respond within 72 hours of a suspected case. Brazil's own rule is a ladder:

items: Report cases within 24 hours
Investigate within 48 hours
Vaccinate people close to the case within 72 hours

blocks.text: It has also made hunting for cases a national habit.
In a program called "Dia S", health workers knock on doors and visit schools, daycare centers, and churches to find people who may be sick but have not seen a doctor.
Brazil holds targeted, mass vaccination days called "Dia D". There was one in November, in the area where Brazil borders Colombia and Peru.
If someone is diagnosed with measles, health workers try to track down every person the patient may have met ("contact persons") and they vaccinate them and other people living nearby.
The country has so far provided more than 16 million doses of measles vaccination in 2026 and has donated 500,000 doses to Peru.

Brazil isn't perfect, though. According to official estimates from the World Health Organization, only 76% of children got both required doses of the vaccine in 2025 — well short of the 95% target. Experts warn this leaves the country at risk because measles is so highly contagious; a country needs to be as close to 100% immunized as possible to protect people and stop the disease from spreading.
"Elimination is not a trophy that we win once and put on a shelf. It must be protected every day," says PAHO Director Jarbas Barbosa.
Is the US experiencing a vaccine crisis?
Why the US lost its measle-free status

The US lost its measles-free status because the PAHO found that the same strain of the virus had been spreading in the country for 12 months or more. Mexico and Bolivia lost their status on the same day as the US.

The US has had more than 5,400 cases in 2026 (at time of writing), more than twice as many as in all of 2025, and about 19 times as many as in 2024. Nearly everyone who got sick with measles was unvaccinated or had an unknown vaccination status.

In August 2026, when US President Donald Trump signed an executive order on new vaccination recommendations for children, it came at a time, when, as we reported, experts said people had stopped getting vaccinated against measles because infection rates were low. As PAHO's Jarbas Barbosa says above, avoiding vaccination when infection rates are low is a mistake.

To be fair, Trump's executive order listed the measles vaccine in a top category of vaccinations recommended for every child. But the administration's stance on vaccination in general is unclear; Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has often declared opposition to vaccination, including against measles, advising people to take vitamin A instead. In Texas, this led to children being hospitalized with toxic levels of the supplement, and left them with no protection against measles.

Before the COVID-19 pandemic, 95% of US kindergartners had their measles shots. Now, it's 92%, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Protection (CDC). That leaves about 280,000 kindergartners unprotected.
In the Texas counties, where a 2025 measles outbreak began, coverage was as low as 77% at the time.

US children usually need vaccines to start school, but most states let parents opt out for religious or personal reasons, with no doctor involved. In 24 states, so many children were exempt that those states couldn't reach the 95% threshold even if every other child got vaccinated.

But vaccination rates have fallen elsewhere in the world as well, including in Europe. In Germany, where measles infections have also risen, experts blame anti-vaccination rhetoric that emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic.
The 95% measles vaccination rule explained
It all comes down to math.

A person sick with measles can infect up to18 other, unprotected people. With vaccination, it is possible to increase the number of protected people and lower the number of people the sick person can infect.
To prevent a measles outbreak, a community needs about 95% of people to be vaccinated and/or immune. The vaccination consists of two doses of the MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) vaccine.

But even after the two doses, a person can expect to have only 97% protection against measles — 3% short of full protection — so, nearly everyone in the community has to be vaccinated to keep the average level of protect as close to 100% as possible.

"For some diseases like measles, even a small decrease in vaccination rates can lead to more outbreaks of disease [so] community immunity requires over 95% of susceptible individuals to be immunized," says Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics.

And the 95% has to hold everywhere. A good national average can be affected by, for example, a single school where only 70% of the children are vaccinated. And that is where the outbreak start is likely to start.
In the US, where vaccination rates at kindergartens have dropped to 92%, that small difference is big enough to cause a measles outbreak.
The picture is mixed worldwide
Around the world, measles deaths have dropped by 88% since 2000, thanks to vaccines.
But progress has stalled. Only about three out of four children worldwide get both doses of the vaccine. The biggest outbreaks right now are in Bangladesh, Indonesia and Guatemala.
Data from Europe shows that things can get better. In the European Union, cases fell from more than 35,000 in 2024 to about 2,300 the following year, with no measles-related deaths.
Romania went from more than 30,000 cases in 2024 to about 4,200 in 2025.
Hungary, where 99% of children are vaccinated, there have been no measles cases in the past year.
But in January, six European countries lost their measles-free status, including the UK, Spain and Austria. Across Europe, eight out of ten people who got measles in 2025 were unvaccinated.

The Americas are seeing a major surge in measles infections, with more than 58,000 cases in 2026, over four times as many as this time (November) in 2025. Guatemala has been hit hardest, with almost 35,000 cases.

The deadliest outbreaks are in Africa. African Union countries have so far reported nearly 1,800 measles deaths in 2026, about 1,650 of them in Democratic Republic of Congo. Yet, Sudan, despite the war, raised first-dose measles coverage by 22 percentage points in 2025, which was the world's largest gain.
What you need to know about measles
Measles is extremely contagious. One person can infect up to 18 unprotected people, which makes it about 12 times more contagious than the flu.

The virus can linger in the air for up to two hours after a sick person has left the room. And people spread it before they know they are sick. Someone with measles is contagious for four days before the rash appears and four days after.

It's not just a rash. About one in five unvaccinated people who get measles in the US ends up in the hospital. Measles can weaken the immune system for years, making it harder to fight off other infections.
But it's preventable. Two doses of the MMR vaccine (which also protects against mumps and rubella) protect 97% of people for life.

articles.title: US Senate approves bill to speed up permitting reviews for energy projects and datacenters
articles.summary:
Bipartisan legislation now goes to the House amid concerns by some Democrats and environmental groups

The Senate approved bipartisan legislation on Thursday aimed at speeding up permitting…

blocks.text: The Senate approved bipartisan legislation on Thursday aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation’s energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower electricity prices.

The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to start big energy projects and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over datacenters and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths.

The 62-33 vote is the first major action by Congress since midterm elections that soundly repudiated Donald Trump and congressional Republicans. The bill now goes to the House, which approved a more limited, industry-friendly version last year.

The Senate bill would overhaul several environmental laws to make it easier to build energy infrastructure, drawing criticism from Democrats and environmental groups about limits on judicial review and changes to bedrock laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act.

Trump urged approval of the bill, calling it a “BIG WIN for US ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE” in a recent social media post. The bill, formally known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, will ensure the US can build pipelines, mines and power plants more quickly, “lowering Energy Costs for American Families”, Trump wrote.
Fifteen Democrats, including Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer, voted for the bill. Two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, voted no.
Fear of weakening safeguards

Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and the oil and gas sector support the bill as a way to deliver more electricity to the grid and avoid delays for infrastructure projects that can stretch a decade or more.

However, many environmental organizations have denounced the measure, saying it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals.

“Make no mistake: This backroom deal will pave the way for even more fossil fuel projects like gas power plants for data centers, oil and gas pipelines and (liquefied natural gas) terminals while sacrificing fundamental and common-sense public health and environmental protections for communities across the US,” said Jen Duggan, executive director of the Environmental Integrity Project.

Benefits for renewable energy are outweighed by likely increases in greenhouse gas emissions and air and water pollution from the fossil fuel industry, Duggan and other critics said. She called the bill “a gift to some of the biggest polluters in America” and complained that it was being rushed through a lame-duck Congress without public hearings or sufficient debate.
Democrats push for amendments
A final vote on the measure was held up this week as Oregon’s two Democratic senators pushed to add amendments, including one to ban datacenters on public lands.

Senators Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden are among several Democrats in both chambers who say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that boosts clean energy, such as solar and wind power, while limiting expansion of oil, natural gas and other fossil fuels.

“Getting more renewable electrons where they are needed doesn’t tackle climate change if you simultaneously promote the burning of more fossil fuels. Unfortunately, this bill does exactly that,” Merkley said.

Majority Republicans stymied Merkley’s effort to ensure votes on a host of amendments, including one that would block the Trump administration from continuing to cancel clean energy grants and other Democratic priorities for “purely political purposes”.
The bill’s sponsors reneged on promises of “a robust amendment process”, he said. In the end, the measure was approved without amendments offered by rank-and-file senators.
“I do think that this bill is very consequential to the future of this planet,” Merkley said.

Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, oppose the bill, citing concerns about limits on judicial review and changes to the National Environmental Policy Act and other laws. The environmental policy law, known as Nepa, requires agencies to consider a project’s possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved. The current review process often takes five years or more, and shortening that time frame is a key goal of the bill.

“In America today, it takes too long and costs too much to build,” said Wyoming senator John Barrasso, the No 2 Republican in the Senate. “Energy projects that would help lower prices remain frozen for years” as they await approval by the federal government.
“Construction cannot start without first spending years in the regulatory penalty box,” driving up costs and creating uncertainty, Barrasso said.
The bill’s four main champions – two Democrats and two Republicans – have released a detailed set of amendments designed to bolster support for the legislation.

The four senators, who lead the chamber’s energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal a few weeks before the election. Republican senators Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic senators Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years.
“We are going to make it easier to build in America again, and make life more affordable for American families,” Lee said.
‘The floor, not the ceiling on climate

Whitehouse, a longtime climate hawk who has been criticized by some allies for supporting the permitting bill, said the measure is “the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations”, adding that he hopes “to accomplish big things with our big Democratic majorities” over the next two years.
But Democratic senator Maria Cantwell of Washington state said the bill has been rushed and its impacts are not fully considered.

Cantwell, who met Tuesday with tribal, outdoor recreation and conservation leaders, said the bill would undermine tribal nations and weaken protections for the nation’s bodies of water, land and wildlife.

“Now is the time to slow this process down, to actually have a formal process” to debate and amend the bill, she said. “Don’t sacrifice the Clean Water Act or hunting or fishing grounds, historic or sacred sites, or protections of tribal sovereignty. We all need new sources of energy and power. But this bill, as it’s currently drafted, is not the answer.”

articles.title: Far-right activist Daniel Thomas jailed for slashing dinghy in Channel
articles.summary:
Thomas sentenced to 15 months after admitting to criminal damage to vessel that had been carrying asylum seekers

The far-right agitator Daniel Thomas has been sentenced to 15 months in jail…

blocks.text: The far-right agitator Daniel Thomas has been sentenced to 15 months in jail after slashing a dinghy that had been carrying asylum seekers in the Channel.
Thomas had taken a boat out to observe the occupants of a dinghy being assisted by the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI), Border Force and the French coastguard on 22 September.

He instructed his boat to be steered towards the empty vessel, which was adrift, and then armed himself with a knife as rescue crews also approached the dinghy and a French man boarded from a rescue vessel.

After slashing the dinghy with the knife, Thomas could be heard saying: “This is what needs to happen to everyone in these boats. Right, you’re on English territory. This is England; this is not France any more. Get off the boat; you have time to get off the boat. This is not France. Take them back.”
The incident was captured on Thomas’s live stream and the 37-year-old, also known as Danny Tommo, admitted criminal damage when he appeared at Portsmouth crown court via video link from prison.
After footage of the incident emerged, Thomas’s actions were condemned as violent and dangerous by the refugee charities Stand Up to Racism and the Joint Council for the Welfare of Immigrants.
According to the RNLI, the rescued asylum seekers had been onboard the dinghy for 36 hours, which was thought to be the longest time small-boat passengers had spent crossing the Channel.

The RNLI said there were concerns for their deteriorating health and fears of a “catastrophic failure” of their dinghy. The French coastguard said about 60 people on a small boat had spent more than 33 hours at sea “in precarious conditions” and refusing help as they were “determined to take all risks to reach the United Kingdom”.

articles.title: ‘Forever our Fiona’: fans of the famous hippo mourn her death at zoo
articles.summary:
Flowers and notes appeared next to sculpture of hippos at Cincinatti zoo within hours of Fiona dying, days after swallowing a visitors’ hat

Tributes are pouring in and an impromptu shrine…

blocks.text: Tributes are pouring in and an impromptu shrine has popped up at the Cincinnati zoo in Ohio as fans of the famous hippopotamus Fiona mourn the animal’s death on Thursday, following failed attempts to save her after she ate a knitted hat.

Flowers and notes began appearing next to a sculpture of hippos at the zoo within hours of Fiona dying on Thursday despite numerous treatments aiming to help her eliminate the object that got stuck in her digestive tract.

One note with flowers said: “Forever our Fiona”. Amy Hackey said to Cincinnati’s Channel 7 TV station: “I thought she was going to make it.” As the tributes continued arriving, Hackey added: “I think it will be our equivalent of Princess Di”, referring to the late Diana, Princess of Wales, the first wife of Britain’s King Charles, whose sudden death in a car crash in 1997 prompted an outpouring of grief and tributes.

Yolanda Gould, who was visiting from Kentucky, told the TV station that she’d been following Fiona’s story since she was born, when her survival after a premature birth made her famous and a symbol of strength for many.
“Cincinnati has such an incredible bond with her because of her journey and what’s she’s been through. She taught us all to be resilient.”
The nine-year-old hippopotamus earlier in the week mistakenly swallowed a visitor’s hat that had accidentally fallen into her enclosure. It was not possible to operate on the adult animal.

Her zoo keepers placed her under surveillance and she was initially asymptomatic, then her appetite waned. Despite round-the-clock care from the zoo’s veterinary team and care staff, and various treatments, the Nile hippo became increasingly sick and later on Thursday it was announced that she was dead.
Fiona became a global sensation in 2017 as a tiny newborn who was unable to stand on her own and weighed just 29lbs. As her legend grew, she inspired books and a line of beer.

The Cincinnati zoo was also where 10 years ago bouquets and tributes accumulated after zoo keepers were obliged to shoot dead an adult gorilla, named Harambe. The male western lowland gorilla, 17, was executed in 2016 after a child fell into his enclosure and was grasped by Harambe.

articles.title: Is Pakistan backing anti-Taliban groups in Afghanistan?
articles.summary: The Taliban rulers in Afghanistan have accused Pakistan of aiding and sheltering armed resistance groups. The allegations come amid heightened tensions and are likely to deepen the rift between the…

image.caption: Islamabad has repeatedly demanded that the Taliban take action against anti-Pakistan militant groups operating from Afghan soilImage: Abdul Basit/AFP

blocks.text: The Taliban authorities in Afghanistan claim that the Pakistani government is supporting armed Afghan groups that are opposed to their rule, an accusation Islamabaddenies.
Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi recently alleged that Pakistan had launched a "project to destabilize Afghanistan."
He claimed that "thousands of armed individuals have gathered along the Durand Line (Afghanistan-Pakistan border) to undermine the stability achieved in Afghanistan."
The accusations come after months of border clashes between Afghan Taliban and Pakistani forces.

In July, the Afghanistan Freedom Front (AFF), an anti-Taliban group, reportedly clashed with Taliban forces in the Zebak district of Badakhshan, a northeastern Afghan province. The group said it also carried out attacks in Nooristan and Kunar provinces in October.
Another "resistance group," the United Front of Afghanistan, claimed it attacked Taliban forces in Kandahar province along the border with Pakistan.

"The people who created insecurity in Badakhshan crossed from Chitral [in Pakistan] and later fled back to Chitral. They had been brought in. Even Pakistani military personnel were with them," alleged Zabihullah Mujahid, Taliban's main spokesperson, in an interview with DW's Pashto-Dari service in September.
Pakistan's Ministry of Information swiftly dismissed the allegations as propaganda.
Groups that oppose the Taliban rule in Afghanistan say they are not supported by any external force, and their resistance is purely indigenous.
How 5 years of Taliban rule have changed Afghanistan
Pakistan's 'leverage' amid tense ties
More than five years since returning to power in Kabul, the Taliban have consolidated their control over Afghanistan and largely suppressed both armed resistance groups and political dissidents.

Shinkai Karokhail, a former Afghan member of parliament, told DW it would be logistically difficult for anti-Taliban Afghan groups to cross the Pakistani border and enter Afghanistan without Islamabad's support, referring to clashes in Badakhshan and Nooristan provinces.
"It is simply impossible," she said.

The Taliban themselves maintained close ties with Pakistan in the 1990s during their first stint in power. Some US officials even claimed that Islamabad didn't relinquish its support to the Islamist group even after September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in the United States. Islamabad has always refuted these allegations.
But Afrasiab Khattak, a Pakistani political analyst and former senator, believes that Pakistani support for anti-Taliban groups is "real."
"Taliban opponents come to Islamabad, hold meetings, and it is a part of Pakistan's policy toward Afghanistan," he told DW.
Qandil Abbas, an associate professor of politics and international relations at Quaid-i-Azam University in Islamabad, disagrees.
"Pakistan may provide political support [to Taliban opponents], but not military support," she told DW.

Ali Ahmad Jalali, a professor at the Near East South Asia Center for Strategic Studies at the National Defense University in Washington DC, said it is possible that Islamabad is backing Taliban opponents as a "leverage."

"When such incidents take place along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border, and given Pakistan's history of support for Afghan groups, it would not be surprising if Pakistan is supporting these groups," Jalali said.
Are Pakistan and Afghanistan heading for war?
Islamabad accuses Taliban of similar tactics

Pakistani officials have repeatedly demanded that the Taliban take action against anti-Pakistan militant groups, particularly the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), a militant group responsible for attacking Pakistani civilians and soldiers, and the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA), an outlawed armed separatist group active in its western Balochistan province.
Islamabad alleges that these groups organize and launch attacks inside Pakistan from Afghan territory with Taliban support.

"Meaningful progress requires Afghan authorities to address legitimate security concerns of neighboring countries, particularly the threat of terrorism," Pakistani Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said this week at the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO) summit in Islamabad.
Islamabad said on Friday that Afghanistan was not invited to participate in the ECO gathering as Pakistan does not recognize the Taliban regime in Kabul.
Analyst Jalali, who served as Afghanistan's interior minister from 2003 to 2005, argues that Islamabad is demanding something the Taliban may neither be willing nor able to provide.

"Pakistan wants the Taliban to cooperate in fighting against groups such as the TTP. But the TTP has long fought alongside the Afghan Taliban. There are ideological as well as friendly ties between the two. They seek a similar political system, and some Afghan Taliban members may even be among TTP fighters," he added.
Analysts also point to the Taliban's efforts to strengthen relations with India, Pakistan's long-standing regional rival, as a cause of concern for Islamabad.

Malek Sitez, Afghan expert and researcher of international relations, argues that Pakistan, among other things, doesn't want Kabul to be close to New Delhi. But Pakistan no longer has the kind of influence over Afghanistan that it had in the past, he said.
Under Taliban shadow, Afghans in Pakistan look to Germany
Is Pakistan seeking to remove the Taliban from power?
Despite these accusations and counteraccusations from both sides, Jalali believes Pakistan still does not seek to remove the Taliban from power.

"I do not think Pakistan can or wants to overthrow the Taliban and replace them with another group," he underlined. Instead, he stressed, Islamabad's objective is to pressure the Taliban into cooperating against the TTP.

Aziz Barez, a political analyst of Afghanistan and regional affairs, is of the view that Afghan groups opposed to the Taliban can also not fully trust Islamabad, adding that they may welcome alleged Pakistani support but are also aware that such backing could be temporary.
"It is possible that Pakistan and the Taliban will resolve their differences tomorrow and become close allies again," he told DW.
Ahmad Waheed Ahmady and Helay Asad contributed to this report.

articles.title: ‘You can’t get experience if no one’s employing you’: the vicious circle facing Blackpool’s Neets
articles.summary:
The English seaside town tops the list for 16- to 24-year-olds out of work and education, but not for lack of young jobseekers’ efforts

Speaking random words like “cat” and “box” into her…
articles.byline: Josh Halliday North of England editor

blocks.text: Speaking random words like “cat” and “box” into her phone while filming herself in her pyjamas, Amy Butterworth’s relentless search for a job had reached a new level of absurdity.
The 19-year-old from Blackpool was applying for a role at Marks & Spencer, but first had to prove she was not a robot.

After downloading an app, filming her face from different angles, speaking particular words, inputting numbers and sharing a picture of her passport, she eventually received an email offering interview slots.

Yet within two minutes of the message arriving, all the slots were gone. In the small print, the retailer admitted it could not promise an interview to everybody offered one. “I just felt kind of stupid,” Butterworth said.
This is the demoralising reality for many young people in Blackpool, where more than one in five 16- to 24-year-olds are out of work and education, the highest proportion in England.

Alan Milburn, the former Labour minister, this week urged “full throttle” overhaul of policy across healthcare, education, benefits and employment regulation as Britain reckons with a growing crisis of nearly 1 million young people not in education, employment or training (Neet), a far higher rate than many other western European nations.

Eight of the 10 English local authorities with the highest Neet concentrations are in the north or the Midlands. Top of the list is Blackpool, where the town’s reputation as a pleasure resort sits uncomfortably with its deep-rooted issues of poor health, housing and addiction.

blocks.caption: Blackpool has England’s highest proportion of Neets, with more than 20% of its young people not in work or education. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian

blocks.text: On Saturday, dozens of seasiders will put on their glad rags hoping for a ticket to the BBC’s Strictly Come Dancing, which is filmed in the Blackpool Tower Ballroom for one week each year. Yet the queues are unlikely to match the town’s annual jobs fair earlier this year, when more than 4,000 jobseekers lined the promenade.
One local official described the enormous turnout in February as a “sad indictment” of the British economy. Of the 2,000 jobs on offer, 1,200 were given out on the spot.

The huge demand for work makes life more difficult for teenagers such as Butterworth, who say they are constantly told by employers they need more experience but find few willing to take a chance on them.
Describing this vicious circle, she said: “You need to get a job, but to have a job you need some experience. And you can’t get experience if no one’s employing you.”

The lucky ones find seasonal work cleaning hotels or serving up chips to day-trippers. But the lack of year-round jobs means competition is extremely high, with some employers receiving 200 applications for every vacancy.

Companies have started using AI to sift through CVs, putting applicants at the mercy of algorithmic bias. Less scrupulous firms use “postcode screening”, effectively blocking applicants from some parts of Blackpool, according to a report by the Social Mobility Commission in September – a practice Chris Webb, the Labour MP for Blackpool South, described as “abhorrent”.

blocks.caption: Amy has recently found work at a bar and food hall, and is hoping to train as a tattooist. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian

blocks.text: Since finishing her art diploma at Blackpool and the Fylde College, Butterworth has lost count of the amount of job applications she has submitted. Despite volunteering at a local primary school, she has had no end of knockbacks.
“It really knocked my confidence a lot and I felt really disadvantaged, because nearly everyone I knew had got their first job because they knew someone,” she said.
after newsletter promotion

Butterworth is bright, articulate, hard-working and full of character, with a cuttingly dry sense of humour. But in school she struggled with concentration. Her autism was only diagnosed in February after a years-long wait.

The Covid pandemic, which struck when Butterworth was in her second year of secondary school, left her marginalised. Her mother had just finished cancer treatment and was classed as highly vulnerable, so teachers put Butterworth “behind a wall on a desk on my own”.
“It was very isolating,” she said. “It made me very socially anxious, which definitely didn’t help when I was originally trying to find a job.”

Blackpool has one of England’s highest school exclusion and absence rates, and one of the lowest levels of attainment for GCSEs. Experts say both are a result of the challenging backgrounds of many of the town’s children, as well as mental or neurological conditions that often go unsupported.

Last November, headteachers started adopting less punitive measures to try to keep more children in class. The number of pupils excluded or suspended has since fallen by 33% and 29% respectively, according to Blackpool council.

Local leaders are working to reverse the town’s position as England’s Neet capital. A brightly coloured youth skills hub called the Platform gives 16- to 24-year-olds personalised support with writing CVs, training, doing interviews and securing work or volunteering.

Kath Benson, a Labour councillor who is the council executive’s member for young people, said: “There’s a massive perception about young people that they just want to stay in bed and play on their phones. I know that’s not the case. In Blackpool, they’re queueing up for jobs.”

The Platform was launched in 2022 with £5m of funding from the UK’s shared prosperity fund, which replaced EU money previously given to disadvantaged areas. Since then, it has supported more than 2,350 young people into learning, training or work, according to the council.

Butterworth was one of those it helped, finding her training to work behind a bar while she tries to establish a career as a tattooist. She pulled her first pint last month at Abingdon Street Market, a trendy food-and-booze hall, and is hoping to start an apprenticeship at a tattoo parlour where she showed off her artwork.
Things are now starting to look up, she said: “I just feel very grateful that I was in a situation for once where I actually know someone that can give me an ‘in’ somewhere.”

articles.title: ‘A source of inspiration’: series of public events celebrate life of Dolores Huerta
articles.summary:
A public vigil and celebration of life honor the civil rights activist and co-founder of United Farm Workers union

Hundreds honored and celebrated the life and legacy of California civil…

blocks.text: Hundreds honored and celebrated the life and legacy of California civil rights activist Dolores Huerta this week with a series of public events including a vigil and celebration of life in Bakersfield.
Huerta, a feminist icon who co-founded the United Farm Workers (UFW) in 1962, died on 28 October aged 96.

“Our family has been deeply touched by the condolences, remembrances, and tributes we’ve received from people whose lives our mother, Dolores, impacted,” said Huerta’s family in a statement on Thursday afternoon. “Countless people have shared how she changed the course of their lives, and each story has reminded us of how fully she committed her life to helping and supporting others.”
The week was filled with events dedicated to Huerta’s memory, her courage, resilience and her impact on the community.

On Monday, Huerta was honored in Sacramento by state government officials including Monique Limón, the senate president pro tempore, Robert Rivas, the assembly speaker, Xavier Becerra, the California governor-elect, and community leaders and the public who paid their respects to the world-renowned labor rights leader and activists in a historic ceremony.
Huerta became the first female, first Latino and first non-elected leader to lie in honor at the state capitol. Her casket was escorted in after a march organized by local unions.

“Our mother devoted her entire life to fighting injustice and lifting up communities too often left out and treated unfairly,” said Huerta’s family. “As a lifelong organizer, her activism has been a source of inspiration and empowerment for people around the world.”

For more than six decades, Huerta spearheaded historic boycotts, fought tirelessly for farmworkers’ rights, women’s equality and environmental justice, and coined the enduring national rally cry, “¡Sí, se puede!”
Huerta has received numerous honors including the Eleanor Roosevelt Human Rights Awards. In 2012, Barack Obama awarded Huerta the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor.
A two-day tribute started on Thursday evening with a public rosary and vigil in Bakersfield, where she had lived since 1990. The public was invited to pay their respects after the rosary.

On Friday, an interfaith memorial service and celebration of life will begin with an opening blessing by Aztec dancers followed by the memorial service and the celebration of life program. Music groups Los Lobos, Ozomatli, Las Cafeteras, Nancy Sanchez and Trio los Dados are expected to perform. The event will also feature speakers including Becerra, Rob Bonta, the California attorney general, Teresa Romero, the UFW president, actor Eva Longoria, and Cristela Alonzo, a comedian, among others.
Both public events will be live streamed on the Dolores Huerta Foundation YouTube channel.

Her legacy will continue through the work and empowering mission of the Dolores Huerta Foundation. In 2003, Huerta founded the grassroots community organization to create leadership opportunities for community members, while organizing underserved communities, and pursuing social justice.
Huerta kept on working even as a nonagenarian, dedicating her life as an organizer.

In the Central valley, Huerta supported minorities to run for office to make a difference at the local, state and federal level. In 2022, Huerta spoke at a USCIS Special Children’s Ceremony in Delano, encouraging new US citizens to fulfill their civic responsibilities, especially voting.

For her 94th birthday, Huerta asked people to help her celebrate her birthday by getting others involved in elections either by talking to somebody about voting and about registering to vote. She encouraged legal residents to become US citizens to exercise their rights to vote.

Huerta urged uninsured Latinos and Californians to enroll in health coverage with the passage of the Affordable Care Act partnering with Covered California to spread the message. Huerta also had several schools named after her throughout the state. Last year, Huerta joined Central valley educators to demand David Valadao, a US representative from California, to defend funding for schools.

articles.title: ‘Gloucestershire nouveau’: UK vineyard uncorks its 2026 answer to beaujolais
articles.summary:
Three Choirs unveils First Release white wine after long, hot summer led to earliest harvest start in 50 years

Forget beaujolais nouveau: a Gloucestershire vineyard has uncorked its 2026…

blocks.text: Forget beaujolais nouveau: a Gloucestershire vineyard has uncorked its 2026 vintage, giving the first taste of this year’s long, hot summer – and an answer to France’s autumn tradition of opening young wine straight after harvest.
Three Choirs near Newent has unveiled its First Release white wine after the earliest harvest in its 50 years of producing wine.

The First Release is what the vineyard calls its “Gloucestershire nouveau” – its tongue-in-cheek nod to beaujolais nouveau, a young, fruity red that is released on the third Thursday in November. Beaujolais nouveau was traditionally made for local consumption and was a way for workers and villages to enjoy the first sip of that year’s harvest.

Vines were first planted on the Gloucestershire site of a fruit farm in 1973, while Three Choirs has been bottling a young wine every November since the 1980s. Customers can buy the wine directly from the vineyard’s shop or try it in its restaurant.
In the 1980s, the harvest used to begin in mid-September, about a month later than it did this year, according to Three Choir’s winemaking director, Martin Fowke.

blocks.caption: In the 1980s, the harvest used to be begin in mid-September, about a month later than it did this year. Photograph: Three Choirs vineyard

blocks.text: This year’s prolonged summer of warm temperatures – and rain at the right time – meant the first grapes were picked on 20 August, a week earlier than the previous record set in 2025. The harvest ended on 9 October, by which time 200 tonnes of grapes had been collected across the vineyard’s 30 hectares (74 acres).
The 2026 First Release is a run of 5,000 bottles of a dry, white wine containing solaris, bacchus, siegerrebe and madeleine angevine grapes.

“We now have an extra month to make the wine. We had riper raw material and longer in the winery,” said Fowke, calling 2026 a “record-breaking year”. He added that higher sugar levels and lower acidity allowed winemakers to make a product that was not possible in Britain 30 years ago.

The early timing of the harvest surprised even the Three Choirs winemaker Jack Abbotts, who was on his summer break when picking started. “It’s usually a safe week for me, but this year it all snowballed,” he said.
The changing climate has made it possible to grow grapes on a commercial scale in Britain, but it also brings challenges.

“We found it hard this year,” said Fowke. “People kept saying: ‘This hot weather must be good for you’, but it was difficult because we knew the heat and lack of rain was challenging for farmers. We don’t need it to get any warmer, that’s for sure.”
Vines have been planted as far north as Yorkshire and Scotland, as Britain’s wine industry expands. More than 1,100 vineyards are now registered in Britain.
after newsletter promotion

While Britain remains far down the list of global wine producers in terms of volume – behind countries including Uzbekistan and Tunisia – it is the fastest-growing wine region in the world, according to the property group Knight Frank. The area of planted vineyards in the country has quadrupled since the turn of the century, it reports.

Some of the newer, smaller vineyards do not have their own winemaking facilities, relying on contract winemakers such as Three Choirs. The Gloucestershire vineyard also produces wine for about 40 others, including Llanerch, located west of Cardiff.
English and Welsh wine producers had their second-largest harvest in 2025, when the equivalent of 16.5m bottles, or 124,377 hectolitres, was produced, according to the industry body WineGB.

blocks.caption: Grapes are harvested at the Three Choirs vineyard in Gloucestershire. English and Welsh wine producers had their second-largest harvest in 2025. Photograph: Three Choirs vineyard

blocks.text: The data for the 2026 harvest will not be available until early next year, although WineGB said in August it was “optimistic” about the size and quality after the hot growing season.

If the UK climate continues to change and summers such as 2026’s become the norm, Three Choirs may consider growing new varieties. “We can evolve and change, but we would be planting cabernet sauvignon like they did in Bordeaux 50 years ago,” said Fowke, noting the shift from white to red grapes. “But that is not what we set out to do.”

In the fog and damp of November in Gloucestershire, pruning of the vines ready for the 2027 growing season has already begun. “To have two good years in a row is not uncommon, to have three is unusual,” said Fowke.

articles.title: Germany face belgium in Nations League quarterfinals — Klopp plays down favorites tag
articles.summary: Germany coach Jürgen Klopp is looking to "carry positive momentum forward" as his team draw neighboring Belgium in the quarterfinals of the UEFA Nations League.

image.caption: Based on their FIFA rankings, the Germany-Belgium matchup should produce a closely contested tieImage: Peter Schatz/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany, who finished top of Group A2 following their 5-0 win over the Netherlands in Berlin on Monday are to face Belgium in the Nations League quarterfinals—after they finished second in Group A1. The Belgians recently came up with a statement result of their own, beating Italy 4-1. The match-up between the neighboring countries promises to be closely contested, with Belgium sitting at No. 8 in the men's rankings, three places above Germany.

The head coach of Belgium is former Bayern Munich player Mark van Bommel, who took over from Rudi Garcia following the World Cup, where they were knocked out by eventual champions Spain in the quarterfinals.

Germany head into the knockout phase on a high note, not only because they won their group, but also the way they performed in their last two matches, against Serbia and the Netherlands in the group stage.
Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp followed the draw, held in Nyon on Friday, from the German FA's (DFB) Frankfurt offices. He played down the notion that Germany enter the tie as the favorites.
"I've practically never given it any thought. It's never interested me," he said.

"An awful lot can happen in that time. We're very happy with the final impression we left, yet we're also fully aware that we're only at the very beginning of a development process. We want to carry this positive momentum forward—there's still a great deal to be done."
Historical success for Germany against Belgium
The matches are slated for March 25 and March 30, 2027, and having won their group, Germany will have home-field advantage for the second leg.
Germany and Belgium have faced each other 26 times to date, with West Germany and Germany having the upper hand with 20 wins, five defeats and one draw.
Should Germany advance to the semifinals, they will go on to face the winner of England and Norway – a World Cup quarterfinals rematch.
In the other two semifinals matchups, the Netherlands drew Portugal, while the top pairing sees Spain face France in a rematch of one of last summer's World Cup semifinals.
The "Final Four" mini tournament is to be held from June 9 to 13 but the host venue won't be determined until the semifinal lineup has been completed.

articles.title: Marcos rejects call to reassess economic team amid 'malaise'
articles.summary: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Friday stood by his current economic team even as he was urged by a senator to take a closer look at his Cabinet amid a so-called “economic malaise.”

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 10:44pm
President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Friday stood by his current economic team even as he was urged by a senator to take a closer look at his Cabinet amid a so-called “economic malaise.”

In a Kapihan with the media in Shenzhen, China, the President said he disagrees with the call of Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson, who earlier raised concerns about the dipping Philippine stocks, the weakening peso, and rising inflation, among other issues.
“No, I don’t…I disagree with him. I’m sorry, but I disagree with him,” Marcos said.
“All the difficulties we’re going under can be clearly directly traced to the war in Iran,” he added.
Cabinet revamp
Marcos likewise addressed speculations about recent changes in his Cabinet, saying that he is only trying to “put the best people to the best use” amid developments worldwide.
“Everything was done for a particular reason. There’s no general reason that I’m not happy with the Cabinet or anything like that. No, not at all. Quite the contrary,” he said.
“Issues come up that didn’t exist before in certain departments. So we’re trying to put the people who are best able to address those issues into the proper department,” he added.
The President said that the reshuffle also had something to do with his administration’s plans.
“[We’re] trying to get the best people into whatever position we need to best be able to push our priorities for the future,” he said.
Marcos also stood firm that shifting one Cabinet member to another position does not produce instability in the government.

“The job of a Cabinet secretary does not remain exactly the same from day one until day whatever it is six years later. Nagbabago talaga ‘yan (it really changes). And then we make our own plans as we go along,” he said.

“And then we have to worry about shocks like the war in Iran, so we have to adjust also to that. And then now with AI coming up, we have to adjust also to that. And then the different developments in geopolitics, we also have to adjust to that,” he added. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Defense witness can’t explain discrepancy in Cale88 sales, cash inflow
articles.summary: DTI Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo's testimony on Cale88 raises more suspicions about the banana chips exporter's inward remittances from China

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – A defense witness for Vice President Sara Duterte on Friday, November 20, admitted he could not explain the discrepancy between the cash inflows and declared sales revenues of Cale88 Foods Corporation, a company being linked to the Vice President.

On Day 45 of the impeachment trial, the defense presented Ceferino Rodolfo, Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) undersecretary for industry development and investment promotions, to establish the legitimacy of Cale88.

Rodolfo testified that Cale88 is registered as an export enterprise under the DTI-Board of Investments (BOI) and has complied with the agency’s registration requirements. He also identified the company as a micro, small, and medium enterprise (MSME).

In his interjection, Senator-judge Sherwin Gatchalian questioned the huge disparity between Cale88’s declared sales and its reported cash inflows, asking Rodolfo to explain the possible reasons behind the discrepancy.

“In relation to the operations of the company and the documents they submitted to us, we don’t see any reason for the inward remittances to exceed the declared sales revenue submitted to us,” Rodolfo said.

Rodolfo later admitted that it was his first time encountering such a discrepancy involving a company. He stressed, however, that he was not qualified to explain the figures, saying Cale88’s president, treasurer, operating officer, and export sales manager would be in a better position to do so.

Cale88, a banana chips production company partly owned by Duterte’s husband, Manases Carpio, came under scrutiny during the impeachment trial after Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) records showed that it received P776 million in cash inflows despite having only P125,000 in paid-up capital and declaring P208 million in sales.

Lawyer Alex Cabrera, who prepared a forensic financial report on Duterte’s bank and financial records, described Cale88’s business model as “implausible.” He likened its operations to a “revolving door,” which he said was a symptom of money laundering.
Senator-judge Panfilo “Ping” Lacson said the central issue was not Cale88’s legitimacy as a registered company but allegations that it may have been used as a front for money laundering.
“What we want to see is proof or records – waybills, shipping records,” Lacson said.

“I know you said earlier that those are with the Customs, but we are all wondering, at least, if the defense could refute the forensic financial analysis, and erase our doubts that Cale88 might have been used,” he added.
Defense counsel Michael Poa clarified that Rodolfo’s testimony was only preliminary, assuring senator-judges that the defense would present other witnesses to address the allegations.
“We understand what you are looking for. We have witnesses for that,” Poa said.

Senator-judge Risa Hontiveros said on October 6 that an investigation by her office showed that Cale88 Food Corporation received remittances from Chinese companies, including entities linked to China’s state-owned sector.

Prior to that, Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura told the impeachment court that Cale88 received P319 million from China and Hong Kong, based on covered transaction reports (CTRs) and suspicious transaction reports (STRs).
The National Security Council (NSC) responded to these disclosures last October by saying it would look into the reported inflow of Chinese funds to Cale88.

Vice President Duterte has generally been silent and uncritical about China’s harassment of Philippine vessels in the West Philippine Sea, which critics say could be linked to her family’s business ties with Chinese companies.

Im a related development, the Senate impeachment court has set a new schedule for the trial as it takes a brief break to give way for the Senate plenary deliberations on the proposed 2027 national budget.

Impeachment Court Presiding Officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero initially announced that the trial would resume on Thursday, November 26, reverting to its original schedule of 10 am to 2 pm. However, lead defense counsel Sheila Sison asked for the indulgence of the court, saying their witnesses are unavailable on November 26 and November 27.

“We would like to be candid to the court and say that our next witnesses are not available on November 26 and 27. Also given that we are only informed today that there will be hearings for next week and as you know, this is not our only commitment and we had also made commitments to our other engagements,” Sison said.

“We are not interested in a protracted, prolonged trial of this case and as this court has seen, the defense has been prudent with the time of this court, has not abused this court, and has not wasted three months time presenting witnesses that will eventually be withdrawn,” she said.
House prosecutor Terry Ridon asked for Sison’s remarks to be stricken from the records. He also called for consequences to be placed on the defense for lessening the days of presentation.
Escudero said he would take under advisement Ridon’s manifestation. He also said the impeachment proceedings will resume next month with the following schedule:
December 1 to 4: 10 am – 3 pm
December 14 to 17 (if necessary)

articles.title: Turkey takes control of opposition broadcaster Sozcu TV
articles.summary: In the latest in a series of raids and arrests, another major pro-opposition Turkish broadcaster has been brought under state control. This is the third in a year.

image.caption: Sozcu is not the first government-critical television channel in Turkey to be brought under state controlImage: Berk Ozkan/AFP

blocks.text: Another important opposition media outlet in Turkey has been placed under state control. On Tuesday morning, authorities raided the offices of the television broadcaster Sozcu TV and the news portal Sozcu.com.tr, and arrested several executives.

A trustee has also been appointed: The state deposit protection fund, TMSF, which usually administers the assets of insolvent companies, has been put in charge. Sozcu was one of the last big media companies in Turkey to regularly report critically on the government of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

A large police contingent raided the broadcaster's headquarters in Istanbul, with counterterrorism officers searching the offices. According to Sozcu, its chairwoman, Funda Tuncer Sidali, and Asim Akgul, the former chief executive of the Sozcu group, were among those arrested.

The broadcaster did not initially announce the appointment of the trustee on its digital channels. It did call on its audience to follow it under a new account. The leader of the main opposition party, Ozgur Ozel, declared on X: "You will never be able to prevent this nation's voice from rising, its rebellion from being heard, its cry from echoing."
Accused of ties to the Gülen movement

The Istanbul public prosecutor's office has confirmed the arrangements. It justified the investigation with claims of a suspected connection between the owner of Sozcu, Burak Akhay, and the Gülen movement. The Turkish government blames this movement, which was once allied to Erdogan, for the attempted coup in 2016, and has designated it a terrorist organization.

According to the investigators, Akbay is said to have used foreign bank accounts to finance two companies involved in media activities on behalf of the Gülen movement. They claim there is strong suspicion that he was able, in this way, to hold a leadership position in the organization.
A familiar pattern in Turkey

It is not new for the Turkish state to take over media organizations by appointing trustees. Many media companies accused of being close to the Gülen movement were brought under state control in this way after the attempted coup in 2016. What is new is that for about a year now this is also happening to media seen as pro-opposition.

blocks.caption: Turkish counterterrorism officers searched the Sozcu offices Image: Berk Ozkan/AFP

blocks.text: Sozcu is not the first opposition broadcaster to be targeted by the authorities. The TELEI TV channel was searched on October 24, 2025. Its editor-in-chief, Merdan Yanardag, was arrested on charges of espionage and remains in custody. The offices of Halk TV were raided on October 14 this year. There, too, a trustee was put in charge.

In the space of just over a year, three of the most important opposition television channels have been brought under state control. Observers see this as another step toward an increasingly authoritarian and politically isolated system.
The opposition is being silenced
Berk Esen, a political scientist with Sabanci University in Istanbul, sees these measures as a significant weakening of the opposition in the public domain.

Esen told DW that the government may first have acted behind the scenes and tried to bring Sozcu to heel politically. When this didn't succeed, it invoked the judiciary. Esen says Turkey is increasingly moving toward an authoritarian system. The attempt to prevent opposition organizations and media from gaining strength and influence is part of this.

Esen describes the opposition's success in local government elections in March 2024 as a political turning point. Since then, he says, the government has seen its chances of winning political competitions at the ballot box receding. "It's become harder for the AKP to win elections," says Esen. "That's why it's attacking the opposition and the free media both at once."

Several opposition mayors have also been arrested in recent months and replaced by trustees. They include the mayor of Istanbul and presidential candidate Ekrem Imamoglu, who has been in detention since his arrest in March last year. He is regarded as one of Erdogan's most promising challengers.
No future in Turkey? Growing exodus of young Turks
'Black winter for press freedom'

The Turkish Journalists' Association (TGC) spoke of a "black winter for press freedom," and announced its solidarity with all those affected. It described the recent developments as a serious attack on press freedom. The fact that a trustee had been appointed, first at Halk TV and now at Sozcu, showed how the media climate in Turkey has deteriorated, it said.

"These days, too, shall pass," the TGC declared. "When that day comes, those journalists who seek the truth today will be remembered, as will the decisions that prevent the public from hearing that truth."
This article has been translated from German.

MANILA, Philippines – One of the co-accused of former House speaker Martin Romualdez has surrendered to the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI), the bureau said on Friday, November 20.

The NBI said Samchan Foreign Exchange Corporation president Felicito Guevarra surrendered the day before on November 19. Through his counsel, the accused, who faces a plunder case alongside Romualdez, relayed his plan to surrender.
“On 19 November 2026, at approximately 9:00 am, NBI agents proceeded to the agreed meeting place at Santuario de San Antonio Parish, 3117 McKinley Road, Forbes Park, Makati City,” said the NBI.
“At approximately 10:00 am, Guevarra voluntarily submitted to NBI custody in the presence of his counsel,” it added.
Guevarra was read his rights during the surrender and was later brought to the NBI headquarters to undergo standard booking procedures for arrested or surrendered suspects.
On Friday, NBI agents returned the warrant to the anti-graft court Sandiganbayan and presented Guevarra before the 3rd Division, where their case is pending.

Guevarra surrendered after the Office of the Ombudsman moved to cancel his passport. The investigative body said it granted the Samchan president conditional immunity because they will use his testimony to further strengthen their case.

“The Office granted Mr. Guevarra conditional immunity under Section 17 of Republic Act No. 6770 because his testimony and records are necessary to establish the truth in this case. The immunity rests on his full and truthful testimony,” the Ombudsman said.

“Mr. Guevarra personally handled Samchan’s operations. His testimony and records will help the prosecution trace the movement of funds alleged in the charge sheet. The charges against the other accused stand as filed,” it added.
If Guevarra breaks any condition, the Ombudsman said it will revoke the immunity. The conditions are as follows:

items: cooperate fully and truthfully with the prosecution
turn over all of Samchan’s records and devices
remain in the country
stay under the Department of Justice’s protection

blocks.text: Romualdez, Guevarra, former Ako Bicol representative Zaldy Co, and Josely Serenio are facing plunder, a non-bailable offense, due to alleged P7.44 billion in kickbacks from government projects.
The Ombudsman filed the plunder charge against them with the Sandiganbayan on September 7. On the same day, the 3rd Division issued a warrant of arrest against the accused.
Romualdez was subsequently arrested and has been detained in the New Quezon City Jail in Payatas since September 14. But his co-accused remained at large, until Guevarra’s surrender. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Africa at COP31: Will climate cash finally flow?
articles.summary: As the curtains draw to a close on COP31 in Antalya, one question looms large for African countries: will climate promises finally translate into the funding African communities need to cope with a…

image.caption: Some African countries are currently coping with El Nino-induced weather patternsImage: Thomas Mukoya/REUTERS

blocks.text: For millions across the continent, climate change is no longer an abstract environmental concern debated in conference halls. It is already reshaping daily life, livelihoods and even decisions about where people can live.

In Zimbabwe, Harare resident Tsitsi Moyo says the effects are becoming increasingly difficult to ignore. "The extreme heat wave we have been experiencing I think also has issues to do with rainfall patterns."
Jane Okello has witnessed similar changes in Uganda, describing increasingly erratic weather, including periods of unusually heavy rainfall associated with El Nino.

Their experiences reflect a wider trend across the continent. Communities that depend on predictable seasons for agriculture, water supplies and income are finding it harder to plan for the future as weather patterns become more extreme and less reliable.
Africa: How climate change is reshaping the continent

For some, the consequences go beyond disrupted harvests or shrinking water supplies. Climate pressures are also influencing migration patterns. According to Professor Alfred Ngomanda, Permanent Secretary of the Gabon Climate Council, environmental stress can push people to leave their homes in search of more favorable conditions and more secure livelihoods.

Climate change is rarely the sole reason people migrate. However, droughts, floods, declining agricultural output and other environmental strains often intensify existing economic and social challenges, making displacement more likely.
As African countries prepare to make their case at the climate negotiations, Ngomanda stressed that the continent must emphasize the global importance of its natural resources.
"We will go to Ethiopia to assert that the Congo Basin is a stabilizing element for the global climate, and not just for Africans."
Why climate finance matters
At the heart of the discussions at COP31 is climate finance, the funding used to help countries reduce greenhouse gas emissions and adapt to the impacts of climate change.

COP, or the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, brings together governments from around the world to negotiate action on global warming. The talks build on the Paris Agreement, adopted at COP21 in 2015, which aims to keep global temperature rise well below 2 degrees Celsius while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5 degrees.
For African countries, the challenge is not simply making climate commitments, but securing the resources needed to turn those commitments into reality.

Opening the conference, United Nations (UN) Secretary-General Antonio Guterres highlighted what he described as a fundamental injustice in the global response to climate change. "Developing countries face a double injustice: they bear the brunt of climate change but struggle to access the finance they urgently need," Guterres said.

The scale of the financing gap remains stark. According to the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa, the continent received about $52 billion (€44.5 billion) in climate finance in 2022, far short of its estimated annual requirement of $190 billion. Much of that funding also comes as loans, adding pressure to already strained public finances.
The shortfall is especially significant given that Africa contributes only about 4% of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet remains one of the regions most vulnerable to climate change.

African governments are therefore calling for funding that is more predictable, accessible and affordable, particularly for programs intended to help communities adapt to extreme weather, strengthen resilience and protect livelihoods.
From commitments to action

African negotiators say the focus now must be on making sure that climate commitments produce tangible results on the ground. Speaking at a press conference on November 19, Veronica Nonhlanhla Jakarasi, lead negotiator for the African Group of Negotiators, argued that the continent needs a dedicated mechanism to translate climate proposals into funded projects.
"What we need is a mitigation implementation facility that moves Africa's proposals into actual financing and projects on the ground."

She said such a facility would help direct more resources to the continent while supporting economic growth, green industrialization and the development of Africa's critical minerals sector without driving up emissions.

blocks.caption: Africans countries bear much of the impact of climate change despite contributing less greenhouse emissionsImage: Emmanuel Herman/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: Mitigation focuses on reducing greenhouse gas emissions, while adaptation involves preparing for and responding to climate impacts. African countries insist both are essential if the continent is to pursue development while coping with increasingly severe weather events.

Negotiations remain difficult. A revised COP31 draft circulated on November 19, removed references to phasing out fossil fuels and dropped a proposed annual adaptation-finance target of $120 billion. While talks are ongoing and the text does not represent a final agreement, the changes underscore the political and financial battles that still shape international climate action.

For women like Moyo and Okello, however, the significance of COP31 will ultimately be measured far from the conference venue. Climate finance can support drought-resistant farming, improved water management systems, early-warning networks and infrastructure intended to withstand floods and extreme heat. But pledges alone will not deliver those outcomes. Countries must be able to access the money, implement projects effectively, and ensure support reaches the communities that need it most.
After recent floods, Nairobi braces for El Nino extremes
Gerauds Wilfried Obangome contributed to this article

articles.title: Tech stocks pull U.S. markets lower, Anthropic shares fall

image.caption: Stocks on the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange fell on Friday, the day after Anthropic's historic IPO booked double-digit gains. (CP/AP images)

blocks.text: Business·Updated
U.S. markets are pushing lower on Friday, including Anthropic shares on their second day of trading.
U.S. stocks are sliding the day after Anthropic's blockbuster IPO
Stocks are wobbling on Wall Street and Bay Street as a retreat in artificial intelligence shares contrasts with a modest rebound in consumer staples and Canadian telecoms.
The S&P 500 index shed 1.2 per cent on Friday, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 62 points, or 0.1 per cent. The Nasdaq composite slumped 2.3 per cent.
In Toronto, the S&P/TSX Composite index is down by less than one per cent. Canada's benchmark index has slipped about eight per cent since hitting an all-time high in August.
On Friday, BCE and Telus were among the most influential stocks as investors digest news about proposed consolidation deals in Canada's telecom sector.

On the Nasdaq, Anthropic slipped over 10 per cent in a reversal from its big market debut on Thursday. The company behind the popular Claude chatbot was pitched to investors as a pure play on the AI boom.
Unlike the other AI "hyperscalers" on the market — such as Google and Meta — Anthropic's business is solely focused on building and selling AI models.
The company's Nasdaq-listed stock ended its first trading day on Thursday with a 17 per cent gain.
AI stocks have been losing ground recently, due in part to worries among investors that their market values and massive spending are unjustified.
Nvidia is among the heaviest weights on the market on Friday, falling about six per cent. Shares of Intel and SpaceX are also among the most influential decliners.

Tech stock analyst Dan Ives says the fear and anxiety behind today's tech stock sell-off is akin to levels seen during the COVID-19 pandemic and U.S. President Donald Trump's so-called "Liberation Day" tariff announcement last year.

Ives points to a "perfect storm" of factors roiling the tech trade. These include the leadership crisis at Nvidia, U.S. regulators putting tighter controls on China's access to AI chips and fears of a data centre slowdown in the U.S. driven by the "blue wave" of Democrat victories in the recent midterm elections.

articles.title: As the Coalition stares down One Nation in NSW, a new threat is rising: the teals
articles.summary:
The opposition’s struggle is creating an opportunity for progressive independents who are boosted by shrewd political operator Chris Minns

  • Get our

blocks.text: The New South Wales Coalition is facing a renewed threat to its heartland seats on Sydney’s north shore.
This time, the threat is from independent candidates – and they’re backed by the same community activists who put a swathe of teal independents into federal parliament.

The challenge, which has so far remained under the radar, comes as the NSW Coalition tries to shore up its right flank against a surging One Nation before the March state election. This has resulted in the Coalition lurching to the right on issues ranging from gun control to law and order, and, in the case of the NSW Nationals, to abandon climate targets altogether.

As former opposition leader Mark Speakman resigned from the Liberals on Thursday – joining an exodus of MPs announcing they wouldn’t contest their seats in March – he warned his party against becoming “One Nation lite”.

But the move to the right has also created an opportunity for progressive independents running in urban seats usually held by Liberal moderates, with several candidates about to launch their campaigns.

This weekend, Amelia Loye, a management consultant who specialises in stakeholder and community engagement, will announce she is running in the seat of Willoughby, on Sydney’s north shore. She will attempt to oust Liberal MP Tim James, who holds the seat on a 2.6% margin.
Loye is backed by community group Willoughby Votes, which came close to securing an independent in the 2023 election with 47% of the two-party preferred vote.
“Willoughby has already shown it is ready for an independent,” she said. “Nearly half of voters backed one last time. I want to earn their support, and the support of those still deciding.”

She joins high-profile candidate Elouise Massa, a small business owner, who became a household name after campaigning for Northern Beaches hospital to return to public hands after her toddler’s death in emergency.
Massa will run in the Sydney seat of Manly against Liberal Adelaide Cuneo, who is seeking to replace the retiring MP, James Griffin.

The independent deputy mayor of Mosman, Michael Randall, announced last weekend he will run in North Shore as a community independent. Several of the people behind former independent federal MP Kylea Tink’s campaign are supporting him.
Monica Wulff, another independent, has announced a run in Davidson.
Voters on the northern beaches have already sent two independents to Macquarie street – and both have a good chance of being returned.

blocks.caption: NSW opposition leader Kellie Sloane has not ruled out a preference deal or a post-election arrangement with One Nation. Photograph: Sarah Wilson/AAP

blocks.text: At the federal level, teal independents Sophie Scamps, Zali Steggall and Nicolette Boele hold McKellar, Warringah and Bradfield respectively. Tink held North Sydney for one term before the seat was abolished.
The NSW Liberal party is not giving up on the northern beaches and the north shore, despite the trend towards independents.
“We’ll keep making our case directly to voters, including why we oppose Labor’s gun buyback that targets law-abiding owners rather than criminals and terrorists,” a Liberal spokesperson said.
This time, however, the independents have a boost in the form of NSW Labor premier, Chris Minns.

During the final weeks of parliament before the NSW election, Minns joked that independent Jacqui Scruby, who won Pittwater at a byelection, should be known as “the member for Mona Vale road” for her tenacity in seeking an upgrade. It’s now being fast-tracked by the Minns government.
Minns has also appeared with Massa, and praised her for her advocacy.
But Minns, a shrewd political operator, has not fallen in love with independents – he’s just hedging his bets.

A year ago, with the Liberals languishing in the polls, Labor could have expected to increase its majority in 2027. But with One Nation storming to a primary vote as high as 30% in some polls, that prospect has dimmed.

In the current parliament, Labor has support of three independents – Greg Piper, Joe McGirr and Alex Greenwich – to ensure confidence and supply for its minority government. An expanded crossbench would give more options and provide a buffer for Labor losses to One Nation in western Sydney, the Hunter and possibly the Central Coast.
If all independents were successful – and that is a big if – almost the entire north shore region would go to state independents, except the seat of Wahroonga.
Most of the commentary about the 2027 election has focused on the likely Armageddon facing the Nationals, who could lose as many eight or nine of their 11 seats in the regions.

But a teal wave also remains a threat to the Liberal party, especially as the Coalition try to position themselves to fight off One Nation in the regions with policies that don’t sit well with urban voters.

One Nation could also prove helpful to independents if it makes good on its promise to run candidates in every seat. The party is more likely to shave votes from the Liberal primary vote, making it easier for the independents to overtake the Liberal on preferences from Labor and the Greens.

NSW’s optional preferential voting makes it hard to predict how strong flows will be – and it depends what parties advocate on how to votes. But in 2023 only 41% of One Nation voters nominated preferences, compared to 70% of Green voters and 49% of Labor voters.

The opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, has not ruled out either a preference deal or a post-election arrangement with One Nation, describing such options as “hypothetical”. But if they do end up preferencing One Nation, it may alienate moderate Liberals and ultimately work against them.

items: Disclosure: Anne Davies worked as a media and policy adviser to the independent federal MP Sophie Scamps from October 2023 to October 2024.

articles.title: P.E.I. horse makes harness racing history with 29 straight wins
articles.summary: A Prince Edward Island horse has made harness racing history, winning her 29th consecutive race Thursday night to set a modern-day North American pacing record.

image.caption: Earl Watts, trainer of Windemere Skye, says the filly will have the winter off and return to race next summer. (CBC)

blocks.text: PEI
A Prince Edward Island horse has made harness racing history, winning her 29th consecutive race Thursday night to set a modern-day North American pacing record.
3-year-old filly breaks modern-day North American pacing record in Charlottetown
The three-year-old filly Windemere Skye took the lead early at Red Shores in Charlottetown and held on for the win. She remains undefeated in all 29 races of her career.
Her trainer, Earl Watts, said he was still taking it all in after the race.
“Unreal. It’s hard to believe we just set a record,” Watts said.
The previous record of 28 consecutive wins was first set by Cam Fella in 1983 and matched by Firms Phantom in 2001, according to Lee Drake, Red Shores’ manager of racing and broadcast.
Windemere Skye, with Marc Campbell in the driver's seat, at Red Shores in Charlottetown on Thursday night. (CBC)
Watts called Windemere Skye “a very special filly” and credited driver Marc Campbell and the team caring for her at the farm.
“You won’t get too many like her. In my lifetime, you won’t get another one,” he said.
The record-breaking win came against a field of older mares. Drake had said before the race that the competition would be strong, and Watts said he was nervous going in.
“I had faith in her,” Watts said. “But no, I’m glad it’s over.”
Watts said the plan is to give Windemere Skye the winter off before bringing her back to race next summer.
