articles.title: Myanmar genocide ruling: Rohingya say struggle for justice not over
articles.summary: The ICJ held Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya and ordered restitution and reparations. Members of the community hailed the ruling but cautioned that achieving real change would…

image.caption: Some 700,000 Rohingya crossed the border into Bangladesh after Myanmar military's operartions in 2016-17Image: Mohammad Ponir Hossain/REUTERS

blocks.text: The International Court of Justice (ICJ) on Thursday ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the country's Rohingya community a decade ago, in a historic judgment hailed by the long-persecuted minority and rights groups.

The United Nations' top court also ordered the Myanmar government to prevent a repeat of the crimes, undertake legal reforms to protect the Rohingya, and provide the victims with reparations or, where it cannot, compensate them.

The judgment came seven years after The Gambia filed the case with the court in 2019, accusing Buddhist-majority Myanmar of a deliberate campaign of arson, rape and murder against the country's predominantly Muslim Rohingya community in 2016 and 2017.
It is the ICJ's first finding of genocide against a state, and the first ruling in any of the cases filed against Myanmar or its leaders in multiple courts around the world.
How do Rohingya see the ruling?
Lucky Karim was 14 when she and her mother and brothers were forced to flee their village in Rakhine State to escape the Myanmar military's advance in August 2017.
She joined the roughly 700,000 other Rohingya who crossed the border into Bangladesh at the time.
Now a prominent Rohingya activist, Karim heard the court's judgment in person in The Hague.
"For me … it's a very personal day, a personal moment, as someone who survived and escaped genocide in 2017. It took nearly a decade for the world to finally hear our voice," she said.

"For generations the [Myanmar] military stripped away our identity, our citizenship, tried to erase us from our homeland, told the world that what they did to us in 2017 was merely clearance operations, or worse, that we didn't even exist," said Wai Wai Nu, another Rohingya activist and former political prisoner.
Myanmar's Rohingya case: What it takes to prove genocide
Today, she said, their decades of persecution "is actually validated, and the truth has come out."
Tun Khin, a Rohingya activist and plaintiff in a universal jurisdiction case against Myanmar in Argentina, called the judgment "a historic moment" and "a big day for the Rohingya."

The press bureau of the Myanmar president's office did not respond to DW's requests for comment. The government's main mouthpiece, the state-run New Light of Myanmar newspaper, has made no mention of the ruling online.
'Far in excess of what was justified'

Throughout the trial, Myanmar claimed that its actions in Rakhine State were strictly part of legitimate counterinsurgency operations against the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, an armed group in the area that had been attacking police and military posts.

The ICJ flatly rejected the argument. "The court views casualties and damage far in excess of what was justified by military necessity," ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said, reading from the 15-judge panel's 9-6 ruling in The Hague.

"The execution of Rohingya men and boys in some locations, the widespread sexual violence, the targeting of children and babies, the methodical burning of villages and attacks on fleeing civilians are not consistent with an intent to conduct counterinsurgency operations," he added.
A UN-backed fact-finding mission concluded that some 10,000 people likely died in the pogroms. By some estimates, about 1 in 5 of them were children.

Michael Becker, an associate professor of international human rights law at Trinity College Dublin, said the court's ruling was both historic and "monumental" not only because it found a state responsible for genocide, but also because "it demonstrates that establishing genocidal intent is not impossible."

He noted that the panel took pains to show that The Gambia's case passed the court's established "only reasonable inference" test for genocidal intent. The ruling also "helpfully affirms" that forced transfer, targeting children and sexual violence could be relevant factors, he added.
Myanmar committed genocide — what happens after the verdict?
'Not conditions amenable to … relief'
Amid the elation among the Rohingya and rights groups, their focus quickly turned to making the court's prescribed remedies real.

The ICJ said Myanmar was now obliged to allow the "safe, voluntary and dignified" return of those who fled, investigate the crimes, and prosecute those found responsible. It also told Myanmar to return or replace all stolen property or, within two years, show the court it was compensating victims for what it could not.
But those behind the genocide, including former military chief and current President Min Aung Hlaing, have remained in power since toppling Myanmar's democratically elected government in 2021.

Much of the country, including Rakhine State, is still in the midst of a brutal civil war between the military and an array of armed resistance groups. And the group that now controls most of Rakhine, the Arakan Army, is widely accused of persecuting the Rohingya as well.
"These are not conditions amenable to realizing the relief ordered by the ICJ anytime soon," said Becker.

Enforcing the court's orders ultimately falls to the UN Security Council. But China and Russia, which both back the Myanmar government and keep it well armed, would "almost certainly" veto any proposed Council resolution that aims to punish Myanmar, said Richard Horsey, senior Asia adviser at the International Crisis Group.
"Whatever pressure there is will come from governments and the General Assembly, not the Council," he said.
Immediately after Thursday's ICJ judgment, the UK said it was expelling Myanmar's defense attache in London and would call for a UN Security Council session to discuss the court's decision.
'This is just the beginning'
A number of Western governments have already buried Myanmar under round after round of sanctions over the past decade, but with little to no apparent effect.

Myanmar is even taking tentative steps to shake off its global pariah status and restore regular relations with the rest of the world. Min Aung Hlaing has been warmly hosted by eight Asian and Eastern European countries since arranging his transition from army general to president earlier this year following rigged elections.
Horsey says the ICJ judgment will slow those efforts but not reverse them.
"Most governments in the region will keep engaging, but those with Muslim-majority publics, especially Malaysia and Indonesia, will find it harder to justify at home," he said.
Bangladesh: Could the UN help the Rohingya return home?

Japan and South Korea, which maintain extensive business ties with Myanmar, are likely to remain cautious, he added, while the United States, which has reportedly had recent meetings with senior government officials, would keep up a transactional relationship.
"For [Myanmar], the real cost is that every government that deals with it will now have to explain why it is engaging a state found responsible for genocide," Horsey said.
'They want to return home'
The Rohingya, meanwhile, expect a long and hard fight for real change.

"A judgment in The Hague will not on its own stop the bombs or feed starving families or stop the atrocities in Rakhine State," said Wai Wai Nu. "It is imperative that the international community take action to enforce the ruling," she added.
Karim said other countries should use the ICJ judgment "as a tool to open every possible door to help us and protect the people on the ground."

The Gambia's lead counsel in the case, Arsalan Suleman, said the genocide ruling could be used to help hold the perpetrators to account in other courts. The International Criminal Court, for one, is weighing an arrest warrant request for Min Aung Hlaing for alleged crimes against humanity, also against the Rohingya.

Tun Khin said the wish of most Rohingya is simple, if still hard to foresee. "They want to return home, to their houses and own villages," he said, but this time with full citizenship rights and legal protection.
"It will take time," he acknowledged. "This is just the beginning."

articles.title: FIFA presidential election 2027: Infantino facing Diallo and Tashima — could an alliance change everything?
articles.summary: Two challengers to Gianni Infantino have registered for next year's FIFA presidential election. What do Philippe Diallo and Kozo Tashima stand for – and do they stand a chance against the incumbent?

image.caption: Three men are vying to become the most powerful man in world football when FIFA elects a new president next MarchImage: Ennio Leanza/EPA/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Three men are vying for one of the most powerful positions in sports when delegates from more than 200 FIFA member nations cast their ballots at the FIFA presidential election, to be held in Rabat on March 18, 2027. DW looks at the field of candidates.
Gianni Infantino – the powerful incumbent

Gianni Infantino was first elected FIFA president in February 2016, promising greater transparency and a fresh start in the wake of the corruption scandals that marked the Sepp Blatter era. Under his leadership, FIFA's revenues have continued to grow, the Club World Cup has been revamped, and the men's World Cup has been expanded to include 48 teams.

During his decade in office, the 56-year-old Swiss has built a global network of support. Infantino enjoys significant backing in Africa, South America, and large parts of Asia—a result of multi-billion-dollar development programs and financial grants provided to national associations. Many smaller member associations view him as a president who takes their interests more seriously than his predecessors did.

At the same time, critics accuse Infantino of consolidating power within the organization around himself. During his tenure, oversight and control bodies have been restructured multiple times, and key positions have been filled with his own loyalists.

blocks.caption: Gianni Infantino had been credited with increasing FIFA's revenue, but he has also faced strong criticismImage: Harry Langer/DeFodi Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Infantino's ostentatious closeness to political leaders has also sparked debate—whether it be his conduct during the World Cup in Qatar, his tight ties to Saudi Arabia, or his public appearances alongside US President Donald Trump (though that relationship is said to have cooled significantly following the 2026 World Cup). Detractors accuse him of seeking proximity to authoritarian rulers and intermingling political interests too closely with football.

A failed initiative to grant private investors a larger stake in lucrative FIFA competitions (FIFA Forward Enterprise) has placed Infantino under considerable pressure. As the FIFA election approaches, he faces the prospect of legal challenges; European football's governing body UEFA is aiming to take action over the investment plan, while other critics are calling for an investigation by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).
However, his time in office has brought many of FIFA's 211 member associations additional development funding and other revenue. This makes him the man to beat in the March vote.
Philippe Diallo – Europe's principled alternative

Philippe Diallo is Europe's candidate. The 63-year-old, who was elected president of the French Football Federation in 2023, is seen as an experienced sports administrator with a pragmatic and measured leadership style.
He has the backing of UEFA, as well as many of its 55 member associations, including the German Football Association (DEB).

blocks.caption: Former FFF President Philippe Diallo is Europe's candidateImage: Bruno Bebert/Bestimage/IMAGO

blocks.text: "Philippe Diallo stands for a version of football that embraces responsibility and tackles future challenges with determination," DFB President Bernd Neuendorf said in a statement announcing the German FA's position.
"We want a FIFA that serves the sport in the interest of all its member associations. That is why we support Philippe Diallo with great conviction."

Diallo is positioning himself as a clear alternative to Infantino. His supporters see him as a candidate who stands for sound leadership, transparency, and a stronger dialogue with member associations. Unlike the incumbent, however, he lacks a global network of allies.
Kozo Tashima – an underdog as a possible king maker?

The third man in the race is Kozo Tashima. The 68-year-old was president of the Japan Football Association (JFA) from 2016 to 2024 and has been one of the most influential officials in Asia for decades.
During a press conference in Tokyo on Friday, Tashima mentioned the words "integrity, fairness, trust and transparency" several times in explaining his decision to run.
"I just don't only want to be the FIFA president, my intention is to make FIFA better," he said.

blocks.caption: Kozo Tashima say he wants to reform FIFA, but acknowleges that he is a dark horseImage: Kyodo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "Being the president is the shortcut to making that happen. I just want to clean up the federation and make it a fair organization. I want to help rebuild the whole organization."

Tashima also acknowledged that failing to have won the endorsement of any of the regional confederations – the Asian Football Confederation is supporting Infantino – makes him a longshot to win the election.

But he could still play a key role in the outcome. At a press conference on Tuesday, Diallo said he intended to reach out to Tashima to "unite forces" to defeat Infantino. Tashima hasn't ruled out the notion.
"We do share some moral or ethical positions, so he's a great person to team up with," Tashima said.
"Diallo is also very strict in governance and he does have a lot of experience in management," he added.
However he also noted that he hadn't had any thoughts of withdrawing from the race.
If Infantino's challengers do manage to join forces in some way, they might just stand a chance of upsetting the highly favored incumbent.

articles.title: Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk
articles.summary: Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.

blocks.text: Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday and Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.
Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.

The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".
Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near Mołodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.
He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.

Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," he said.

A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine.

"It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa Dęba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.

The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.

At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.
This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland and in July a cruise missile also landed in Poland.

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 8:53pm

A co-accused of Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez and former Ako Bicol Rep. Zaldy Co in the plunder charges they are facing before the Sandiganbayan surrendered on Friday to the National Bureau of Investigation.

According to the Office of the Ombudsman Felicito Guevarra, the president of Samchan Foreign Exchange Corp., was granted conditional immunity "because his testimony and records are necessary to establish the truth in this case."

"Samchan has returned to the Bureau of the Treasury all its earnings from the questioned transactions. Restitution does not erase criminal liability. It is also not the basis of the immunity," the Ombudsman said in a statement.

"The Office granted Mr. Guevarra conditional immunity under Section 17 of Republic Act No. 6770 because his testimony and records are necessary to establish the truth in this case. The immunity rests on his full and truthful testimony," it added.
The Ombudsman said the conditions are as follows:

items: that Guevarra will cooperate fully and truthfully turn over all of Samchan's records and devices;
that he will remain in the country; and
that he will stay under DOJ protection.

blocks.text: "If he breaks any condition, his immunity will be revoked and his prosecution will resume," the Ombudsman said.
Guevarra personally handled Samchan's operations, said the Ombudsman.
"His testimony and records will help the prosecution trace the movement of funds alleged in the charge sheet. The charges against the other accused stand as filed," the Ombudsman said.
"All accused are presumed innocent. The evidence will be presented in court," it added. —NB, GMA News

articles.title: Texas death-row inmate screams as execution takes more than one hour
articles.summary: This prolonged execution comes weeks after Christa Pike survived the lethal injection of the same drug.

blocks.text: A US death row inmate has screamed in apparent pain during his Texas execution which lasted more than an hour.
This is "not working the way it should be," Reinaldo Dennes, 70, said as he was being injected with the drug pentobarbital, according to witnesses.

A spokeswoman for the Texas Department of Criminal Justice said there had been unsuccessful attempts to find veins for the injections, but added that Dennes had reported pain in parts of his body where there were no attempted injections.

Dennes's case comes weeks after the botched execution of Christa Pike, who survived two lethal doses and is believed to be the only individual to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.
Dennes was sentenced to death over the 1996 murder of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer who was found shot multiple times.
His execution came on the same day another inmate was put to death in Florida.
Executions with a lethal drug usually last from a few minutes to over an hour.

Michael Graczyk, an Associated Press reporter who has witnessed many such executions, described how they had waited for an unusually long time before being taken into the chamber. According to him, such delays are usually due to an inmate resisting the procedure or difficulty in finding veins.
When the witnesses were finally allowed in, Dennes almost immediately exclaimed, "The pain! Go! Go!", Graczyk said. He then uttered an expletive and asked "the father" to "take this pain".
He then shouted: "My right leg is killing me!", describing it as a cramp. After another expletive, he grunted and said, "I don't think this is normal."
Another witness, the reverend Jeff Hood, told USA Today that Dennes's execution was "by far the worst one" he had seen.
"He [Dennes] screamed out, 'my leg, my leg, my leg'," Hood said. "He screamed out twice, 'it's not working like it's supposed to.'"

articles.title: Fallout over tuition fees may snag Burnham’s EU deal, say insiders
articles.summary:
No 10 pushing back on claims in Brussels that lack of agreement on fees for EU students could sink agreements

The UK and EU have agreed a reset deal, Downing Street has said, although the…
articles.byline: Peter Walker, Jennifer Rankin and Lisa O’Carroll

blocks.text: The UK and EU have agreed a reset deal, Downing Street has said, although the level of tuition fees EU students will pay to study at UK universities remains unresolved.

“The deal is done – negotiations have concluded,” a No 10 statement said, less than an hour after the prime minister, Andy Burnham, arrived at the summit venue in Brussels, where he was greeted by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, and António Costa, the European Council president.

The reset means there is agreement on three deals – food and drink, emissions trading, and a youth mobility scheme – but EU sources say these deals will not enter into force unless the UK reaches a settlement with the bloc over tuition fee rates for European students.
The statement came shortly after headlines on Friday suggested that the tuition fee issue could cause other parts of the process to collapse.

However, after the deal was announced, UK officials pushed back strongly against the idea that the three plans could be jeopardised by a failure to agree on tuition feels, saying the issues were completely separate. Earlier, EU officials had indicated that progress on the main deals would be contingent on tuition fees.

While talks on tuition fees are scheduled to last another six months, the officials said that new arrangements for food and agriculture would come into force in March 2028 regardless of an agreement on the issue.

They said the UK had also won sign-up to the potential idea of inclusion in the EU’s yet-to-be finalised “Made in Europe” policy, a protectionist plan intended to limit China’s increasing influence on European industry. One official called this “a big win”, especially as it was achieved before a deal on tuition fees.
The arrival on Friday morning of Burnham, von der Leyen and Costa was met with a brief burst of the UK and EU anthems from a string quintet. None of the leaders made a statement.

In a sign of how seriously the summit is being taken by London, the prime minister was accompanied by a phalanx of cabinet ministers that included: Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state; John Healey, the chancellor; Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary; Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary; Angela Eagle, the environment secretary; and Anneliese Midgley, the chief whip.

Speaking earlier to business leaders, Burnham said: “It just makes sense to get closer.” He described the summit as “a big day and hopefully a positive day”, and said his aim was to “put the country on a better path, more hopeful about the future, more sense of possibility and positivity around the country,” as he wanted to break with “a decade of low, stagnant growth … [and] rising costs”.
Brussels insiders said on Friday that equal treatment for EU students at British universities would be essential for the success of the deal as a whole.

A statement seen by the Guardian from the main EU institutions spelt out the link: “The Council and Commission consider that this agreement is to provide for equal treatment with nationals as regards tuition fees for all students. The Council and Commission acknowledge that these four agreements form a package of the 2026 EU-UK summit.”
An EU official said: “I think our position has been clear. We think this is an issue that needs to be addressed.”

The EU wants to ensure its students pay UK domestic rates for tuition fees, which are capped at £9,790 for the current academic, rather than the international rate that can be four or five times higher. In a concession last night, the bloc agreed to defer agreement on tuition fees by six months, but will continue to press for domestic rates.

In 11th-hour talks over tuition fees, the UK suggested it could go as low as £12,000 for EU students, according to two EU sources, which is more than £2,000 in excess of the charge for UK students. The EU continues to seek “equal treatment” for its students, suggesting that tough negotiations lie ahead.

Earlier, the two sides agreed that 100,000 young people from each side could take part in the youth mobility scheme that allows the freedom to live, work, travel and study on both sides of the Channel for up to three years.

Even with the deal not yet finalised, Burnham has begun to face a strong pushback from anti-Brexit politicians in Britain, notably Nigel Farage, the leader of Reform UK, who is also in Brussels and will host a press conference later on Friday.

Speaking to LBC radio, Farage said Burnham was “rejoining a chunk of the European Union’s single market”, which would result in the UK becoming a rule taker. “It is wholly unnecessary, and he’s being led by the nose by the European bureaucrats,” Farage said.

articles.title: Russian missiles and drone reportedly hit Poland during attacks on Ukraine
articles.summary:
Polish PM calls strikes, which took place amid western military exercises, ‘an intentional provocation’ by Moscow

Two Russian cruise missiles and a jet-powered drone are reported to have…

blocks.text: Two Russian cruise missiles and a jet-powered drone are reported to have crashed in Poland during Russian air attacks on Ukraine that took place amid major western military exercises by allied countries.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said it was “one of the largest attacks” since the full-scale Russian invasion in 2022, with at least eight people killed and nearly 30 injured in Ukraine.
“The Russians spread this attack across many cities and regions of Ukraine. Absolutely all the targets were ordinary civilian infrastructure – things that literally sustain people’s lives,” he said.

Zelenskyy said Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, went ahead with the strike after “weak meetings” with the US president, Donald Trump, and China’s Xi Jinping, and his “failure to attempt to somehow redraw the world”.
The Ukrainian president added: “Russia is trying to compensate for its military and diplomatic impotence with precisely this kind of terror.”
Poland’s defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, confirmed three violations of Polish airspace, with no injuries reported.

He said he believed it was “not accidental” that the incident took place on the same day as major western military exercises involving troops from 11 countries in the “coalition of the willing”, including the UK.
The incidents were reported in Nowy Lipowiec, Mołodycz and Rudnik nad Sanem in south-eastern Poland, between 50km (30 miles) and 100km from Nowa Dęba, where the exercises are taking place.
Poland’s prime minister called the incident “an intentional provocation” by Russia.

Donald Tusk said he had spoken with Nato’s secretary general, Mark Rutte – who will visit Warsaw on Saturday – who agreed with him that “it does not seem to be a coincidence” that the attack took place on the night before the drills.
“It clearly shows … that coming months … will certainly pose great challenges for all of us,” he said.

“Today’s incident shows clearer than ever before why Poland must participate in decisions on Ukraine’s future,” he added, arguing that Warsaw has a “better understanding” of the threat posed by Russia.

blocks.caption: Security personnel secure the area after reports of a possible unidentified object falling in Rudnik nad Sanem, south-eastern Poland. Photograph: Piotr Polak/EPA

blocks.text: Rutte said on X: “Spoke with @donaldtusk about the grave violations of Polish airspace overnight. NATO jets were scrambled in response. We stand in solidarity with Poland and will continue to strengthen our ability to deter and defend.

“This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine. I condemn Russia’s attacks as well as its ongoing war. We continue to stand united as Allies and will continue to support Ukraine.”

​The UK defence secretary, Wes Streeting, who is in Poland for the exercises, described the incursion as “very serious” in a post on X, adding: “The impact of Russia’s illegal war is being felt across Ukraine and increasingly in neighbouring countries. The UK stands in solidarity with our allies.”
Maj Gen Ireneusz Nowak, commander of the operational command of the Polish armed forces, said as many as 11 objects had been identified as posing a danger to Polish airspace.

He also highlighted the unprecedented scale of the overnight attack on Ukraine, saying Russia used seven bombers and fired 26 Kalibr cruise missiles, 72 Kh-101 cruise missiles and more than 500 drones.

Air traffic control at Rzeszów-Jasionka airport – an international passenger hub and major transit point for military aid to Ukraine – was briefly evacuated overnight, for the first time since the start of the full-scale war in Ukraine.
After the incidents, Tusk summoned army and security service chiefs to an emergency meeting to discuss the situation.
Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said the latest violations “demonstrate the threats posed by Russian aggression to the whole of Europe and the transatlantic community”.

He added: “While Moscow tries to initiate discussions about the ‘new security architecture of Europe’, Russian missiles and drones directly undermine the existing security order in Europe. The first step toward strengthening it would probably be to cease such attacks.”
Polish authorities repeatedly warned in recent months against potential security incidents as they feared an escalation in Russia’s war against Ukraine.
In July, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile fell in Poland’s Lublin region after veering off course during a nightly Russian attack on Ukraine.
In September last year, more than 20 Russian drones crossed into Polish airspace, with Tusk warning that the country was “closer to military conflict than at any time since the second world war”.
In November 2022, a Russian missile Kh-55 crashed near Bydgoszcz, more than 400km from Ukraine’s territory, but was only discovered in early 2023.

articles.title: Duterte in ICC jail, but families still afraid – Callamard
articles.summary: 'How can it be that years after the killings, accountability here is still not possible?' asks Amnesty International secretary general Agnes Callamard

items: Former President Rodrigo Duterte is detained in The Hague, but families of victims from his anti-drug campaign still fear seeking justice in the Philippines.
Amnesty International's Agnès Callamard highlighted the ongoing lack of accountability for the killings, questioning why justice remains elusive despite Duterte's trial for crimes against humanity.
The launch of 'Walang Pahimakas,' an anthology of poems honoring the victims, emphasizes the importance of remembrance and the need for independent investigations into unlawful killings.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
QUEZON CITY, Philippines – Former president Rodrigo Duterte is detained in The Hague, but the families of those killed in his war on drugs are still afraid to seek justice in the Philippines.
Nearly a decade after the killings began, their fear has not gone away.
“How can it be that Duterte is in prison in The Hague, and yet people are scared here now?” Amnesty International secretary general Agnès Callamard asked Friday, November 20.

Callamard, returning to the Philippines after a Duterte-era immigration ban was lifted, raised the question during the launch of Walang Pahimakas (No Farewell), an anthology of poems remembering those killed in the anti-drug campaign.

blocks.caption: REMEMBERING. Amnesty International officials and editors of Walang Pahimakas discuss poetry, remembrance, and accountability for drug war killings, on November 20, 2026. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno

blocks.text: She had spent the previous 48 hours meeting victims’ families. Their message, she said, was that justice remained beyond their reach.
“How can it be that years after the killings, accountability here is still not possible?” she asked.
“That is an indictment not of President Duterte. It is an indictment of the current government.”
Her remarks came 10 days before the scheduled opening of Duterte’s trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) on November 30.

The former president faces charges of crimes against humanity, including murder and attempted murder, over killings allegedly committed during his anti-drug campaign and earlier operations in Davao City. He has denied wrongdoing.

Callamard welcomed the coming proceedings but said the Marcos administration must also deliver accountability through independent investigations, witness protection, and prosecution of those responsible for unlawful killings.

At the book launch in Quezon City, National Artist for Literature Virgilio Almario, better known as Rio Alma, read his poem Pag Nahimlay ang Katwiran (Pagkatapos ni Francisco Goya), written on May 3, 2020.

blocks.caption: RIO ALMA. National Artist for Literature Virgilio Almario reads his poem Pag Nahimlay ang Katwiran, a warning against injustice and abuse of power, on November 20, 2026. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno

blocks.text: “Pag nahimlay ang katwiran, lumalabas ang halimaw.” (When reason falls asleep, the monster emerges.)
Cordilleran poet Susie Bangles-Baldo, writing as Layad Ya Ikigai, read Magay Inges Na Ay Sakit, a poem in Kankanaey about a family whose hopes for their child’s future are shattered by loss.

blocks.caption: POETRY. Cordilleran poet Susie Bangles-Baldo reads her Kankanaey poem Magay Inges Na Ay Sakit, a story of sacrifice, hope, and loss, on November 20, 2026. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno

blocks.text: Their works are among those featured in Walang Pahimakas, Amnesty International Philippines’ first published book, with contributions from more than 70 writers and artists.

First unveiled at the Manila International Book Fair in September, the anthology tells the stories of people whose deaths were often reduced to police reports, statistics, and the familiar claim that suspects had fought back.
Its editors, poets Ronald Atilano and Harold Fiesta, said the collection challenges the narratives that helped normalize the killings.
Atilano described the poems as testimony against forgetting, recalling how violence could be presented as necessary or even as service to the nation.
Fiesta said poetry could not bring back the dead, but it could keep their stories from disappearing.
“Those who were denied a proper goodbye should not also be denied remembrance,” he said.
During the launch, Amnesty presented a symbolic check for P69,300 to representatives of victims’ families, representing sales of Walang Pahimakas and Suong at the Manila International Book Fair.

blocks.caption: SUPPORT. Amnesty International presents ₱69,300 in proceeds from book sales at the Manila International Book Fair to support families of drug war victims, on November 20, 2026. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno

blocks.text: Callamard last visited the Philippines in 2017, when she was serving as United Nations special rapporteur on extrajudicial executions.

Her criticism of Duterte’s anti-drug campaign and calls for an investigation into the killings drew the administration’s ire. In 2018, she was barred from entering the country and declared an undesirable alien.
The immigration restriction was lifted in September 2026.
“A ban may keep a person out, but it cannot suppress the truth,” she said.
Callamard’s return comes as Duterte faces proceedings before the ICC, which is investigating alleged crimes committed while the Philippines was still a party to the Rome Statute.

blocks.caption: Duterte in ICC jail, but families still afraid – Callamard

blocks.text: Police figures recorded more than 6,000 deaths during anti-drug operations under Duterte. Human rights organizations have estimated a much higher toll, including killings attributed to unidentified assailants.
Amnesty International Philippines section director Ritz Lee Santos III said accountability through Philippine courts remains limited.

Citing the organization’s assessment, Santos said only five cases involving nine police officers had resulted in convictions, despite thousands of deaths. (READ: [Pinoy Criminology] The hidden impact of Duterte’s drug war)
He questioned how families could pursue justice when filing complaints meant spending money on transportation, missing work, and risking their safety.
“A mother should be able to ask these questions without being passed from one office to another,” he said.

Amnesty International called on the government to investigate unlawful killings, protect witnesses, and replace punitive drug policies with voluntary treatment, healthcare, and evidence-based harm reduction programs.
Callamard, who plans to attend the opening of Duterte’s trial in The Hague, said international proceedings should not become an excuse for inaction in the Philippines.

She also warned that sanctions and political pressure against the ICC, particularly from the United States, threatened an institution on which victims of serious crimes depend when domestic justice systems fail them.

As the launch ended, the poems returned attention to the people at the center of the case: children who waited for parents who never came home, families still looking for answers, and survivors who remain afraid to speak.
Callamard promised them that Amnesty International would continue pressing for investigations and accountability.
“You are not alone, we stand by you and we will fight with you.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: US reacts cautiously to Myanmar genocide ruling as EU praises ‘critical’ role of UN’s top court
articles.summary:
Reactions to ICJ ruling underline global divisions over court with China raising concerns about judicial overreach

The US has greeted with caution the world’s highest court’s ruling that

blocks.text: The US has greeted with caution the world’s highest court’s ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, while China has raised concerns of judicial overreach.

Reactions to Thursday’s historic ruling underlined deep international division over the role of the court and similar institutions. The international court of justice (ICJ) had never previously found a state responsible for genocide and the decision could set a precedent for future genocide claims, notably a case against Israel.

The EU hailed a “landmark” judgment from the ICJ, while the UK reaffirmed “full support” for the court and the international legal order. Australia called on Myanmar to comply fully with the judgment and its obligations under international law.

But China, which has offered rare international support for Myanmar’s military rulers since they seized power five years ago, highlighted “issues such as jurisdiction overreach and expanded interpretation”.

“China … believes that such practices are not conducive to the settlement of disputes,” the foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, told a news briefing when asked about the ICJ ruling. “The international community should make joint efforts in this direction to avoid complicating this issue.”
Western nations cut ties with the unstable and poor south-east Asian country after the 2021 coup that ousted a civilian-led government.

Myanmar’s presidential spokesperson said on Friday that the ruling was “unfair”, noting the judges’ nine to six vote. The country’s military rulers have denied carrying out a genocide, claiming their actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted insurgent attacks.

“When we look at the result, not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” said Khaing Khaing Soe, speaking at a press conference in the capital, Naypyidaw. “So this was not a unanimous decision … I would say it is not fair.”
The US state department said on Thursday that Washington was examining the judgment, while stressing the need to avoid “politicisation” of the ICJ.
Donald Trump’s administration has taken a dim view of international law, vowing to dismantle the international criminal court (ICC), but has yet to question the legitimacy of the ICJ.

The state department reiterated US support for the people of Myanmar and said it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups”, noting that the US was the largest single humanitarian donor to the Rohingya humanitarian crisis response.
In Brussels, the EU said Myanmar must fully implement the ICJ’s ruling “without delay” and that “compliance with ICJ’s decisions is not optional, it is an obligation under international law”.

“The European Union holds the ICJ in the highest regard and remains steadfast in its support for its critical role in the peaceful resolution of disputes and the upholding of the rule of law at international level,” an EU spokesperson said in a statement.

blocks.caption: Rohingya refugees attend a rally addressed by the UN general assembly president, Khalilur Rahman, in Cox’s Bazar in Bangladesh on Friday. Photograph: Mohammad Ponir Hossain/Reuters

blocks.text: “The Rohingya people have endured immense suffering, including displacement and violence, and their plight must not be forgotten. This landmark ruling underscores the imperative of justice for victims and the necessity of upholding international law.”
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, called the ruling “a demonstration of international justice and a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand”.
The UK expelled Myanmar’s defence attache and called for measures to “ensure the court’s ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity”.

The ruling caps a lengthy legal campaign since August 2017 when Myanmar’s military launched what it called a “clearance campaign” in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. Reports rapidly emerged of mass rapes and killings by security forces, as well as the burning of thousands of homes.

Judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.

The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the ICC – which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states – on allegations of crimes against humanity.

The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited.
While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.
Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya “in whole or in part”.

About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across the Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.

blocks.caption: An aerial view shows the Rohingya refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. Photograph: Salahuddin Ahmed/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: Judges at the court based in The Hague have also been asked to rule on other allegations of genocide.

South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies. That case is years from completion. An interim ICJ judgment in 2024 ordered Israel to ensure its forces do not commit acts of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia. Shortly after Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.

articles.title: EU and UK strike 'landmark deal' to strengthen ties after Brexit
articles.summary: The European Union and the United Kingdom have agreed on "landmark" deals on youth mobility and trade. Leaders on both sides praised the agreement as they seek to rebuild ties.

image.caption: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham is seeking to build closer ties with the EU after BrexitImage: Yves Herman/REUTERS

blocks.text: European Union top officials and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced deals on trade and youth mobility at Friday's Brussels summit.
This might be the first step to rebuild ties, a decade after Britain voted to leave the EU.
During the delegations' meeting, Burnham said the deal was a "landmark agreement," while European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called it a "turning point" in relations.
"This is a good day for Britain. This is a good day for Europe," Burnham said.

Speaking at the joint press conference, European Council President Antonio Costa said the bloc respected the British decision to leave the EU and would respect its choice to strengthen ties in the post-Brexit era.
He said jokingly that the EU and UK "may drive on the opposite sides of the road, but what matters is they are heading for the same direction."

blocks.caption: Von der Leyen, Burnham and Costa had kind words for each other following the talksImage: Marius Burgelman/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Burnham said that the deals were made with young people in mind, adding: "This deal is for you. This deal really is about lifting your life chances.
He went further and said "Brexit took opportunities from young people," and that they have to "open up new opportunities" for young people.
Von der Leyen said the youth experience project would "open horizons and create friendships that will last a lifetime."
She said the trade agreement is a "two way street" and it means "more choice for the customers."
Von der Leyen also mentioned the agreement on the carbon market, saying that it would cut emissions and generate investments in cleaner industries.
She also said Britain will rejoin the Erasmus+ program, adding, "We miss them so much."
What did Burnham say ahead of the EU-UK summit?

In September, Burnham said he would seek a political consensus on the country's future relationship with the EU, even suggesting he could campaign to take Britain back into the bloc at the next election.
Brussels said the agreements would only take effect if a deal is reached to lower university tuition fees for EU students studying in the UK.

"Britain and Europe share values, interests and a global neighborhood. In a more dangerous world, we are stronger together. A closer partnership with Europe is good for working people, good for Britain and good for Europe," Burnham said as he arrived in Brussels.
UK prime minister, who was greeted on arrival by a string quintet, said Britain should explore different options for its future relationship with the EU, including rejoining the bloc.
On Monday, he said it ​was the "obvious truth" that ‌Britain had lost more than it had gained from Brexit.
What do the deals involve?
The three key agreements establish ways to:

items: Simplify food exports by reducing red tape
Link the UK and EU emissions-trading systems
Establish a youth experience scheme

blocks.text: The "youth experience scheme" would allow 100,000 people under 30 from each side to reside for up to three years in each other's territory for work, study or travel without being subject to existing visa requirements.

No deal was reached on tuition fees for EU students studying in Britain, a deal-breaker for the bloc. The EU has pressed for the UK to reduce university tuition fees for EU students to the same level paid by British students
"There will be further discussions coming out of it on issues including on tuition fees," Burnham said.

On the food deal, the EU and UK have agreed to scrap certificates and border checks on food and animal products to ease post-Brexit trade. In return, Britain will align more closely with EU food safety and animal health rules.
How do Brits feel about Brexit now?
As UK debates rejoining the EU, Brexit divides Newhaven residents
Polling firm YouGov runs a regular tracker on whether the UK was right or wrong to vote to quit.
Since mid-2022, a majority of people surveyed said Britain was wrong to leave.In September, the "Bregret" camp rose to 60% — the highest ever.

articles.title: ‘Traumatizing’: hunger striker in ICE detention tells of force-feeding ordeal – and what made him crack
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Luis Alejandro Cora Perez says in messages to Guardian from inside Texas facility pain of force-feeding caused him to break strike

The text message that came from inside the…

blocks.text: The text message that came from inside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center was stark: “I have spent five days eating regular food. If I don’t eat it, they put the tube in me to feed me.”

A Cuban asylum seeker, Luis Alejandro Cora Perez, 32, said in messages to the Guardian this month that he was still weak and dizzy after three months without eating, but that he had broken his hunger strike because being force-fed was just too painful.
The Trump administration responded to requests for comment by denying it had force-fed Cora Perez. But the detainee sent more details – and his is far from an isolated case.
Cora Perez was one of two men on hunger striker at a Texas facility for whom ICE sought and received a federal judge’s permission to force-feed in recent weeks, a Guardian investigation found.

Cora Perez and the other man were locked up inside the Port Isabel service processing center, an ICE detention facility in south Texas, just a few miles from the US-Mexico border, on the coast near where Elon Musk’s SpaceX launches rockets. Cora Perez began a hunger strike in August to protest against his prolonged detention by federal immigration officials while his case plays out. At first he only drank water, then after three weeks, he says he began to drink one Ensure nutritional shake per day.
On 30 October, court records show ICE received permission to forcibly feed and hydrate him, and to restrain him while doing so.

The next day he says six guards at the center held him down, while medical staffers inserted a feeding tube through his nose and down his throat, and pumped nutritional liquid into his stomach – a process he called “traumatizing, both physically and psychologically”.

On 3 November, ICE then received permission from a federal judge to force-feed another hunger striker at Port Isabel, from Uzbekistan, federal court records show. DHS says the Uzbek man has not been subjected to the practice, however.

blocks.caption: The Port Isabel detention center in Los Fresnos, Texas. Photograph: Verónica G Cárdenas/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: On Wednesday night, after weeks of communications, Cora Perez was suddenly transferred to another detention center in Texas. His relative says neither of them were alerted to any plans to transfer him, or a reason for it.
DHS did not specify why Cora Perez was transferred, adding that ICE makes custody determinations on a “case-by-case” basis based on “various factors”.

The revelations come as ICE’s detention practices continue to come under fire amid allegations of mistreatment, and as an increasing number of sporadic hunger strikes have been breaking out in ICE facilities across the country.

The two men’s cases in Texas, revealed here for the first time, are some of the most recent instances of government lawyers seeking a federal judge’s permission, as required by ICE policy, and receiving the go-ahead to force-feed detained hunger strikers. The Guardian’s reporting is based on court records, interviews, dozens of messages exchanged and an interview conducted with Cora Perez via a facility phone. It further reveals how the Trump administration is increasingly obtaining such court orders to force-feed detained immigrants, a secretive practice widely condemned as torture by human rights organizations and medical ethics groups.

Detainees driven to hunger strike are typically using it as a last resort to protest against poor conditions and the Trump administration’s preference for arrest and prolonged detention while their civil immigration cases proceed through the system.

Cora Perez said detention center staff inserted the feeding tube and left it in his body, a not uncommon practice, according to experts, and introduced nutrition – first a “clear liquid”, followed by a “milky liquid”, he recalled – through the tube twice more that day, before he cracked and said he broke his hunger strike, citing what he called “horrific torture”. He began voluntarily drinking nutritional shakes the following day, he said.

“ICE does not hold back on anything, and they do anything they want, like we have seen, even killing their own US citizens,” he wrote to the Guardian, referring to the fatal shootings of Renee Good by an ICE officer and Alex Pretti by a border patrol officer in January of this year during Trump’s pivotal immigration crackdown on Minneapolis.

blocks.caption: Children look at posters honoring Alex Pretti and Renee Nicole Good, shot dead by federal agents in Minneapolis in January. Photograph: Tim Evans/Reuters

blocks.text: Detained hunger strikers subjected to involuntary medical procedures, including force-feeding, have rarely spoken out about their cases or revealed their identities, much less while still detained. Cora Perez’s messages offer a rare glimpse at conditions inside a detention center’s restricted medical unit where hunger strikers and suicidal detainees are held.

“They just took [the Uzbek man] in an ambulance after [him] fainting in front of the medical lobby where they take our vitals, our weight and our temperature,” Cora said in an alarmed message last Monday morning.
The Uzbek man was returned the following day to the facility, Cora Perez said.
“I see him every day because I see him in the room in front of me, but they don’t let us talk to each other,” he added.

The Guardian independently confirmed the Uzbek’s man identity but is not publicly naming him, because efforts to contact him have been unsuccessful. The man arrived at the Mexico-US border in April 2022 and was released into the country while navigating his immigration case. He was arrested by border patrol officials in April of this year and placed in detention. The man does not appear to have any criminal record and DHS did not point to any criminal history.
In a statement, DHS said that after they received the court’s permission to force-feed the Uzbek man, he “has voluntarily taken in fluids and there has been NO force-feeding or forced hydration”.

Security operations at the sprawling Port Isabel facility in Los Fresnos, Texas are run by a private prison company, Akima Global Services, while healthcare is primarily handled by government workers.

blocks.caption: An examination area of the Port Isabel facility. Photograph: Verónica G Cárdenas/AFP via Getty Images

blocks.text: “ICE respects detainees’ rights to exercise self-expression and medical autonomy by refusing nourishment and medical care,” DHS said in a statement. “ICE Health Services Corps may provide involuntary medical treatment only to prevent imminent life-threatening harm or death. Medical staff may provide treatment only to medically stabilize the patient, bringing the detainee outside the imminent harm, incapacitation, or death.”

The US attorney’s office in the southern district of Texas, which represented ICE in its force-feeding request, did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Virginia-headquartered Akima Global Services, and its parent company Nana Regional Corporation, based in Alaska, did not respond to a request for comment.

Force-feeding cases are shrouded in secrecy. After a detainee launches a hunger strike, ICE often sequesters them in medical isolation cells for monitoring, according to ICE’s detention standards. DHS said that ICE continues to offer hunger strikers three meals per day.

After a certain period of not eating, which varies per case, ICE will request a federal judge’s permission to force-feed the hunger striker. Many court records, and sometimes entire court dockets, are sealed and hidden from public view. In Cora Perez and the Uzbek man’s cases, like in others, they did not have any legal representation to challenge the force-feeding requests.

The Guardian found at least five instances in which ICE requested permission to force-feed hunger strikers in Port Isabel since January 2025. The federal judge who ruled on Cora Perez and the Uzbek man, Rolando Olvera, has similarly ordered in at least three other cases, records show. Olvera’s judicial assistant said the court had no comment for this article.

ICE is known to have requested permission to force-feed at least 21 detainees across the US since January 2025, the Guardian found, but the number is likely higher since an unknown number of records and dockets remain sealed, unsearchable and not feasible to locate. Most of the cases coinciding with the second Trump administration and tracked by the Guardian are in Texas and Florida, with others in Georgia, Arizona and Washington state. Under the Biden administration, ICE force-feeding requests were also made in Louisiana and California.

Amy Zeidan, an emergency medicine physician based in Atlanta and an expert on healthcare in immigration detention, said force-feeding hunger strikers can amount to “torture”, and lead to significant psychological distress. She also said it is a violation of medical ethics.

“Essentially it’s like inserting a straw into your nose,” Zeidan said. “You have a gag reflex, so most times people will gag, and that’s really uncomfortable. And people will even vomit repeatedly if it continues to irritate their gag reflex.”
Zeidan added that the forceful insertion of a feeding tube can lead to the swelling of the nostrils and the throat, and even tear them, leading to bleeding.

“It is like torture – somebody is doing a painful procedure to you that you don’t consent to,” Zeidan added. “Autonomy is a fundamental principle of medical ethics. We can’t do something to patients if they don’t want to, even if we think it’s good for them.”

There are numerous cells and rooms inside the Port Isabel medical unit, including isolation cells and shared rooms for ill detainees, according to Cora Perez. In recent weeks, there were five people in the Port Isabel medical isolation cells used for hunger striking or suicidal detainees, he added. He described the cells as “practically freezing”, constantly surveilled with a security camera, and with just a bed, toilet and sink. As well as himself, he says he observed the Uzbek man, a Middle Eastern man, a “tall” eastern European man and a Black man of unknown nationality in the isolation cells. Unit detainees are escorted by facility staff to showers and sometimes receive yard and television access, he said.

blocks.caption: A security guard at Port Isabel. Photograph: Verónica G Cárdenas/AFP via Getty Images

blocks.text: Cora Perez worries for the other detainees. The Black man, whose identity or nationality he does not know, seems to have “serious mental health problems”, Cora Perez observed.
“He harms himself and spends the night yelling and hitting the door, and does not let anyone sleep,” he said.

The Guardian has independently confirmed the eastern European and Middle Eastern men’s identities, but is not publicly naming them because efforts to contact them have been unsuccessful. DHS did not comment on the other men inside the medical isolation unit, saying they could not comment without the Guardian providing their identities.

Cora Perez had left his son and parents in Cuba and requested asylum at the Mexico-US border in 2023, according to a relative who spoke to the Guardian on condition of anonymity due to fear of retaliation by immigration authorities. Cora Perez went to live with the relative in Florida, where he worked in maintenance at a hotel and as a food delivery worker, he said.

In March 2025, Cora Perez was arrested by local police and later convicted of two misdemeanors, including “breach of peace” and “obstructing an officer without violence”, according to local records. He was sentenced to two months in jail, his relative said. But ICE placed a hold on him and as he was being released in June 2025, immigration officials took him into custody – a common system – and soon transferred him to the Adelanto detention center, a privately-run facility in California.

Days in Adelanto turned to weeks, then months, then a over year, according to a federal court order denying one of his petitions requesting his release. His multiple requests to immigration and ordinary federal courts for release from detention, while he fights his asylum case, have been unsuccessful.

“All his claims will be heard by an immigration judge, and he will receive due process. This administration will not ignore the rule of law,” DHS said. “Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the US.”
In August, he stopped eating to protest against his protracted detention.

“I have spent two birthdays behind ICE’s bars,” he wrote. “The reasons I did the hunger strike in Adelanto are for my political asylum, for the time I have spent detained, [and] because I have a 14-year-old son who is starving to death in Cuba because he does not have my help.”
“Also due to the mistreatment by the officials,” he added.

Cora Perez did not tell his family about the hunger strike, so as not to further worry them. It was not until he was transferred to Port Isabel in late September that he confessed to his relative he had been on a prolonged hunger strike.
“He doesn’t share details so that I won’t get upset or worry,” the relative said in a phone interview.

blocks.caption: The barbed-wire fence at Port Isabel. Photograph: Verónica G Cárdenas/Reuters

blocks.text: Cora Perez’s mother, who is in Cuba, “does not know anything, because she is sick, and with his detention she has gotten worse”, the relative added, between tears. “I don’t want her nor his grandmother to know anything about it,” the relative added.

On October 30, the federal prosecutors requested permission for ICE to forcibly feed and hydrate Cora Perez. Hours later, a federal judge approved the procedures without hearing from Cora Perez. Cora Perez told the Guardian in various instances he felt it was unfair he was not given the opportunity to present his case to the judge before the judge approved his force-feeding.

“It’s very disturbing because the judge is basically making a decision on information that is only provided by one side,” said Linus Chan, a professor of clinical law and the director of the detainee rights clinic at the University of Minnesota law school. “That just seems ridiculous.”
Cora Perez was force-fed the following day, he said in his messages and in a phone call, adding that he did not physically resist because he “had seen a lot of mistreatment of others detained”.
“[ICE does] what they want with us, whatever they want, because a federal judge gave them permission,” he added. “I have suffered on the island [of Cuba] and now at the hands of ICE.”

After asking Cora Perez about DHS’s denials that he was force-fed, he repeated that he was. “Brother, ICE says and does whatever they want. They deny, punish, retaliate and do everything at their own will. They have even sent Cubans to Africa,” he said.

The number of people detained by ICE has soared under the Trump administration. And due to policy and legal changes, tens of thousands of people are forced to stay in detention for long periods while they fight their immigration cases.
Chan, from the University of Minnesota, says prolonged detention and delays in their cases lead to logical conclusion. “That’s exactly when people protest,” he said.
“And the only form of protest, for many of these people, is a hunger strike,” he said.
As Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown continues and people are detained as a first resort while their cases play out, Chan said: “Hunger strikes will become more common.”

articles.title: Senate ethics panel to Bato dela Rosa: Respond to prolonged absence complaint
articles.summary: The Senate committee on ethics and privileges has transmitted to Senator Ronald "Bato" dela Rosa the complaint lodged against him due to his prolonged absence.

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 7:00pm
The Senate committee on ethics and privileges has transmitted to Senator Ronald "Bato" dela Rosa the complaint lodged against him due to his prolonged absence.

The Wag Kang KuCorrupt group on Friday posted the panel's transmittal letter to Dela Rosa on Facebook. Committee chair Senator Tito Sotto, who signed the document dated October 22, 2026, later confirmed the complaint to reporters.

"This is to inform you of the action taken by the Senate Committee on Ethics and Privileges… on the complaint filed by Wag Kang KuCorrupt, represented by Barry Gutierrez, Cielo Magno, et al., against you for alleged prolonged absence from official duties," the document read.
The ethics panel gave Dela Rosa 15 days upon receipt of the complaint to provide his written response and any information regarding the matter.
Dela Rosa started missing Senate engagements in 2025 following reports that the International Criminal Court (ICC) had issued an arrest warrant against him.

He resurfaced on May 11, but left Senate custody in the early morning of May 14 after a shooting incident erupted inside the legislative chamber's premises. He has not been seen publicly ever since, and now faces a P50-million bounty for information leading to his arrest.

According to the transmittal, Wag Kang KuCorrupt's initial complaint was filed as early as February 25, but it was returned after the panel found it did not comply with rules. Supplemental affidavits to support the complaint were later submitted on September 14.
The panel then deemed the complaint "in substantial compliance, both in form and in substance" during an executive session on October 22, the same date of the letter.

"You (Dela Rosa) are invited to provide the Committee with any information relevant to the complaint, including a written response, within 15 days from receipt of this notice. A copy of the complaint, the Supplemental Affidavits, and the Rules is attached for your reference," the document read.
The group's petition reasoned that Dela Rosa's prolonged absence showed a dereliction of duty and a grave abuse of privilege.

"Under ordinary working conditions in both the public and private sectors, employees who fail to report for work without authorized leave are ordinarily subjected to disciplinary measures, including salary deductions, suspension, or even outright termination. Breadwinners across the country work tirelessly, often under difficult conditions, precisely because their families' welfare depends on daily accountability and performance," the group's original complaint read. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: International court's ruling on Myanmar genocide means little for victims, but much for future cases
articles.summary: Legal experts say the International Court of Justice's first ever finding of genocide committed by a state may also help shape how that case and others like it are decided in the future. Victims,…

image.caption: Judge Yuji Iwasawa, centre, president of the United Nation's International Court of Justice, reads the court's landmark judgment that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in a brutal 2017 military operation. The ruling took place Thursday at the International Court of Justice in

blocks.text: World·Analysis

Legal experts say the International Court of Justice's first ever finding of genocide committed by a state may also help shape how that case and others like it are decided in the future. Victims, human rights activists and legal observers had hoped that the case, filed against Myanmar in 2019, would open a new pathway for delivering justice on the international stage.
Court's finding that Myanmar committed genocide provides little change for Rohingya victims

In the days after the world's top court was asked to weigh in on accusations of genocide against Myanmar, legal experts, activists and victims alike hoped the case might, for the first time in decades, open a new pathway for delivering justice on the international stage.

That was back in 2019. The International Court of Justice's finding seven years later that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority was indeed celebrated as recognition of the decades-long suffering of the Rohingya people. But it came at a high price.
"For the first time the world has heard the Rohingya," said John Jonaid, a survivor of the genocide who is now an Ottawa-based Rohingya journalist and human rights advocate.
"But at the same time, it's too late, I would say, for us to get any justice for our suffering."
Rohingyas hail UN top court ruling that Myanmar guilty of genocide
The Myanmar military conducted "clearance operations" in Rakhine state in 2017, systematically destroying Rohingya villages, perpetrating brutal sexual violence and killing thousands of people.
Most Rohingya now live in the world's largest refugee camp in Bangladesh and beyond, with little prospect of return.

items: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya ethnic minority, International Court of Justice rules

blocks.text: In its judgment, the ICJ demanded that Myanmar provide reparations and allow Rohingya to return to their villages — but most of those villages have been erased, and the country's leadership has long disregarded international scrutiny, rejecting allegations of genocide.

The tension between a legal victory in the case against Myanmar, launched by the Muslim-majority African nation of Gambia, and the reality for Rohingya victims of genocide was inevitable from the start: while the court has the power to hear and rule on cases filed by states against other states, it has no real means with which to implement its rulings.

Gambia's Justice Minister and Attorney General Dawda Jallow, right, with lawyer Arsalan Suleman, speaks to the media after International Court of Justice ruling in The Hague, Netherlands, on Thursday. Gambia launched the proceedings at the court in 2019. (Patrick Post/The Associated Press)
And yet even before the Thursday ruling, the case still had a profound legal impact.

Five new cases involving genocide were subsequently filed at the ICJ, each with its own unique circumstances. They include the highly anticipated case brought forward by South Africa against Israel, accusing it of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza following Hamas's attacks on Oct. 7, 2023.

items: South Africa accuses Israel of 'genocidal' acts in Gaza; Israel rejects filing to top UN court 'with disgust'
As UN court prepares to hear genocide claim against Israel, Canada still hasn't taken a position

blocks.text: And now, legal experts say, the court's first ever finding of genocide committed by a state may also help shape how that case and others like it are decided in the future.
Not everyone agrees on exactly how.

At minimum, Thursday's ruling — the first of its kind at the ICJ — has brought the 1948 UN convention on genocide "back to life," said Canadian human rights lawyer Payam Akhavan, one of the attorneys who served as counsel for Gambia in the case.

"This is a landmark judgment of the ICJ, and it comes at a crucial point in the evolution of international law, including unprecedented attacks against both the international court and the ICJ," he said in an interview with CBC.

While Akhavan says the ruling is "grossly inadequate" in addressing the immediate plight of the victims of Myanmar's genocide, he notes that how the court has interpreted the law in this case could still play a role in shaping the outcome of future ones.

Canadian human rights lawyer Payam Akhavan, centre, sits at Gambia's counsel table for the January 2020 reading of the first International Court of Justice judgment on urgent measures concerning Myanmar. (Submitted by Payam Akhavan)
Ruling underlines sexual violence is a genocidal act

Significantly, the majority of the judges in the Myanmar case rejected the country's argument that the "clearance operations" it conducted against the Rohingya in 2017 were defensive military operations aimed at neutralizing a threat and therefore precluded genocide.
Priya Pillai, a lawyer and international law specialist, told CBC News the court ruled that "the fact that you have a conflict doesn't preclude the fact that you might have genocidal intent as well."
"The two things can exist at the same time."

Other strands of the ruling, says Akhavan, demonstrated an expansive approach to the genocide convention, which was adopted in the wake of the Holocaust and the murder of millions of Jews during the Second World War.

Crucially, the ICJ judges strongly affirmed that genocidal acts were not limited to murder or displacement, but could also include crimes of sexual violence and attacks on reproductive capability to prevent procreation.
Breaking down the ICJ's first-ever ruling on state genocide
Countless Rohingya women reported a campaign of mutilation and brutal sexual violence at the hands of Myanmar's military forces.

Marianne Vitug, legal advisor for the Global Justice Center, said at a news conference in The Hague Thursday that the court looked at how sexual violence was directed at women and girls of reproductive age and sometimes pregnant women, and how young and unmarried women were targeted with extreme and brutal violence.
"The targeting of reproductive capacity is now very clearly a genocidal act, so that is a significant finding in this case."

items: UN report condemns sexual violence by Myanmar military against Rohingya

blocks.text: Vitug says the court's reliance on evidence gathered by NGOs and fact-finding missions is also "very significant in relation to upcoming cases that will rely on similar findings."

Unlike in other cases, NGOs cannot intervene directly in cases before the ICJ. Only member states can do so, and in Gambia's case, that included Canada, jointly with France, the Netherlands, Denmark, Germany and the U.K., supporting Gambia's effort to end Myanmar's impunity.
Their intervention focused on how the court should interpret the genocide convention, including the role of sexual violence.
In 2018, Parliament voted unanimously to recognize that Myanmar's military actions against Rohingya people constituted genocide.
John Jonaid, a survivor of the genocide who is now an Ottawa-based Rohingya journalist and human rights advocate. (Nicole Williams/CBC)
A 'painfully long' process

Rohingya activists are skeptical that pressure by the international community will do anything to persuade Myanmar's current president, Min Aung Hlaing, who led the military during its operations in Rakhine State, to accept them back.
There is also the question of what they would be returning to.
"Their entire villages have been burned and their history has been erased from Myanmar, as if they never existed [there]," said Jonaid.
"There is no trace."

items: Rohingya man whose mother was abducted calls for refugee pathway to Canada

blocks.text: While they await the right conditions for return, Jonaid says countries like Canada that have taken an interest in the plight of Rohingya must do whatever possible to ensure they thrive — including providing opportunities for education and employment wherever they currently live.
Akhavan suspects meaningful change in the international justice system will take time.
"We have to understand that the fight for universal human rights is a painfully long historical process."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Nahlah Ayed is the host of the nightly CBC Radio program IDEAS. A veteran of foreign reportage, she's spent nearly a decade covering major world events from London, and another decade covering upheaval across the Middle East. Ayed was previously a parliamentary reporter for The Canadian Press. She has received several awards for her journalism, including the 2025 Edward. R. Murrow Award.
