articles.title: Have we missed our chance to stop climate change?
articles.summary: From record-breaking heat to devastating floods and wildfires, the warning signs are everywhere. Can rising temperatures still be brought under control?

image.caption: Has the world acted too late to stop catastrophic climate change?Image: Abriansyah Liberto/REUTERS

blocks.text: When world leaders agreed to do what they could to stop the world from overheating back in 2015, it was heralded as a victorious moment. Hope rippled from Paris, where the historic deal was made.

Since then, efforts to curb the use of planet-warming fossil fuels have achieved some success, with coal, oil and gas falling to a record low share of global primary energy supply. But they still account for around 86% of the world's energy.
"We're still burning stuff like [it's] the 19th century," Mark Maslin, professor of Earth System Science at University College London, told DW.

And that has consequences. The United Nations now says overshooting the temperature threshold agreed in Paris 11 years ago is inevitable. That means even more extreme weather events, like storms, flooding, droughts and deadly heat waves and resultant crop failures and water shortages across the world.

The impacts are already being felt globally. This summer, Europe alone recorded 50,000 heat-related deaths in urban areas. In Delhi, India, summer heat waves saw temperatures soar above 45 degrees Celsius (113 Fahrenheit). Even in the relative cool of the evening, there was little respite.
"It feels like your eyes are burning," said Disha Ravi co-founder of the India chapter of youth climate movement Fridays for Future (FFF). "I always describe it as being cooked alive in an oven."
Heat waves and other weather extremes are killing people now, says Ravi, and she is aware that as the global average temperature continues to rise, life is only set to become tougher.
"Even at this moment where we haven't even reached the worst of what it could be, it's already difficult," she said.
"We should have dealt with climate change 10, 20 years ago," Maslin said.
Shoulda, woulda, coulda: Is it too late to bring temperatures under control?
The UN now says that the world must keep the time it spends in overshoot as brief as possible, bringing global heating back down by the end of the century.

The longer the planet spends above the threshold, the greater the risk of triggering irreversible, self-perpetuating tipping points, such as massive forest die-back and permafrost melting that would release huge amounts of carbon into the atmosphere.

blocks.caption: As permafrost melts, it releases carbon dioxide which adds to the greenhouse gas effect that continues to warm the planetImage: MAXIM SHEMETOV/REUTERS

blocks.text: A recent report by science-based assessment Climate Action Tracker says limiting overshoot will require policies to rapidly and steeply reduce the emissions warping the climate.

"The stark choice for governments is to continue to support the fossil fuel industry, which would consign humanity to insurmountable economic damages, rising mortality from heat and climate-driven diseases and disasters that they are unable to adapt to — or pivot to the solutions which are available and cheaper than ever," the authors said.

Failure to cut emissions quickly has made it significantly harder to get climate change under control, and the window for doing so is rapidly closing. But Maslin refers to a Chinese proverb: "When is the best time to plant a tree? Yesterday. When's the next best time to plant a tree? Today."

He points to the massive expansion in renewable energy as reason not to despair. Wind, solar and hydropower accounted for around 34% of global electricity production in 2025 and are increasingly being used to meet rising demand.
Last year, record growth in solar power meant that clean energy met all new global electricity demand, stifling new fossil fuel generation, according to an analysis by energy think tank Ember.

blocks.caption: Solar energy has experienced record growth for years Image: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "At the moment, $2 trillion is being invested in new renewable energy projects around the world, which is twice as much as fossil fuels," Maslin said.
But no country is weaning itself off fossil fuels quickly enough to limit the time spent in overshoot. "The transition is happening, it's just not happening fast enough," he added.
The countries pushing for a fossil fuel phaseout

One of the problems is that most climate and energy plans focus on building a green energy system rather than creating policy to shift away from fossil fuel use and production, according to recent report on how to manage the transition by nonprofit research organization, World Resources Institute.
A group of 57 states is working together to manage and accelerate the complicated task of phasing out oil, coal and gas by creating specific roadmaps to do so.

Under the Transition Away from Fossil Fuels initiative (TAFF) initiative, Brazil has published a global roadmap that suggests various measures that can be tailored to each country's financial circumstances and capabilities.
So far, a small but growing number of countries, including, Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, France, Germany, and Finland, have released national roadmaps.
COP31: Can electrification replace fossil fuels?

Yet renewables advocacy group Oil Change International says they largely repackage existing commitments rather than offering new ones, when "what we need is an accelerated timeline for a clean, secure energy system."

France is sticking to a previously announced deadline of phasing out fossil fuels entirely by 2050. The Netherlands has not published binding dates for quitting oil and gas, and will continue to extract gas in the North Sea.

Germany, however, explicitly mentioned transitioning away from fossil fuels by 2045 for the first time, in line with its existing climate neutrality target. The country has also reduced its emissions by 48% compared to 1990 levels.

And while Finland has not set a hard and fast target for phasing out the fossil fuels that still account for 26% of its total energy consumption, it already generates more than 96% of electricity from non-fossil sources.

"None of these examples is a perfect template," according to the WRI report. "But together, they show that countries are already developing many of the core ingredients of a fossil fuel transition plan."
Every fraction of a degree matters
Limiting the time spent in overshoot would mean fossil fuel use falling 20% by 2030 and being phased out completely by 2070, according to research institute Climate Analytics.
It also means removing hundreds of billions of tons of CO2 from the atmosphere using carbon removal technologies that remain unproven at scale, as well as nature-based approaches like reforestation.
And it requires fast action on the short-lived but highly potent greenhouse gas methane. A 45% cut would reduce warming by 0.3%, according to the UN.

blocks.caption: Each fraction of a degree of warming will bring with it escalating climate extremes so it's still all to play for, say scientistsImage: Apu Gomes/AFP

blocks.text: Scientists stress that every fraction of a degree matters as the world blows past the threshold of 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) of warming above pre-industrial levels. That's because every increment will bring more extreme heat, heavier rainfall, rising seas, and greater and more catastrophic risk for everyone around the world.
Still, even in the face of accelerating climate change, FFF co-founder Ravi rejects the idea that it is too late to act.
"I refuse to believe we'll ever run out of time. No matter how bad it gets," she said. "We owe it to ourselves. We owe it to each other to always try to get out of this mess."

articles.title: California’s coastal communities on alert as biggest waves in years hit state
articles.summary:
Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recorded

Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive…

blocks.text: Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.

Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.

blocks.caption: A large wave pours over the seawall in Pacifica. Photograph: Fred Greaves/Reuters

blocks.text: Nearly 72,000 people have been evacuated from areas of Odisha in eastern India as Tropical Cyclone Akvan approaches land. Akvan is expected to make landfall on Friday between Narsapur and Puri, prompting cyclone warnings from the India Meteorological Department for north Andhra Pradesh, Yanam and south Odisha coasts. Peak wind gusts are expected to reach 70mph, with rainfall totals through Friday and Saturday potentially exceeding 200mm for northern coastal Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.

blocks.caption: Fishers carry a boat to a safer place along the shore before the expected landfall of Tropical Cyclone Akvan near Gopalpur in Odisha, India. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: Following a Yellow Level 2 severe thunderstorm warning by the South African Weather Service on Tuesday, torrential rainfall and large hail were reported across parts of Johannesburg. The storms triggered flash flooding and caused infrastructure damage in the township of Soweto. One person died, while another remains missing after the severe storms.

articles.title: Ever buy more than you mean to when shopping online? This could be why
articles.byline: Stephanie Kampf, Daniela Silva, Katie Swyers, Asha Tomlinson

image.caption: Marketplace tracked popular online shopping sites to reveal tactics companies use to influence your behaviour. (Adobe stock)

blocks.text: Ever buy more than you mean to online? It could be by design.
CBC's Marketplace tracked popular online shopping sites Amazon, Shein, Temu and Walmart, revealing the tactics companies use which can influence your behaviour.
Can you trust every sale countdown timer? How about that inventory counter? Not necessarily.

They can be part of what experts call "dark patterns," a type of design on a website or app that can steer you into a decision that might not be in your best interest, and something that can be found across the internet.

"What's spooky about it is that people don't even know it's happening, and so their choices as shoppers are being guided invisibly," said Ryan Fritsch, an advocate for protecting consumers in the digital marketplace and a lawyer for the Law Commission of Ontario.
Ryan Fritsch, lawyer for the Law Commission of Ontario, says dark patterns 'try and trick consumers into making choices that may not be in their interest.' (Will Arnold/CBC)

Marketplace put it to the test in a series of spot checks, tracking sites and apps each week for about a month, and found several pressure tactics. Here’s what to be aware of the next time you're shopping online.
False urgency
The team saw a pair of leggings on Amazon with a stock counter that said only one left, so they bought what appeared to be the last pair. But eight minutes later, they were able to buy a second pair.
A message from Amazon saying we recently ordered what they said was the last pair of leggings, before we ordered a second pair. (CBC)

That second pair shipped a few days later than the first, but Fritsch said, "I think that if they're telling you there's only one left, that should be an honest statement. Otherwise, they are deceiving consumers. It's unfair."
Amazon’s stock count said these leggings were the last pair, but Asha Tomlinson and Ryan Fritsch show two pairs of leggings. (CBC)
Similarly, the Marketplace team saw coupons on Shein with a 24-hour countdown timer. But when the time ran out, the sale simply started over again.
"It's creating a false sense of urgency," said Jacquelyn Burkell, a professor in the faculty of information and media studies at the Western University in London, Ont.
"They're playing you, right?" said Fritsch. "The consumer is being induced to make an impulsive purchase that may not be in their best interest when other, better options might be available to them."
Pre-selected options

Another tactic is pre-selected options, which can also work against a consumer’s best interests. When buying the leggings on Amazon, Marketplace noticed the company had pre-selected slightly faster paid shipping for $7.98 as the default — even though free shipping was an option.
Fritsch said a busy shopper might not even notice.
Paid delivery was a pre-selected option on Amazon Canada, even though free delivery was available. (CBC)
Visual interference

Something else experts say to watch for are bright colours that can draw your eye and lead you into a decision. During checkout, both Walmart and Amazon used bright colours to attract attention to signing up for their membership programs, while the option to decline was on a white background.
A pop-up message on Amazon promoting their membership with a yellow button saying 'Start 30-day FREE trial.' (CBC)
Burkell said "a big bright yellow thing is going to be more evident to you" and "when it attracts attention…you're more likely to act."
Shoppers who Marketplace spoke with at the CBC Broadcast Centre in Toronto agreed.
Trisha Arocena said she’s seen this on Amazon before and "it makes the decision almost easier for you. So you're prompted to go ahead and click."
Ritu Gill said if she’s in a rush, "Your eyes do follow … the bright blue button. 'Let me just click yes, yes, yes, get through this and make the purchase.'"
A pop-up message on Walmart Canada promoting their membership with a blue button saying 'Confirm Plan.' (CBC)

In a statement, a spokesperson for Walmart Canada said the company's goal is to provide customers with a transparent and easy-to-navigate online shopping experience. They said the membership offer is optional and clearly presents consumers with "both the membership option and the option to close the offer and continue with their checkout."
The statement added that Walmart is "committed to complying with applicable laws and regulations."
An Amazon spokesperson said in an email that they "work hard to offer customers a transparent and trustworthy shopping experience."

"When Amazon displays how many units of an item are left in stock, that information reflects inventory on hand and ready to ship with a specific delivery estimate. The Amazon.ca store complies with all applicable Canadian laws, including consumer protection, competition and privacy laws."
Nagging

After the Marketplace team left items in the shopping cart on Temu, the company immediately emailed saying "Action required" and "Complete checkout" with a price drop. Temu continued to email and text about the cart multiple times in the following days.
This type of dark pattern, called nagging, can wear people down, says Burkell.
"Eventually people are just going to give in and say, 'Oh fine, I'll buy it.'"
It’s a tactic that works, says Arocena.
"If it was on my cart, chances are I was somewhat ready to check out … so that price drop ultimately convinces me to move forward with the purchase."
Gamification
Another design tactic to watch for: games on shopping sites that can keep consumers locked in to the site.

While browsing on Shein, the Marketplace team spotted an animated promotion that offered the chance to grab three free items: an iPhone Duo, an iPhone Max and a pair of AirPods Max. The chance to win didn’t come until about a week later but the prizes were first come, first serve and the stock was limited to one of each.
Fritsch says the game keeps consumers in the habit of visiting the site and "captured as a customer."

In an email, a Shein spokesperson said the company "is committed to complying with applicable laws and regulations in the markets where we operate." They added that they provide a transparent shopping experience and regularly review features on their platform as well as identify opportunities to improve customers’ shopping experience.
Confirmation shaming

On a "spin to win" game on Temu, the Marketplace team got a $350 credit. Although the game said they were just one step away from claiming it, they didn’t manage to get the credit, despite making multiple purchases.
When the Marketplace team left the app, a message said "Cancel your account rewards?" The options were "Stay and withdraw" or "I don't want cash."
Fritsch says that language is called confirmation shaming, which manipulates a consumer's emotions.

"The idea here is that a consumer has made a choice and they want to exercise that choice. And then at the last step, the vendor says, ‘Whoa, whoa, whoa, are you sure you wanna do this? You're walking away from all this potential money.'"
A message on Temu’s app that appeared when trying to leave a game saying 'I don’t want cash.' (CBC)

A Temu spokesperson said in a statement that "the interactive elements in our app are intended to make shopping more engaging and give users opportunities to unlock additional discounts. Users have a choice: they can shop without playing games, close a game and return to shopping, and turn off game-related notifications in the app’s settings."

In response to the repeated notifications, the company said users can unsubscribe from texts and email promotions. They added that they "listen to customer feedback ... and continue to refine platform features."
Possible solution?
In the European Union, lawmakers are making a push to specifically ban dark patterns through their Digital Services Act.

Marketplace checked out some of the same shopping sites using a VPN set to Sweden and found some differences. For example, on Amazon, free shipping was the pre-selected option, rather than paid shipping. Temu didn’t send emails after items were left in the cart. And coupons on Shein actually seemed to expire. (Walmart does not operate in Europe.)

"This is precisely what our services are monitoring," said Thomas Regnier, spokesperson on digital tech sovereignty for the European Commission. He said the differences between the North American and European shopping experiences on these sites show that the approach in the EU is working.
Even so, the European Commission wants to strengthen consumer protection further through the Digital Fairness Act.
"We need to reach that level where the Wild West is completely over in the online world, where platforms operate in a regulated environment, just like shops do in real life," said Regnier.
Thomas Regnier, spokesperson on digital tech sovereignty for the European Commission. (Fernando Moreno/CBC)

articles.title: PNP identifies 70 social media posts encouraging protests, violence
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Friday said it has identified around 70 social media posts allegedly encouraging people to participate in protests and engage in violence.

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 5:00pm
The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Friday said it has identified around 70 social media posts allegedly encouraging people to participate in protests and engage in violence.
At a press briefing, PNP spokesperson Police Brigadier General Allen Rae Co said the PNP Anti-Cybercrime Group is working to identify the individuals or groups behind the posts.
“Marami po, marami ang na-ano natin na, several. Siguro nasa mga 70, more or less, 70,” Co said.
(There were several. Maybe more or less 70.)

Among the posts monitored by authorities were messages urging people to take to the streets, join demonstrations, oust certain government officials, and resort to violence over alleged government’s wrongdoing.
Co said the PNP is still validating the identities of those behind the posts.
According to him, authorities have noticed similarities in some of the messages, including the use of identical punctuation marks and spacing.
“It could have come from a single source na marami pong naglalabas (and many people posted them),” he said.
Co said the PNP is examining possible violations of Philippine laws in connection with the posts.
During the ASEAN Summit 2026, protesters expressed opposition to the Pax Silica initiative as well as the visit of United States President Donald Trump to the Philippines. —NB, GMA News

articles.title: A Montrealer died in Istanbul. Authorities blame food poisoning but what we found suggests something else
articles.summary: A young Canadian woman travelled to Turkey after graduating from medical school. In her last days there, she fell ill and died within hours. Authorities there blame food poisoning, but a joint…
articles.byline: Michelle Gagnon, Jacaudrey Charbonneau, Judith Plamondon

image.caption: Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino visited Capadoccia, Turkey, in 2025 as part of a trip celebrating her recent graduation from medical school. During that trip, the 24-year-old Montrealer died suddenly in Istanbul. (Submitted by Deveaux-Cattino family)

blocks.text: Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino, a healthy 24-year-old Montrealer, died suddenly in Istanbul on June 17, 2025.
A Turkish autopsy report concluded the cause of death was food poisoning.
But for her family, that doesn't add up.
A joint investigation into Deveaux-Cattino's death by Enquête and the fifth estate revealed a different poison at work and 12 similar deaths.
The recent medical school graduate had decided to celebrate by taking a trip with a few of her closest friends.
"She'd never been to Turkey," said her sister, Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino. "She thought it was a super beautiful, vibrant country."
The group hit the tourist trail and its highlights, including the requisite balloon ride in Cappadocia.
Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino had never been to Turkey before her trip in 2025, says her sister, Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino. ‘She thought it was a super beautiful, vibrant country.’ (Radio-Caanda)
With only two days to go, Bérengère and one of her friends headed for Istanbul, a city she'd longed to visit.

items: Watch the full documentary, "The Invisble Killer," from the fifth estate on YouTube or CBC-TV on Friday at 9 p.m.

blocks.text: They checked into Room 108 at the Seven Days Hotel and went straight out to explore. They soaked up the sights and street food, then settled down for a proper meal, a chicken casserole followed by Turkish tea and baklava.
The next morning, they woke violently ill.
Laurie recalls the final days

The details of those final days come from Laurie, the woman who travelled to Istanbul with Bérengère. What happened on that trip left her traumatized and we've agreed to protect her identity and not use her real name.
She said that within minutes of waking, Bérengère was throwing up.
"Then I started feeling unwell," Laurie said, "and suddenly we were taking turns running to the bathroom to vomit until we realized that whatever it was, it wasn't just going to pass."
They called the front desk and an ambulance took them to hospital.
‘My sister is younger than me,’ said Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino, right. ‘I’d never imagined a life without her.’ (Submitted by Deveaux-Cattino family)
'Things aren't going well'
That same day, across the ocean in Montreal, Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino saw her screen light up: Laurie was FaceTiming her.

"I thought: 'This isn't normal. Something's off. This is going to be bad news,'" said Deveaux-Cattino. "She says 'Élo, we're in the hospital in Istanbul, and things aren't going well. I've been told to contact the family.'"
Deveaux-Cattino and her father, Henri Cattino, scrambled to find flights to Istanbul. While waiting for their connection in Paris, Deveaux-Cattino called the embassy.
"I said: 'Please, can you tell me if my sister has died?'" said Deveaux-Cattino. ”And she said: 'I'm very sorry, Éléonore, but your sister is dead.'"
Three days into their trip to Istanbul in November 2025, the Böcek family from Hamburg fell ill. Five days later, all four family members were dead, poisoned by phosphine gas. (@ismailsaymaz/X)
The Böcek family
The Deveaux-Cattinos repatriated Bérengère's body and asked the Quebec coroner's office to examine it. They buried their daughter and sister without confirmation of the cause of death.
As they waited for answers from Turkey, the family speculated about what else could explain Bérengère's death: Organ trafficking? Alcohol poisoning? Medical malpractice?
Then, in November, as we were investigating, a diplomatic source texted with a tip that pointed to an entirely different explanation.
"A family of four has just died in Istanbul. Watch this report."
The Böceks, a Turkish-German family from Hamburg, were visiting Istanbul. Their hotel was blocks from where Bérengère and Laurie stayed. All four fell ill and died within days of each other.

Investigators initially suspected food poisoning there, too. But within days, authorities concluded that another poison had been at work: aluminum phosphide, a highly toxic agricultural pesticide used to kill rodents and insects.
The 'bomb'

Exterminators call aluminum phosphide "the bomb." It is used in pellet form. Once the pellets are exposed to air, they release phosphine gas. Exterminators say that when placed in a sealed room, the gas kills every living, breathing thing within 72 hours. In Turkey, it's illegal to use in urban areas.
But, like all big cities, Istanbul has a bedbug problem.
Safe extermination of bedbugs
Exterminator Birkan Cihan said he can barely keep up with calls from desperate home and hotel owners. Some ask whether he treats bedbugs with "gas." He doesn't.
"We tell them their neighbours could die from it, and that they could, too. But they say: 'We have no choice, it's the only thing that works,'" Cihan said
The phosphine gas these pellets emit is so potent and volatile that it can spread through a building, even if the area being treated is sealed.
In the case of the Böcek family, fumigation in the neighbouring room was determined to be what killed all four of them.
Investigations by Enquête and the fifth estate have found similar cases. In 2012, two sisters from Quebec, Audrey and Noémi Bélanger, died of phosphine poisoning in Thailand.
In 2012, two sisters from Quebec, Audrey and Noémi Bélanger, died of phosphine poisoning in Thailand. (Submitted by Bélanger family)
'That doesn't make any sense'

Just before Christmas 2025, the Deveaux-Cattinos received the autopsy report from Turkey. It concluded that food poisoning caused Bérengère's death. Unconvinced, they handed the report to the Quebec coroner's office.

"The coroner here ran some tests, and she couldn't confirm that food poisoning was the cause of death because, usually, there are signs of intestinal irritation," Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino said. "There were none in my sister's case."
We showed the Turkish autopsy report to another Quebec pathologist. Although not authorized to speak publicly, he also questioned the autopsy's conclusions.

"Two young, healthy women who end up in the hospital with food poisoning — OK, I'll buy that. But to die of it so quickly, without any signs of bloody diarrhea or other complications, that doesn't make any sense."
Turkish freelance journalist Ayse Adanali covered the story of the death of the Böcek family in Istanbul in 2025. (Radio-Canada)
Women and children
In Turkey, we started working with Ayse Adanali, a freelance Turkish journalist who'd covered the Böcek story.
Together, we documented nearly 30 cases of phosphine poisoning, including a dozen deaths, since 2023 in Turkey.

Some were tourists, like the two Dutch teenagers found dead by their father in their Istanbul hotel room in August 2025. But most of the victims were Turkish, like Karan Yazıcı, a three-year-old boy poisoned in Istanbul in April 2025 following a fumigation in the neighbouring apartment.

The majority of the victims are women and children. Members of the same family were often poisoned together. While some survived, others died. In most cases, food poisoning was initially blamed for making them sick.
'This is not food poisoning'
Şebnem Korur Fincancı is a human rights activist, professor emeritus and leading forensic pathologist in Turkey.
She's studied aluminum phosphide and knows how difficult it is to identify victims poisoned by phosphine gas.
Turkish forensic pathologist Şebnem Korur Fincancı has studied aluminum phosphide and knows how difficult it is to identify victims poisoned by phosphine gas. (Radio-Canada)
She'd never heard about Bérengère; her death had not been covered by Turkish media.
"This is not food poisoning," she said after reading the Turkish autopsy report.
"I don't think that this is food poisoning because there is no story of diarrhea, only throwing up."
She added that the timing of Bérengère's decline suggests food poisoning couldn't be the culprit.
"Rather, it is the pesticide poisoning."

Fincancı sees one undeniable detail in this report, a finding common to all victims of phosphine gas poisoning she's examined: something called metabolic acidosis, which increases the levels of acidity in the body.
"There is the metabolic acidosis, which also indicates the pesticide intoxication," she said. 'It is one of the main findings of these kinds of cases."
She believes there could be more cases of phosphine poisoning than currently reported.
"With all these misdiagnoses, we have to consider the situation."
Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino and her friend, Laurie, stayed at the Seven Days Hotel in Istanbul. (Radio-Canada)
150 bites
We scoured hundreds of Google and Tripadvisor reviews for the Seven Days Hotel to see if they'd had a bedbug problem around the time of Bérengère and Laurie's stay.
One stood out: A tourist claiming he'd been bitten 150 times during his stay in June 2025.
We tracked him down. He confirmed he stayed in Room 107, the room next door to where the two women stayed 10 days later.
The windows in those two rooms open onto each other.
That left one critical question: Had Room 107 been treated after his stay? And, if so, with what?
We contacted hotel manager Bahattin Demir. He remembered Bérengère and Laurie and had gone to the hospital after they'd been admitted.
We told him about the tourist in Room 107 and asked him whether extermination work in that room could have killed Bérengère.
"I don't think so, because if it was that product, I'm sure that, you know, everybody would have this problem," he said.
Inside Room 108 at the Seven Days Hotel where Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino and Laurie stayed. (Radio-Canada)
He said exterminators spray the rooms in the hotel monthly. He offered to contact them and find out what product they use, but then wrote back, referring us to them for more details.
The extermination company is called Wolves.
A contact called them for us. We're protecting her identity because undercover work can lead to jail time in Turkey.
Posing as an Air BnB owner in Istanbul's Fatih district, she claimed to be struggling with bedbugs.
The employee was cautious on the phone.
He didn't name the product specifically, but his detailed description is similar to how aluminum phosphide is used.
"For 72 hours, nobody goes in, the doors are locked and nothing living enters."

items: Deaths of Quebec women in Thailand may have been caused by pesticide
Phosphine pesticide used to kill bedbugs causes Fort McMurray baby's death

blocks.text: We called Wolves for an interview. The employee who answered the phone was not authorized to speak, but denied using aluminum phosphide.
Neither the hospital that treated Bérengère nor the Forensic Medical Centre where her autopsy was performed replied to our inquiries.
The tourism police similarly declined our interview request.

Going over notes Laurie had shared, we noticed she and Bérengère had left the window open the first night. But the next evening, to avoid being woken by the call to prayer, they closed it and turned on the air conditioning. And that was the night they got sick.
We asked pathologist Şebnem Korur Fincancı whether phosphine gas residue could build up in air conditioners.
"Of course," she said.
'Those who are gone'

The Böceks' case went to trial in June 2026. The defendants were charged with criminal negligence causing the deaths of this family of four. The ruling came down within days. The owners of the extermination company were found guilty and sentenced to 18 years in prison. The hotel owner and employees received 12 to 13 years.
While awaiting the verdict, the paternal grandfather, Yilmaz Böcek, commented that even the stiffest penalty could never bring back his children and grandchildren.
"Those who are gone never come back."
Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino wants Bérengère to be remembered.
"My sister is younger than me. I'd never imagined a life without her. We used to be two against the world … now I'm all alone," she said.
"But I'm stubborn. And since she can no longer speak, I'll speak for her. I'll never let her go."

In the summer of 2026, the government of Canada added a new entry to its travel advisory for Turkey, alerting travellers to "cases of poisoning linked to the use of chemical pesticides in tourist accommodations in Istanbul."
After this story first aired on Oct. 15, 2026, Turkish consular officials contacted us, confirming the investigation into Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino's death in Istanbul remains open.

articles.title: Tenants in Madrid say Toronto-based Brookfield is pricing them out of formerly public housing
articles.summary: Canadian investment firms, led by Toronto-based Brookfield, have become central targets in Spain's Nov. 29 election fight over housing affordability. Long-term Madrid tenants living in former public…

image.caption: Residents protest members of Toronto-based real estate investor Brookfield Corporation at an event in Madrid with signs that say 'Shame!!' in Spanish. (Madrid Tenants Union handout)

blocks.text: At a Madrid apartment complex just outside the city's centre, red maple leaves hang upside down in windows along with defiant posters urging Canadian investment money to get out of their neighbourhood.
"They are pushing us out of our houses," said Rafael Cuadrado, who has lived in the complex for 20 years.
The main target of the residents' wrath is Toronto-based Brookfield Corporation.

A sign on a window of a Madrid apartment accuses Toronto-based Brookfield of treating tenants unfairly. In a statement to CBC News, Brookfield said it complies with all 'applicable Spanish tenancy legislation, including statutory tenant protections and extension requirements.' (Jason Ho/CBC)
One of Canada's premier financial and investment institutions, Brookfield owns 900 units in Cuadrado's residential complex, along with approximately 4,100 others around the Spanish capital.

Cuadrado and other residents accuse Brookfield of planning to let their leases expire and then flip their homes for market prices that few here can afford. He says several of his neighbours have already received notices from Brookfield's management company informing them their tenancies will not be extended.
CBC News has seen one letter sent to a tenant who was told their expiring lease would not be renewed and they would have to turn over the keys to their apartment.
It's not illegal, but the residents say it's unfair.
"Our daughter came here when she was two years old. This is our first house ... so this is our life," Cuadrado told CBC News in his living room.

Many of the residents are long-time tenants who moved into the buildings when they used to be part of Madrid's public housing stock. Most pay rents well below the current market rate, as a succession of lease extensions and government-mandated rent caps have kept their outlay relatively low.

Raphael Cuadrado lives in a Madrid apartment complex owned by Brookfield, one of Canada's top investment firms. He and other residents fear the company plans to flip their units when their leases expire. (Jason Ho/CBC)
Cuadrado says he pays 930 euros a month for his 800-square-foot, three-bedroom apartment. The unit would likely fetch about 1,500 euros on the open market.
"Why do we have to leave our house because there is a big investment company coming from abroad to get a profit [from] us?" he said. "No way."
Clashes in Spain as millions protest nation's housing crisis
'Vulture funds'
Anger over housing in Spain has hit a breaking point.

The eviction of Madrid resident Maricarmen Abascal in late September, after the 87-year-old woman was unable to pay a hefty rent increase, sent protesters into the streets. Authorities evicted her on the back of a stretcher and she died in hospital a few weeks later.
Her eviction prompted Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to call an election for Nov. 29, with housing the central issue.
Spain's public unions, which allied with the tenants, are casting money from institutional investors, such as pension plans, as one of the primary villains. And some of them are Canadian.
"'Vulture funds' are what they call them," said Alicia Del Rio, who is with Sindicato de Inquilinas de Madrid (Madrid Tenants Union), one of the country's most prominent advocates for renters.

Del Rio blames a succession of cash-strapped Spanish governments for laying out the welcome mat for foreign investors, who she says have in turn treated Spanish residential properties as a commodity to be flipped, with little regard for the people living in them.
Alicia Del Rio is with Sindicato de Inquilinas de Madrid, Spain's most prominent tenants union. (Jason Ho/CBC)
"[The government] gave the message, 'Welcome to Spain, this is going to be your paradise.'"
Canadian owners
Canadian retirement funds and investment firms are designed to seek out safe returns — wherever they can find them. And Spain is seen as an attractive place to grow that money.

Along with Brookfield, Canada Pension Plan Investments has a roughly 900-million-euro portfolio ($1.4 billion Cdn) in the Spanish housing sector, although it's focused on student housing rather than residential homes. It owns approximately 13,000 dorm-type beds across Spain and Portugal, concentrated in cities with large universities.
In a statement to CBC News, CPP said its investments help "expand the overall supply of housing available to students without removing existing homes from the conventional residential market."
HOOPP — Health Care of the Ontario Pension Plan — owns approximately 700 million euros ($1.1 billion Cdn) worth of Spanish properties, including 27 residential buildings and 2,300 Madrid homes.
The Spanish tenant unions haven't raised any specific concerns about HOOPP's activities or its properties.
Whether foreign investment firms are cornering the country's housing market has become one of Spain's most fiercely debated issues.
Numbers from the Bank of Spain say institutional investors control only a tiny share — roughly two per cent — of the country's total housing stock.

The tenant unions, however, say the fact that many of those properties used to be public, non-market housing for middle- or lower-income families matters far more than their share of the national total.
Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez appears at a campaign rally in Palma de Mallorca on Nov. 14, ahead of the Nov. 29 general election. (Francisco Ubilla/Reuters)
They also claim that the concentration of apartments in central areas of cities gives companies like Brookfield outsized power to drive up rents across entire neighbourhoods.
Brookfield used to be chaired by Prime Minister Mark Carney, but he had left the company more than a year before it bought the Spanish homes in March 2026 from U.S. private equity giant Blackstone.
Blackstone held the buildings for 13 years. Residents claim Brookfield's intention is to sell the apartments once their existing leases finish.

Residents of the Madrid building told CBC News that when Brookfield eventually puts their apartments on the open market, they believe they could fetch upward of 600,000 euros apiece — a price few of them can pay.
"It is a constant anguish that is affecting our mental health," said Yutzy Fany Vargas Jimenez, who has lived in the complex for 20 years.
Engaging residents
In a statement to CBC News, Brookfield says any allegation that it is forcing people out of their homes is false.
"We comply with all applicable tenancy laws and tenant protections, and allegations that we terminate rental contracts in breach of these protections are inaccurate," said the statement.
None of the residents that CBC News spoke to had suggested Brookfield had cut short an existing lease. Rather, their concerns were about what will happen when their current tenancy contracts expire.

"We are working closely with our local operating partner, to engage with residents and address their concerns, while continuing to invest in the maintenance and quality of these homes and providing opportunities for residents who wish to become homeowners," the Brookfield statement continued.

The company didn't explicitly address whether it plans to terminate leases when current contracts expire, as the residents claim. However, the company did say it will review individual tenancy matters on a case-by-case basis.

Residents of a Madrid apartment complex say Brookfield intends to force them out of their homes when their leases expire. The company told CBC News that all of its rental arrangements in Spain 'reflect the applicable Spanish legal framework, including statutory requirements governing lease duration.' (Jason Ho/CBC)
Election issue
The cost of housing has become a central issue in Spain's upcoming election, although the roots of the problem can be traced back almost two decades.

Sara Herrero, an associate professor and MBA director at the EAE business school in Madrid, says after the 2008 global financial crisis, Spain was broke and its government turned to private capital to bail it out.
"The situation was really horrible," Herrero recalled, as governments and municipalities were forced to unload real estate they had on their balance sheets.
She said at the time, international funds were among the only buyers willing to inject billions of euros into the Spanish economy, helping banks clean up their toxic debt.
"What if they didn't come? What would have happened with these many residential houses if these supposed 'vulture funds' didn't come to Spain?" she said.
"They were doing a legal thing."
Sara Herrero is vice-dean of academic planning and financial management at EAE Madrid, one of Spain's top business schools. (Jason Ho/CBC)
Soaring prices
But recently, property values in the country have soared, rising 34 per cent in the past five years.
"The problem is the basic economic problem of supply and demand," Herrero said. "It's the perfect storm of low salaries, high population growth and high taxes."
The Bank of Spain also estimates upward of 300,000 homes have been converted to short-term tourism rentals, further displacing long-term tenants.
The left-wing government of Prime Minister Sanchez is trying to harness the housing anger to help with his re-election bid — even though the price hikes have all happened under his watch.
People in Madrid take part in a 24-hour nationwide general strike on Nov. 11 demanding wages that allow access to what demonstrators say is decent housing. (Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters)
Sanchez even appeared to give tacit support to the unions leading the general strike, as he passed tenant-friendly decrees that would likely be reversed if he fails to get re-elected.

His opponents on the political right, the People's Party and the far-right VOX, accused Sanchez of creating the crisis by passing legislation that made it hard for landlords to stay profitable, thereby discouraging new supply.
The latest opinion polls in Spain continue to favour a right-of-centre coalition taking power after Nov. 29, although they also indicate Sanchez's party has shown some recent momentum.
Tenant Raphael Cuadrado says he has repeatedly written to the Canadian Embassy in Madrid, hoping someone there can help residents who are worried about their future.
So far, he says he has not received a reply.
"This is day-by-day fighting, and this is not a life," he said.
In a statement to CBC News, Global Affairs Canada said any questions about Brookfield and its activities in Spain should be directed at the company.

articles.title: Large AI companies 'desperate for compute' are crowding out Canadian startups at home
articles.summary: Ottawa's new budget promises to help Canadian AI companies access AI processing power on home soil — something that's been a challenge as smaller startups face fierce competition from larger AI…

image.caption: Wiring sits inside of the Data Hall of the Microsoft data centre campus in Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin, in September 2025. (Audrey Richardson/Reuters)

blocks.text: Ottawa's new budget promises to help Canadian AI companies access processing power on home soil — something that's been a challenge as smaller startups struggle to compete with tech giants for increasingly scarce computing resources.

The federal government is promising 500 megawatts of "sovereign AI compute" to help expand domestic computing capacity using financial tools such as backstops and offtake agreements to encourage private investment, but questions remain about when that capacity will become available and how companies will be able to access it.
For Al Vigier, CEO of Vancouver-based AI company Caseway, accessing computing capacity in Canada is critical to serving his customers.
Caseway develops AI and automation tools primarily for the court system, and also works with law firms and the defence sector. Many of its clients require their information to remain in Canada.

"Most of our clients, the courts, the defence, the Canadian military, they require sovereign AI, which basically means that they don't want their data to leave Canada. They want their data to be governed by Canadian law and they want to enter into agreements with Canadian companies," he said.

But that option doesn't exist in Canada at the moment, Vigier added, so certain Caseway customers won't use the company's AI offerings. For other clients who are more flexible with where their data lands, Caseway has to turn to the U.S. or elsewhere for computing power.
Al Vigier is the CEO of Caseway, a Vancouver-based AI company that builds automation for enterprises and government. (Submitted by Al Vigier)
Canada, like many other countries, relies heavily on U.S. technology companies for cloud services, including remote computing and data storage offered by tech giants such as Amazon and Microsoft.

That dependence raises concerns about data sovereignty, since U.S. laws can give American intelligence and law-enforcement agencies access to information held by technology providers under certain circumstances.

Vigier said the federal government's commitment is exciting because it could help address those concerns. But while he'd like to offer sovereign computing services to clients immediately, he's worried about how the policy will be implemented and when the capacity will become available.
Canadian computing power in high demand

Sean Mullin, a senior fellow at the Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy at the University of Toronto who helped launch Canada's sovereign AI compute strategy, said major technology companies such as Meta, Google and OpenAI are "desperate for compute."
As AI models become more powerful and more people use them, he said "the demand just skyrockets."

For Canadian startups looking to use AI on a larger scale, "it can be hard to secure these contracts because these big hyperscalers can come in and just buy up all the use for five to 10 years into the future," Mullin said.

"And if you're ... a project developer for a data centre, you'd say, 'Oh, it's very easy. I'll just sign one contract with a big, huge company and I've sold all my compute. I don't have to worry about kind of smaller contracts and selling to smaller Canadian firms.'"

items: Supersized data centres are coming to Canada. One province is at the epicentre

blocks.text: The scale of investment by major technology companies is already evident in Canada.

Earlier this year, Meta announced plans to build its first Canadian data centre, a massive one-gigawatt project northeast of Edmonton. Once completed, it is expected to be among the country's largest data centres and the first hyperscale data centre in Alberta.

In October, U.S. AI company Anthropic announced it had signed a long-term lease for the first 95-megawatt phase of a data centre project in Nova Scotia. Canadian clean energy company EverWind Fuels will build and own the facility, while Anthropic will lease the capacity for at least 20 years.
Government partners with Telus on building sovereign AI infrastructure
Ramping up efforts for sovereign AI
Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) says it is working to bring the capacity online "as quickly as possible," but has not provided a firm timeline.

"The government is engaging with a number of proponents on potential projects across Canada that could significantly expand domestic AI compute capacity," a spokesperson said in an emailed statement to CBC News. "These projects are at different stages of development and commercial discussions are ongoing, and it would be premature to confirm specific timelines, projects or locations."

items: Canada wants sovereign AI data centres. What does that actually mean?

blocks.text: ISED said pricing and access arrangements have not yet been decided, although the government expects companies using the capacity to pay market-based rates.
The commitment is part of a broader federal strategy to support sovereign AI. In October, Ottawa also announced it would invest up to $1.6 billion in Toronto-based AI company Cohere.
LISTEN | The Cohere story part one: Carney's $1.6B bet:
Front Burner31:44The Cohere story part one: Carney's $1.6B bet
500 megawatts could be a 'drop in the bucket'
Clay Swerdelian, CEO of Calgary-based Verano.AI, said he'd welcome the opportunity to keep his company's computing operations in Canada, provided the price was right.
Verano.AI primarily supports the energy sector, using AI-powered tools to automate work related to regulatory matters.

Swerdelian says the company has developed their own AI agents and models to handle tasks involving confidential information, including enterprise data and methane emissions data that clients wouldn't want to share with external AI services.
Clay Swerdelian is the CEO of Verano.AI based in Calgary which primarily supports the energy sector with AI-powered automation of workflow on regulatory matters. (Submitted by Clay Swerdelian)
Swerdelian says he expects Canada to experience a "massive boom" when it comes to companies looking for computing power, partly driven by the recent U.S. midterm election results.
"A lot of the red states are now blue states and a lot of the blue states won't allow data centres, so they're shifting to Canada," he said.

"And the place to be is Alberta for the most part, because the gas and all the land that we have and the infrastructure and everything is kind of built out already other than, of course, the data centres themselves."
Given that growing demand, Swerdelian says Ottawa's proposed 500 megawatts of computing capacity could be a "drop in the bucket."

items: Anthropic needs rapid growth to keep up spending, as Canadian AI sector heats up

blocks.text: And with no firm timeline for when that capacity will become available, Mullin said Canadian startups may have little choice but to continue relying on computing services outside the country.
"These firms could try and just buy compute back from hyperscalers, and in many cases that may be south of the border and that just makes us more vulnerable as a country," he said.

"That means things like all that data is crossing the international border subject to U.S. law. It means we don't control these assets, they could be taken away, they can be repurposed for something else and that just makes us overall more dependent."

articles.title: Canada looks to break Starlink's grip on Arctic military communications
articles.summary: Two Canadian high-tech firms have taken a step toward challenging Elon Musk's Starlink with plans for a homegrown military satellite communications system. Dominion Dynamics has signed a $2.2-million…

image.caption: Dominion Dynamics founder Eliot Pence is seen at a conference in Toronto earlier this year. The company has struck a deal with Canadian satellite firm Telesat to develop satellite and autonomous military technology for use in the Arctic. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics

Two Canadian high-tech firms have taken a step toward challenging Elon Musk's Starlink with plans for a homegrown military satellite communications system. Dominion Dynamics has signed a $2.2-million deal with Telesat to develop Arctic-ready technology, part of a broader effort to strengthen Canadian sovereignty and develop an uncrewed combat aircraft.
Homegrown satellite technology could reduce military dependence on Elon Musk

Dominion Dynamics, an Ottawa-based defence technology company, has struck a deal with Canadian satellite giant Telesat, an agreement that opens the door to the development of a homegrown alternative to Elon Musk's Starlink.
The $2.2-million partnership announced Thursday is part of a broader push to give the Canadian military greater control over the technology it relies upon to defend the Arctic.

The deal will see the two companies develop rugged, portable satellite antennas capable of connecting soldiers and uncrewed military aircraft to Telesat's planned Lightspeed constellation of low-Earth-orbit satellites.

Securing the agreement is good news for Telesat, which faces a separate, but critical debt maturity issue. Roughly $3.1 billion in debt related to the company's legacy satellite business is expected to come due between December 2026 and October 2027.
Carney wants Canada to move away from Elon Musk’s Starlink. Can it? | Hanomansing Tonight
Creditors have given Telesat management until Jan. 18, 2027, to reorganize the legacy end of the business, which is separate from the low-Earth satellite group that has signed with Dominion.

The project with Dominion, which includes financial support from the National Research Council, is intended to give Canadian troops a secure communications network that is not dependent on an American commercial provider.
Prime Minister Mark Carney has warned about the dangers of becoming dependent on a single technology provider whose decisions can have profound consequences for national sovereignty.
Eliot Pence, founder and chief executive of Dominion Dynamics, said the experience in Ukraine has demonstrated why Canada needs alternatives.
"Obviously, we've seen Starlink be shut off in Ukraine," Pence said. "What we're really building here is in addition to that [communications] structure."

items: Carney says 'direct casualties' are result of Ukraine's restricted access to Musk's Starshield

blocks.text: The technology being developed would allow military units and autonomous aircraft to communicate directly through the Canadian-controlled Telesat network.
Pence described the concept as something similar to Starlink's portable satellite terminals, but designed specifically for military operations in Canada's harsh northern environment.
"Think of it as a Starlink Mini, but a Telesat Dominion Mini," he said. "It's a sovereign comms link designed specifically for the Arctic" with military specifications.
Starlink difficult to avoid
The partnership does not mean, however, that Canada is about to abandon Starlink.
Pence suggested that the American company's enormous satellite constellation makes it difficult to avoid entirely.
"It'll have to have some interoperability with Starlink because the proliferation of their satellites is just so much more," he said.
He said the goal, instead, is to ensure Canadian commanders have alternatives should one communications network become unavailable, unreliable or politically problematic.
Dominion's existing communications technology is designed to manage multiple networks, allowing military systems to switch between them when necessary.
The company intends to develop two prototype terminals: a lightweight version that soldiers can carry into the field and a larger model for autonomous aircraft and other uncrewed military systems.

items: Experts highlight the 'double-edged nature' of Starlink in the North

blocks.text: Both would be designed to withstand extreme cold and operate in remote locations with limited infrastructure.
The Canadian military is the intended first customer, although no defence procurement contract has been announced.
Dominion says the technology could eventually be used by Canadian Rangers, the Coast Guard, RCMP and emergency responders operating in the North.
There is, however, a significant hurdle.
AI drone warfare is here. Should Canada buy in?
Telesat must first get its Lightspeed constellation into orbit and operational. The company currently expects to begin commercial service at high latitudes around the end of March 2028.

The Telesat agreement is one of several partnerships Dominion has announced this week as it attempts to establish itself as a major Canadian player in the rapidly expanding market for autonomous military aircraft.

On Friday, the company said, in addition to working on the Telesat receiver, Dominion has recruited the satellite-maker and a series of other Canadian firms to work on Scout, its uncrewed combat aircraft.

items: Musk says he was behind Starlink speed restriction in Ukraine
The age of AI warfare has dawned. Is Canada ready?

blocks.text: The other companies supporting the development of Scout include Thales Canada, Top Aces, ITPS Canada, PV Labs, SRC Can, Altitude Aerospace, Groupe DCM, HSB Solutions, North Aircraft Industries and RAMPF Composite Solutions.

Also on Tuesday, the company announced a collaboration with Pratt & Whitney Canada to provide the propulsion system for Dominion Scout, an uncrewed combat aircraft being designed to operate alongside conventional fighter jets.
Scout is intended to fly long distances over the Arctic, conduct surveillance and potentially carry out strikes against hostile targets.
The aircraft will be built around a Canadian-manufactured PW300-series engine.
Pence said securing an engine supplier was a critical milestone for a project still in development.
"You don't really have a plane until you have a propulsion system," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Murray Brewster is the senior defence writer for CBC News, based in Ottawa. He has covered the Canadian military and foreign policy from Parliament Hill for over a decade. Among other assignments, he spent a total of 15 months on the ground covering the Afghan war for The Canadian Press. Prior to that, he covered defence issues and politics for CP in Nova Scotia for 11 years and was bureau chief for Standard Broadcast News in Ottawa.

articles.title: Health-care report highlights chronic conditions, inequities in northern Ontario First Nations
articles.summary: A new report by an alliance of 11 First Nations health and social service agencies highlights health-care inequities facing northern Ontario communities, including high rates of rheumatoid arthritis,…

image.caption: Alvin Fiddler, Grand Chief of Nishnawbe Aski Nation, speaks at the Matawa Training and Wellness Centre in Thunder Bay, Ont., on Thursday during the unveiling of Mamow Ahyamowen's latest health-care report. (Marc Doucette/CBC)

blocks.text: Thunder Bay·New

A new report by an alliance of 11 First Nations health and social service agencies highlights health-care inequities facing northern Ontario communities, including high rates of rheumatoid arthritis, chronic pancreatitis and substance use disorder.
61% of band members dying before retirement age, compared to 22% for Ontario overall

Northern Ontario communities have higher rates of early death and chronic disorders compared to the rest of the province, according to a new report by an alliance of 11 First Nations health and social service agencies.
The report, called “Reclaiming Our Health: Exploring Chronic Conditions in Participating Northern Ontario First Nations,” was released Thursday in Thunder Bay.
The report focused on 22 chronic conditions among members of 70 First Nations between 2003 and 2022, comparing their prevalance with the provincial average.
It found that for northern Ontario First Nations, rates of rheumatoid arthritis were 14.4 times higher, chronic pancreatitis were 4.7 times higher, and substance use disorder were 4.3 times higher.
Some 61 per cent of band members where dying before retirement age, compared to 22 per cent for Ontario overall.
The data comes as no surprise to Alvin Fiddler, Grand Chief of Nishnawbe Aski Nation (NAN), which represents 49 First Nations across Treaties 9 and 5 and was not involved in creating the repport.
“It just reaffirms or validates what we've been hearing from our communities,” said Fiddler.

Maureen Gustafson is the knowledge translation and exchange specialist for Mamow Ahyamowen, an alliance of 11 First Nations health and social service agencies based in northern Ontario. (Marc Doucette/CBC)

But the report offered longitudinal understanding of the health challenges facing northern Ontario communities, said Maureen Gustafson, knowledge translation and exchange specialist for the Mamow Ahyamowen alliance.
“Looking back that far allows us to understand how things have changed over time, looking at trends or patterns,” she said of the report's scope.
Mamow Ahyamowen formed a decade ago with the goal of providing health-care data to First Nations that have historically struggled to obtain this information.
“It's all about giving communities back their data because it belongs to them,” Gustafson said, “but it's often been held by non-Indigenous organizations and institutions.”
Looking back that far allows us to understand how things have changed over time, looking at trends or patterns.Maureen Gustafson, Mamow Ahyamowen
“It's really powerful when the communities can take that back and use it to advance their own goals towards basically self-determination.”
Three of the five most common conditions for community members in 2019 were related to mental health and substance use, the report found:

items: Mood and anxiety disorders.
Substance use disorder.
Other mental health conditions.
High blood pressure.
Osteoarthritis.

blocks.text: The report acknowledges that “health administrative data, by definition, relies on people being able to access the health-care system.” The study only includes data from those in both the Indian Register and Registered Persons Database.

Mamow Ahyamowen receives funding from the Ontario Ministry of Health (MOH). Its study was supported by ICES (formerly the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences), which is also funded by an annual grant from the MOH and Ministry of Long-Term Care.
‘They're not just stories; they're real people’
The report documented big increases in some conditions over time, such as cirrhosis, kidney failure, schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders.
However, there were also decreases in rates of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), osteoporosis and congestive heart failure.

A large group of people gathered at the Matawa Training and Wellness Centre in Thunder Bay, Ont., on Thursday to learn about Mamow Ahyamowen's new report, called “Reclaiming Our Health: Exploring Chronic Conditions in Participating Northern Ontario First Nations.” (Marc Doucette/CBC)
“This could mean that fewer community members are being diagnosed with the conditions, but that they aren’t living as long or that more of them are passing away,” the report said.
While the report dealt in statistics, it was important to remember the humans involved, Fiddler said.
“They're not just stories; they're real people,” he said.
“It's important that we honour those people, people like Miranda that lost their lives trying to access the health-care system that she desperately needed to stay alive.”

Miranda Mamakwa died in September at age 31 after she couldn't get to crucial medical appointments following open-heart surgery in April. The member of Fort Severn First Nation leaves three children behind.
Her story featured in a recent CBC documentary about people from northern Ontario First Nations who say they’re being denied access to critical medical care.
When Canada’s health care fails to be ‘universal’

Fiddler said he hopes Mamow Ahyamowen’s report is sent to the provincial and federal governments so that First Nations can “be given resources for them to address the high disease load that they're currently carrying.”
“I look at it as a very powerful planning tool for our communities to use moving forward,” he said.

items: Jury in coroner's inquest hears how woman from Alberta died in northwestern Ontario
New outpatient addiction program in Thunder Bay, Ont., focuses on Indigenous healing

blocks.text: ‘We need more resources’

The report highlights how health-care partners throughout the region are already at capacity trying to support communities, according to Janet Gordon, vice president of community health for the Sioux Lookout First Nations Health Authority, which is part of Mamow Ahyamowen.
“We need more resources. We need the governments to hear us and to understand what the needs are in all of our communities,” Gordon said.
Janet Gordon is vice president of community health for the Sioux Lookout First Nations Health Authority, which is part of Mamow Ahyamowen. (Marc Doucette/CBC)
It’s also important to recognize the infrastructure needed to support the delivery of health-care services in remote First Nations, she added.
“There's just that demand for workspace and accommodation at the community level and it's not adequate. Our providers could stay longer if there was space,” Gordon explained.

items: Family of First Nation woman who died after being denied medical travel asks OPP to launch investigation
Grand Chief calls Non-Insured Health Benefits program 'Canada's worst insurance company'

blocks.text: Mamow Ahyamowen is developing community-specific reports based on the data it’s gathered. After that, it will issue reports on mental health and substance use as well as injuries.

“For us to know that information, it will inform how we deliver services, how we deliver programs, how we can help communities deal with their community-specific priorities in all those areas — mental health, addictions, heart disease, diabetes,” said Gordon.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Sarah Law is a CBC News reporter based in Thunder Bay, Ont., and has also worked for newspapers and online publications elsewhere in the province. Have a story tip? You can reach her at sarah.law@cbc.ca.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: PhilHealth not offering P5,000 cash aid under YAKAP
articles.summary: PhilHealth has no program that automatically provides cash assistance to all its members

blocks.text: Claim: The Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth) will provide P5,000 cash aid to all its members through its Yaman ng Kalusugan Program (YAKAP).

Why we fact-checked this: Facebook user Cres Jhoerax Vlog posted a video bearing the claim on November 20. The video claims that all PhilHealth members — regardless of whether they are active or inactive paying members — are eligible for the supposed P5,000 cash payout.
It also claims that even those without a Member Data Record or ID are eligible for the cash assistance.

“Nasa aming post ang registration, ang mga requirement, at iba pang detalye. Paki-share po sa iba, para mas marami ang makaalam at makapag-register nang maaga. Mag-follow sa amin at i-share ang balitang ito,” a narrator says in the video.

(Our post contains information regarding registration, requirements, and other details. Please share it with others so that more people can be informed and register early. Follow us and share this news.)
The video has garnered over 100 comments and 200 shares as of writing. Other users have reposted the video bearing the same claim.
The facts: PhilHealth has debunked circulating posts claiming that YAKAP provides cash aid to members.
The agency clarified that it has no program offering cash assistance to all its members, as its mandate is to provide health insurance coverage and access to healthcare services.

The health insurer urged the public to be wary of posts promising unconditional cash assistance or announcing supposed payout schedules accompanied by dubious registration links, particularly those that did not come from any of PhilHealth’s official accounts.
YAKAP is PhilHealth’s national primary care benefit package, giving its members free access to primary care services at accredited clinics. It is an improved version of its Konsulta program.
The program’s benefits include free checkups, laboratory tests, medicines, and cancer screening tests.

AI-generated video, dubious info: The videos about the supposed cash aid are AI-generated. Detection tool HumanMeter flagged one of the videos as 95% likely to be AI-generated, while HiveModeration gave an AI likelihood score of 94.7%.

Meanwhile, similar videos about PhilHealth’s supposed P5,000 cash aid mistakenly reference “AKAP” — referring to the Ayuda para sa Kapos ang Kita Program of the Department of Social Welfare and Development.

Though this program provided cash assistance, it was intended for individuals whose income is insufficient to meet their basic needs. The program has been discontinued as of 2026 and is not affiliated with PhilHealth.
Cash aid fact checks: Rappler has debunked false claims about cash aid and government subsidy programs:

items: FACT CHECK: Registration links to P20,000 AICS, AKAP cash aid are fake
FACT CHECK: UPLIFT cash aid is for eligible beneficiaries, not all national ID holders
FACT CHECK: Post offering cash, livelihood aid under Bong Go’s name is fake
FACT CHECK: Posts promising cash aid, rice subsidy for all national ID holders are fake

blocks.text: – Lourence Angelo Marcellana/Rappler.com

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: Three Kyiv bridges hit during major Russian missile attack
articles.summary: Five people were killed in a wave of strikes which follow Ukraine's successful targeting of the Crimean Bridge.

blocks.text: He added that an unspecified critical infrastructure facility was also damaged and seven medical personnel were injured during the night's assault.
Ukraine's major operation to take out the road section of the Crimean Bridge earlier this week was a tactical and symbolic blow for Moscow.
Since illegally annexing the Crimea in 2014, Moscow has housed troops and military equipment there, with occupying forces travelling through the peninsula towards the front line.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said an operation to weaken the bridge's defences and ultimately cause part of it to collapse had been weeks in the making.
Russian President Vladimir Putin - who personally opened the bridge in 2019 to international condemnation - said the Kremlin's retaliation for the strike would be "far more painful".
Air raid sirens lasted non-stop throughout the night and were ongoing into the morning.
Ukraine's air force says almost 100 missiles were launched by Russia in its overnight attack - one of the largest attacks since the invasion began in 2022. It also involved around 400 drones.
The attack was "one of the most powerful" yet, according to Yuriy Ignat, head of communications for the Ukrainian air force.
Two people were killed in a hit on the Sknyliv railway station in the south-west of Lviv, the city's Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said.
He shared a picture of the ruined remains of what he said was the station's ticket terminal.

articles.title: Marcos concludes 3-day China trip for APEC 2026 summit
articles.summary: President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. on Friday afternoon flew back to Manila after wrapping up his three-day visit in China for the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Conference (APEC) Economic Leaders'…

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 4:28pm

SHENZHEN, China — President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. on Friday afternoon flew back to Manila after wrapping up his three-day visit in China for the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Conference (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting.
The PR001 carrying the President and his delegation left Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport at 4:13 p.m.
They are expected to land in Villamor Air Base in Pasay City at about 6 p.m.

Before departing Shenzhen, Marcos held a Kapihan forum with the Philippine media where he said he used his presence in the APEC summit "to the maximum" by meeting with world leaders as well as business executives.

"So that the opportunities that a conference like APEC provides are fully utilized and we can find ways to engage new partners around the world in the hope that those engagements will bring new business, bring new trade to the betterment of our economy," the President said.

On the sidelines of the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting, Marcos had pull-aside meetings with New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, Vietnamese President To Lam, and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum.
He also had bilateral meetings with Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast, Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori, and Papua New Guinea Prime Minister James Marape.

On Friday, Marcos also led business meetings with Chinese manufacturing company C&U Group, electric vehicle manufacturer BYD Company Limited, and clean-energy technology company Ming Yang Smart Energy Group Limited. — VDV, GMA News

articles.byline: JON VIKTOR D. CABUENAS, GMA News

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 4:26pm

President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. has signed into law a measure that institutionalizes government vouchers to help eligible Filipino students pay tuition at private schools, particularly those who cannot access nearby public schools due to overcrowding or distance.

Under Republic Act No. 12327, or the Basic Education Voucher Assistance Act, signed on November 12, the government will provide financial assistance to Filipino students from middle-middle-income households and below, or those belonging to equivalent income classifications.
The law mandates the Department of Education (DepEd) to implement the program and determine the eligibility requirements, voucher amounts, and participating private schools.

“To achieve quality education, the State shall address classroom backlog and congestion of public schools through the Basic Education Voucher Assistance Act, which shall form part of the broader national strategy to address quality education by resolving classroom shortage,” the law states.

Voucher assistance may be provided, in order of priority, to students enrolled in public schools identified by DepEd as congested, those living in areas without nearby public schools, and those residing in communities with congested public schools.
A public school may be considered congested if its enrollment exceeds classroom capacity based on DepEd standards, or if it has resorted to multiple shifts or alternative delivery modes.

Students living in areas without a nearby public school may also qualify, including senior high school students in areas where public schools do not offer subjects or electives aligned with their chosen pathways. The law defines the covered area as within a walkable distance of three kilometers from the student's residence.

The program budget will be distributed equitably among all regions, including the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), based on official data on public school congestion, available capacity, and open seats, with priority given to areas with the highest public school congestion.

Qualified beneficiaries and their families will be allowed to choose their preferred private basic education institution from a registry maintained by the DepEd. Schools will be required to provide information on their location, available slots, student capacity, tuition fees, and other relevant details.

The law requires DepEd to implement safeguards against fraud, including a centralized system for verifying learner eligibility, stronger audit and monitoring procedures, and mechanisms to protect whistleblowers.

Schools or individuals found to have committed fraud or other prohibited acts may face administrative and legal penalties, such as suspension, disqualification from the program, reimbursement of funds, blacklisting, and prosecution.

The law also requires the government to disburse payments to participating schools within 60 days after the submission of complete documents to the DepEd. Local government units, private sponsors, and other scholarship providers may supplement the assistance.

It also assists private basic education institutions and their teachers, including in-service teacher training, teachers’ salary subsidies, scholarships for qualified private school teachers, and support for school development.

The program will initially cover kindergarten and elementary students beginning in School Year 2027-2028. Meanwhile, existing beneficiaries of the Educational Service Contracting Scheme and the Senior High School Voucher Program will continue to receive assistance until they complete basic education. —LDF, GMA News

articles.summary:
UK and EU have provisionally agreed to allow 100,000 EU citizens to come to the UK every year under a new mobility scheme.

Senior correspondent

France’s insistence…
