blocks.text: UK and EU plan first talks on sending refused asylum seekers to third countries
Rajeev Syal and Lisa O’Carroll
The UK and the EU plan to establish formal talks for the first time about sending rejected asylum seekers to third-country hubs, according to a leaked document.

blocks.caption: A migrant leaves an abandoned warehouse, where some migrants are taking shelter during the winter months, in Marck, near Calais, northern France. Photograph: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: A draft of a joint statement expected to be signed by Andy Burnham and Ursula von der Leyen at a summit on Friday morning states that both sides will establish “a structured dialogue” to discuss “returns to third countries”.
Until now, the Home Office has been seeking bilateral agreements with third countries allowing the removal of migrants, but with no obvious success.
Last week, five EU countries – Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands – announced an agreement in principle with Rwanda to establish a migrant “return hub” there in 2027.

Burnham hinted at possible cooperation with EU countries last week when he told reporters that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that [the five-country deal] with interest, learning from what went on in the past”. He said: “The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”
The UK has been fighting for deeper cooperation with the EU on migration, with the new deal on a “strategic dialogue” secured in the last two weeks by negotiators in Brussels.

It is a key part of the UK-EU reset pact, which also covers a youth mobility scheme, tariffs on Chinese imports, food and drink exports to the EU and a wider restatement of commitment on defence and security.
Informed sources confirmed this was the first time the UK and the EU had agreed to “open a dialogue on returns” after the launch of the bloc’s Channel action plan in June this year.
Whitehall sources said the UK was now open to the possibility of sending rejected claimants to Rwanda – a recent pivot from the position under Keir Starmer’s government, which rejected the move.
According to a draft of the joint agreement, negotiations over third-country hubs will be part of increased cooperation to tackle irregular migration.
Row over voting rights dispels myths that UK comes to negotiations from position of strength - snap analysis

blocks.caption: Lisa O’Carroll

blocks.text: Lisa O’Carroll
Senior correspondent

France’s insistence that the UK could not have voting rights at any stage during the shaping of legislation on food standards and public health risks relating to food and agri products is a line in the sand for Andy Burnham.

blocks.caption: Journalists arrive as preparations are made for the EU-UK Summit at the European Council building in Brussels. Photograph: Virginia Mayo/AP

blocks.text: The last night tensions at the ambassadors meeting will be a sharp lesson for anyone in the UK who clings to the idea that negotiating with the EU comes from a position of strength: the UK is not a member of the EU and despite the warm feelings to the Labour government in European capitals, benefits of the club are not extended to non members.
It also underlines the feeling expressed by several large member states this week that the way forward after this summit is not more iterative reset summits or mini-deals.

Yes, there will be negotiations on allowing the UK into the energy single market as this is in the joint interests of both sides in the wake of the Ukraine war. But no talks on pharma or chemicals, according to some capitals.
As one diplomat said:
“It puts down a marker warning the UK that cherry picking bits of the single market mean you are a rule taker.”
“It makes the choice for Britain starker and more binary” and shows that “the alternatives are basically muddling along with a version of the status quo or rejoining,” they said.

blocks.caption: Jennifer Rankin

blocks.text: Jennifer Rankin
in Brussels
UK prime minister Andy Burnham will be welcomed with a rendition of God Save the King and the Ode to Joy when he attends the opening ceremony around 10.30am local time.

blocks.caption: Musicians rehearse the British national anthem and the European anthem ahead of the EU-UK summit in Brussels, Belgium. Photograph: Olivier Hoslet/EPA

blocks.text: Talks went down to the wire this morning
Talks to seal today’s reset in relations between the UK and the EU went write down to the wire this morning.
In what is known as a “silence procedure”, the EU issued a late night compromise text to all member states after a meeting of crunch hours long meeting of ambassadors in Brussels last night.
Under the procedure if no member states breaks the silence the text is considered “adopted” and would then be made available for signing by the UK – bar any last minute hitches on its side.
This morning diplomats said “no one had broken the silence”. The headline agreements are:

items: Food and drink deal, setting up sanitary and phyto sanitary common area
An electricity carbon emissions deal
Cap of 100,000 EU citizens under 31 years old to come to the UK under a new youth mobility scheme
The issue of tuition fees kicked down the road - a supplementary agreement has been reached to sort this out within the next six months
This allows the UK to hold up the youth deal if the EU does not give it what it needs in the Made in Europe legislation which is expected to reach its final negotiations stages by Easter too.

No voting rights for the UK when the EU comes to writing new laws about food standards; this was never a realistic option as the UK is not a member of the EU, but the French led the resistance as the UK pushed for it equally as hard, instead the UK will be consullted at key stages
Industry groups say that must mean UK regulators are in the room at the early stages. Food regulation is very technical, the say and this is where the real decisions are taken.
The two sides will also open talks on UK entering the energy single market.

blocks.text: Morning opening: Second post-Brexit EU-UK summit gets under way in Brussels

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
The EU and UK will hold a long-awaited summit in Brussels on Friday – the second since Brexit – to hammer out the UK’s longer-term relationship with the bloc.

blocks.caption: A member of protocol arranges the Union flag and EU flag as preparations are made for the EU-UK Summit at the European Council building in Brussels. Photograph: Virginia Mayo/AP

blocks.text: It will be attended by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, the head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and the president of the European Council, António Costa.
As our Brussels correspondent, Jennifer Rankin, explained:

“The two sides hope to announce three deals, which were initiated under Starmer’s government. First, a food and drink agreement that will remove a lot of Brexit red tape on animal and plant products, making it easier to trade meats, cheese, wine and flowers. To secure the deal, which is not expected to take effect until 2028, the UK will align with EU standards, meaning the government, for example, must abandon a planned ban on foie gras imports. A second agreement will link the British emissions trading system with its bigger EU cousin, restoring a link severed by Brexit. It is a significant step for industry because EU and UK businesses will be exempt from each other’s charges on high-carbon imports such as steel, cement and electricity. This agreement also requires alignment with relevant EU rules. The third deal has proved the most contentious: a youth mobility scheme that will give those aged 18-31 the right to live, work, travel and study on both sides of the Channel for up to three years. The scheme may not be up and running until 2030 – which is bad news for anyone in their late 20s.”
The leaders are expected to arrive 9.30am GMT (10.30am Brussels time), with “the leaders’ meeting” between Burnham, von der Leyen and Costa to follow.

A plenary session with UK ministers and EU commissioners is expected at 10.45am GMT (11.45am Brussels), and if all goes well we should then see the leaders tell us what they agreed around half past midday (1.30pm Brussels time).
I will bring you every single detail of the day here today. You won’t miss a thing.
It’s Friday, 20 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

blocks.text: Here is a roundup of headlines from India from Friday, November 20:
Pakistan's Climate Change Minister Musadik Malik arrived in New Delhi on Friday for a Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) cultural forum.

It is the first visit to India by a Pakistani federal minister since Bilawal Bhutto Zardari attended the SCO meeting in Goa in May 2023, and the first since last year's conflict between the two countries.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi is set to inaugurate the Civilizational Dialogue Forum, which runs from November 20 to 22. India invited Pakistan's culture minister in October, but Islamabad sent Malik instead.
Pakistan's Foreign Office said he would present the country's views on dialogue among civilizations and meet other SCO members on the sidelines, local media reported.
Malik said the visit is not a bilateral negotiation, according to NDTV. No breakthrough in frigid relations is expected.

The visit comes after the four-day India-Pakistan conflict of 2025, set off by the Pahalgam attack, which killed at least 70 people on both sides, AFP stated. It also comes two days after Indian forces killed Lashkar-e-Taiba commander Lateef Bhat.
Kashmir tourism struggles post Pahalgam attack
Opposition leaders criticized the government's move to host Malik.

"BJP always says that talks and terrorism cannot happen at the same time. But now, a Pakistani minister is visiting India for the SCO meeting," said Samajwadi Party leader Fakhrul Hasan Chand, NDTV reported.
Congress Member of Parliament Pramod Tiwari also recalled Malik's earlier remarks on the Indus Waters Treaty, calling his language that of a "terrorist," according to NDTV.
Earlier this year, Malik, referring to the Indus Waters Treaty suspension after last year's Pahalgam terror attack, had warned against "water aggression," pressing India to respect the 1960 treaty.
"Whoever touches our water, their hands would be cut off," he said at the time.

articles.title: Sara Duterte's tree planting 'connection' with Calle88 questioned in impeachment trial
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel raised questions Friday regarding the alleged possible connection of Vice President Sara Duterte's tree planting activities with Cale88 Foods Corporation.

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 4:11pm
The House prosecution panel raised questions Friday regarding the alleged possible connection of Vice President Sara Duterte's tree planting activities with Cale88 Foods Corporation.

Cale88, the food firm linked to Duterte's husband Manases Carpio, has come under scrutiny during the vice president's impeachment trial over its profits earned with only two employees and its supposed financial inflows from China.
During the cross examination of Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo on Day 45 of the trial, private prosecutor Erwin Matib flashed photos of Duterte planting trees.
The defense counsel initially objected on the basis of relevance, but Presiding Officer Francis Escudero allowed Matib to continue, granted that he is on a short leash.

"Tama po ba na itong pagtatanim ng mga puno ni Vice President Sara Duterte ay connected sa pag-comply ng Cale88 Foods sa tree planting activities na requirement ng Board of Investment? In fact, ang requirement ng Board of Investment ay magtanim dapat ang enterprises ng at least 100 forest trees. May ganoong requirement, tama po ba?" Matib said.

(Is it correct that Vice President Sara Duterte tree planting is connected with with Cale88's compliance with the tree planting requirements of the Board of Investment? In fact, the requirement of the Board of Investment is to plant at least 100 forest trees. There is a requirement for this, right?)
Before Rodolfo could answer, defense counsel Justin Gular objected.

"Objection, your honor, misleading. There is no prior testimony coming from the witness wherein he testified that the vice president participated in the compliance requirement of tree planting," Gullar said.

"The insinuation being made by the prosecution that the pictures being shown or that was displayed of the vice president planting trees had any relation to Cale88 Foods Corporation's registration is misleading, malicious and callous, your honor," he added.
Escudero sustained Gular's objection, telling Matib to carry on to the next point.
Rodolfo affirmed that tree planting was part of Board of Investment's (BOI) requirements. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Defense witness: Cale88 has zero employees in 2024, two in 2025
articles.summary: Cale88 Foods Corporation, a listed business interest of Vice President Sara Duterte"s husband, Manases Carpio, in their joint wealth statement, recorded zero employees in 2024 and two employees in…

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 4:08pm

Cale88 Foods Corporation, a listed business interest of Vice President Sara Duterte’s husband, Manases Carpio, in their joint wealth statement, recorded zero employees in 2024 and two employees in 2025, a defense witness said Friday.

Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo of DTI’s Industry Development and Investment Promotions Group made the testimony during the cross-examination of private prosecutor Erwin Matib wherein the witness was confronted with General Information Sheet (GIS) submitted by Cale88 to the Board of Investments (BOI).

Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero allowed the prosecution to confront Rodolfo, who also serves as the BOI’s Managing Head, with Cale88 Foods Corp. GIS for years 2024 and 2025 because he was familiar with such documents. Cale88 Foods Corp. changed ownership to Pikimong Pikimong Philippines Corp.
Asked by Matib how many rank-and-file employees Cale88 Foods Corp. had in 2024 based on GIS, Rodolfo said, “Wala po.” (None.)
Matib then asked Rodolfo if Cale88 Foods Corp. had a manpower complement in 2024 based on GIS, to which Rodolfo replied, “Wala rin po.” (There’s also none.)
Likewise, Rodolfo said he did not see any Cale88 Foods Corp. submission on its employees’ Social Security System and PhilHealth benefits.
He also explained that the BOI would not readily know the list of employees of a business entity unless the company applies for an incentive before the BOI.
“Ang pangbangga kasi namin iyong incentives. Pag nag-avail po sila ng incentive, hihingin po namin ‘yun (list of employees),” Rodolfo said.
(We base it on the incentives. If a firm seeks an incentive, we’ll ask for a list of incentives.)
“Dahil hindi naman siya nag-avail na incentive, wala pong pang bangga ho,” Rodolfo added.
(Because they did not avail of an incentive, we won’t have that record [of employees].)

Rodolfo earlier said during the same impeachment proceedings that based on Cale88 Foods Corp.’s BOI form submissions, its number of employees was reduced from 201 in 2024 to 50 in 2025 because of the change in ownership.

Lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro of Batangas, in a separate interview, noted that such a discrepancy in Cale88 Foods Corp. submissions proves that the testimony of the prosecution witness and CPA-lawyer Alex Cabrera is an implausible business model.

“We saw the inconsistency [in submitted documents]. When you say it is an implausible business model, it does not necessarily mean a zero operation. We have to read that terminology on the basis of the entire procedure of the expert witness. For me, the fact that BIR documents (GIS) do not tally with the data with BOI makes it an implausible business model already,” Luistro told reporters.

“Because we need to be very consistent on the business data that we are submitting to the government agencies such as the DTI, Securities and Exchange Commission, and take note of the inward remittances reported by the AMLC (Anti-Money Laundering Council). Implausible is a very general term, and it could mean as well that inconsistent data or information which are being submitted or at the very least shown by the different government agencies,” Luistro added.

Defense witness and AML Consulting PH head, Atty. Rainer Dela Fuente, earlier testified that there were red flags in Cale88 Foods Corporation operations given that the firm only has two employees, received P319 million remittances from China and recorded 757 covered transactions and suspicious transactions worth P1.2 billion based on AMLC records.
Dela Fuente, however, said such red flags are not automatically illegal. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: China's Xi praises 'turnaround' in relationship with Australia
articles.summary: The leaders of Australia and China have held talks on sidelines of APEC summit. Australian PM Anthony Albanese is also slated to meet Chinese Premier Li Qiang.

image.caption: China's Xi also called for enhancing cooperation with Australia in agriculture, ​energy, the ‌green economy and artificial intelligenceImage: Lintao Zhang/Getty Images/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Chinese President Xi Jinping held talks on Friday, following which Xi hailed a "comprehensive turnaround" in the ties between two nations and Albanese said his country was engaging "constructively" with Beijing.
The leaders met on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Forum (APEC) summit in China's Shenzhen.
What did Xi say to Albanese?
Xi pointed out to Albanese that they had met four times since the latter became Australia's Prime Minister in 2022.
"I think it is fair to say that together we have brought about a comprehensive ​turnaround in China-Australia relations," the Chinese President said.
Xi also called for enhancing cooperation in agriculture, ​energy, the ‌green economy and artificial intelligence, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported.
Why is China important for Australia?
China is Australia's top trading partner.
The relations between the two countries hit rock bottom under Canberra's former centre-right coalition government, which had called for an independent inquiry into the origins of the coronavirus.
An angry China retaliated by imposing import curbs worth $13 billion (€12.2 billion) on Australian timber, coal, barley, lobsters and wine.
Since Albanese's centre-left Labor party came to power, China has lifted most of its blocks on Australian exports.

But friction in ties has surfaced occasionally on issues such as China conducting a missile test in the South Pacific and Australia tightening a foreign investment screening in the critical minerals sector.
"It is important that Australia continue to engage in a constructive way with China, manage our differences, but not be defined by them," Albanese told the media on Friday.
"What happens in China does matter for Australia," he added.
Iron ore, a pressure point
Albanese is expected to travel to Beijing and meet China's Premier Li Qiang later on Friday.

On Monday, Australia, which is the world's biggest producer of iron ore, called out China's "manipulation" of trade in the commodity over Beijing's formation of a central buying body to purchase ‌ore on behalf of its steelmakers.
A single buyer has increased bargaining power in negotiations with sellers.
Albanese and Li will attend a business roundtable comprising of senior executives from Australian mining giants Rio Tinto and BHP and ​Chinese company executives.

articles.title: Vape users hospitalised after losing consciousness, prompting public health warning in New South Wales
articles.summary:
NSW health issues public warning about vape liquids containing etomidate, a strong and fast-acting sedative used as a general anaesthetic overseas

Three people who lost consciousness and…

blocks.text: Three people who lost consciousness and were hospitalised in New South Wales after using certain vapes have tested positive for the unregulated anaesthetic agent etomidate, health officials have said.

NSW health on Friday issued a public warning about vape liquids containing etomidate, a strong and fast-acting sedative used as a general anaesthetic overseas but not registered for medical use in Australia.
The three people who were hospitalised had used non-nicotine refillable vapes, the state health department said. Testing of their blood and urine confirmed the presence of etomidate.
The department would not confirm how old the three patients were, where they were hospitalised, or their condition on Friday.
The discovery of etomidate in vapes in NSW comes about four months after Victorian health officials announced they had found the powerful anaesthetic agent in an illicit vape sold in Melbourne.
On Friday, NSW health warned vapes sold as space pods, space oil, kpods, piu piu vapes, or zombie vapes may contain etomidate, or other substances, including ketamine, THC and potent opioids.
The medical director of the NSW poisons information centre, Dr Darren Roberts, said etomidate’s effects were unpredictable when used in a vape.
Roberts said etomidate could cause confusion, drowsiness, slow breathing, vomiting, muscle spasms or movements that were hard to control, and people who took it could become unresponsive.
These effects could be life threatening, especially if used with other drugs that could cause sedation, such as alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, and GHB, Roberts said.
He said etomidate could also cause long term harm when used regularly, including the disruption of hormones produced by the adrenal gland.
These hormones are important in regulating stress responses and need to be replaced if they aren’t produced naturally, he said.
“The contents found in non-nicotine vapes vary,” Roberts said. “You can’t assume what’s inside.”
He urged anyone considering using a vape to ask themselves what could be in it.
“You won’t get into trouble for seeking medical care,” he said. If you feel unwell, or if your friend feels unwell, after using a vape, do something about it.”
NSW health officials said it recommended people administer Naloxone to anyone who became responsive after using any drug, in case they had ingested opioids.
Naloxone is an opioid overdose treatment, which is free at pharmacies and does not require a prescription.
Naloxone won’t reverse the effects of etomidate, as the sedative does not belong to the opioid class of drugs, but it is still safe to give, health officials said.
The officials said anyone who witnessed someone experiencing unexpected symptoms after using drugs should call triple zero immediately or seek urgent medical attention.

articles.title: Baby born with heart abnormalities ‘didn’t have a chance’ after non-medical free birth, NSW inquest hears
articles.summary:
Inquest into the deaths of four babies after free and home births hears routine checks and follow-up may have saved their lives

Four babies who died in New South Wales – three after free…

blocks.text: Four babies who died in New South Wales – three after free births and one after a home birth – might have survived if they had had routine checks and follow-up , a coronial inquest has heard.
Baby DH, Baby D, Baby R, and Baby B died in the state’s northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024.
The inquest in Lismore has heard women chose free or home births for reasons including traumatic experiences, a lack of trust in clinicians, and a lack of services.

Baby DH died about eight hours after he was born in a free birth – with a doula but no medical professionals present. The court earlier heard he turned purple, was struggling to breathe and had became floppy.
His parents gave evidence they were worried but the doula kept reassuring them their baby was OK, then left.
The doula denied many of their claims, and denied that she gave them any clinical advice.

Expert neonatologist, associate professor Nicholas Evans, said on Friday Baby DH’s complex heart abnormalities “would have been readily detectable” in a routine pregnancy scan after which he would have been referred to a paediatric cardiologist.
It was a “missed opportunity”, he told the court.
Paediatric cardiologist Dr Paul Brooks said it was “highly likely” all the abnormalities would have been identified in a routine scan before birth.
Even if the extent of the abnormalities wasn’t clear, he told the court, the scan would have shown the baby needed to be born at a major hospital with cardiac surgery capabilities.
“The site of [Baby DH’s] birth meant that he didn’t have a chance.”
Baby D’s mother did not know she was having twins, and at first thought she’d delivered Baby D’s placenta, only to realise it was a stillborn second twin.

Experts at the inquest agreed it was impossible to know exactly why Baby D died. They discussed the possibility it was because self-described birth keeper Sita Tara Kali did not clamp the umbilical cord before cutting it, but ultimately, Evans told the court, it was most likely from respiratory distress because of his compromised heart function.

Baby D might have survived if someone who could do advanced resuscitation arrived in under 10 minutes, he said, but the “root cause” was that it was not known the mother was carrying twins before the births.
“If [twins] had been diagnosed, at 18 weeks, as it would usually in pregnancy, there would have been very close monitoring.”

Baby R likely died of “severe post-maturity” after being born at 43 weeks and one day in a free birth. The standard is to induce birth or perform a caesarean section at 42 weeks, as the ageing placenta puts the baby at risk.
The mother had been for an ultrasound at 12 weeks, which had put the date of birth at 28 July, 2020.
But the mother distrusted hospitals and trusted Kali, her birth keeper, the court previously heard.
Kali told her to calculate her due date from the date of conception, an unreliable measure that put the date of birth in mid August.
That recalculation, Evans wrote in his report to the court, was the “root cause” of the issue.
“The standard practice now is that you don’t allow a pregnancy to go beyond 42 completed weeks,” Evans said on Friday.
Expert midwives earlier told the court they don’t have statistics for babies born beyond 43 weeks, because it’s so rare.

A 19 August ultrasound showed the pregnancy had become a medical emergency – but Kali advised her to “go home and rest”. It is “more likely than not” that the baby would have survived had she gone to hospital after the ultrasound, Evans said.

Baby B’s mother was warned multiple times that she needed to go to hospital to give birth to her twins, but she was determined to have a home birth. Rather than let her have a free birth, four midwives assisted her and the head midwife repeatedly counselled her about the risks.
The mother declined ultrasounds as well as a test for early onset group B streptococcus (GBS) – an organism present in 15 to 20% of women that infects the babies of about 2% of carriers.
Baby B likely died of GBS, pneumonia and sepsis, Evans told the court on Friday, while his twin fell ill but survived. Many infected babies survive in hospital thanks to antibiotics, he added.
The inquest is ongoing.

articles.title: Nigeria moves to end jail terms for attempted suicide
articles.summary: Nigeria's proposed reform follows years of calls from psychiatrists and a parallel Senate bill.

blocks.text: Nigerian President Bola Tinubu has asked parliament to decriminalise attempted suicide, proposing medical support instead of prosecution for those who survive.
The proposal seeks to shift Nigeria's approach from criminal punishment to treatment and rehabilitation.
It follows years of calls for reform from mental health professionals. A separate bill seeking to decriminalise attempted suicide has already passed its second reading in the Senate.
Under Nigeria's law, attempted suicide is a criminal offence with those convicted facing up to one year's imprisonment, a fine or both.
The Senate bill also seeks to replace criminal penalties for attempted suicide with medical treatment, rehabilitation and support.
It was sponsored by Senator Asuquo Ekpenyong, who has argued that prosecuting people who survive suicide attempts could discourage those experiencing suicidal thoughts from seeking help.
He also warned that families might conceal such incidents for fear of prosecution and social stigma.
He stressed that the bill is not aimed at legalising or encouraging suicide attempts but rather protecting the survivors.
Tinubu's proposal has been welcomed by Senate President Godswill Akpabio, who had previously suggested that people who survived suicide attempts should be sent to prison.
"We are saying that suicide is a crime for now. Therefore, if you attempt it, we will send you to prison," Akpabio had said.
However, after receiving the Tinubu's proposal, he sought to clarify his earlier remarks, saying they did not apply to people experiencing mental health conditions.
He added that punishing people whose actions were influenced by mental health conditions would be insensitive.
Tinubu's letter follows sustained calls from mental health professionals for the law to be changed.

At a parliamentary public hearing in May 2024, the then president of the Association of Psychiatrists of Nigeria, Professor Taiwo Obindo, urged lawmakers to remove criminal penalties for attempted suicide.
"Why do we, as a nation, then punish individuals who are ill and need medical attention rather than prosecution?" he asked.
Drawing on his experience as a psychiatrist, Obindo said most people who die by suicide have a history of mental illness.
Akpabio has referred the president's amendment bill to the relevant senate committee for further consideration.
Nigeria is among several African countries where attempted suicide remains a criminal offence.
Ghana decriminalised attempted suicide in 2023, while Kenya's High Court ruled in January 2025 that the law criminalising it was unconstitutional.
If you have been affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line.

articles.title: Mysterious Mercury is about to get a visitor - after spacecraft's eight-year epic voyage
articles.summary: The mission is set to give us our best ever view of Mercury - the closest planet to the Sun.
articles.byline: Rebecca Morelle, Alison Francis, Tony Jolliffe

blocks.text: Mysterious Mercury is about to get a visitor - after spacecraft's eight-year epic voyage
Why is a spacecraft flying to Mercury?
ByRebecca MorelleAlison Francis and Tony Jolliffe BBC News Science
After an eight-year journey travelling almost six billion miles (10bn km), a spacecraft called BepiColombo is about to reach its final destination and get into orbit around Mercury.

It will be entering an extremely hostile environment: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and temperatures can reach a fierce 430C and then plunge to -180C, and it is constantly blasted with intense solar radiation.
Until now, the planet has been little explored but the hope is this mission will solve some of Mercury's major mysteries.
These include uncovering why there is ice in its craters despite its proximity to the Sun, and understanding the mysterious hollows that are dotted all over its surface.

"I think it's a little bit of an under-loved planet in the inner Solar System, but I think that's one of the reasons why it is so compelling," said Prof Emma Bunce, from Leicester University, who is a principal investigator on the mission.

"There are lots of reasons, scientifically, why we really want to understand Mercury, how it formed, how it evolved, what it looks like today, but also how it interacts with the Sun and the extreme space weather that it experiences."

blocks.caption: Image caption, The spacecraft - just seen here - has taken selfies as it has closed in on Mercury

blocks.text: Image source, ESA/JAXA
The spacecraft - just seen here - has taken selfies as it has closed in on Mercury
The BepiColombo mission, which is a collaboration between the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japanese Space Agency (JAXA), blasted off in 2018, launching from French Guiana.
With the spacecraft heading deep into the inner Solar System, it has had to battle the Sun's immense gravitational pull.

So it has had its brakes on for the entire journey, and has also taken a very convoluted path - looping once around the Earth, twice around Venus and six times around Mercury - to slow it down enough to get into orbit.
This journey should have taken seven years, but a problem with BepiColombo's propulsion system meant the already epic voyage was extended by a year.
The final manoeuvre to get into orbit is a perilous one: it needs to perform a 37-minute handbrake turn to be grabbed by the planet's gravity.
If anything goes wrong, the spacecraft could hurtle past Mercury.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A close up view of the scarred surface of Mercury

blocks.text: Image source, NASA
A close up view of the scarred surface of Mercury
Only two spacecraft have visited Mercury until now - both Nasa missions.
Mariner-10 flew past the planet three times in the 1970s, and then the Messenger spacecraft arrived at Mercury in 2011 and spent four years in orbit.
But there is still much to discover about this tiny world.
Mercury is only a bit bigger than our Moon, and is covered in ancient volcanoes, towering cliffs and colossal craters.
And time on Mercury passes in a mind-bending way.
The planet zips around the Sun so quickly, a year on Mercury lasts just 88 Earth days. But it turns incredibly slowly on its own axis, so a single day there lasts 59 Earth days.

blocks.caption: Image caption, These strange hollows have not been seen anywhere else in the Universe

blocks.text: These strange hollows have not been seen anywhere else in the Universe
As well as investigating why Mercury has ice in its craters in the polar regions, the mission will also spend time studying strange dents in the planet's surface.
There are thousands of hollows all over it. They are shallow but with steep sides and often clustered together, and in planetary terms, they are young: about 100,000 years old.
Scientists know they are not impact craters - larger pockmarks on the surface caused by colliding space rocks - but they are not really sure what the hollows are or how they formed.
BepiColombo will also help to study another aspect of Mercury that has been puzzling researchers. Despite the planet's tiny size, it has a huge metal core.
Prof Emma Bunce said that the planet could once have been much bigger, but was potentially the victim of a "hit and run" early in its history.
"One of the explanations is that the mantle was stripped away in a large collision," she explained.
"Or it's a combination of collisions over a longer period of time that then strips away its outer outer regions, its mantle and its crust, and leads to the planet that we see today."
Or she said, it could have just formed that way in a metal-rich part of the early Solar System.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A life-size model of BepiColombo is on display at the Science Museum in London

blocks.text: Image source, Tony Jolliffe/BBC News
A life-size model of BepiColombo is on display at the Science Museum in London
Unusually, this is a sort of "buy one get one free" mission - there are two spacecraft onboard.
A few weeks after arriving at Mercury they will separate.
An ESA craft will study the surface close-up, the other, which belongs to JAXA, will view the planet from a distance.
A life-size model of BepiColombo is on display at the Science Museum in London. It was used to test the craft while it was being put together.
Jessica Marshall, a systems engineer at Airbus, who built the spacecraft, showed us Bepi's key features - and said the moment of separation would be "nerve-wracking" for the team.
The two spacecraft had to be very securely attached together for their launch and long journey, but now, eight years later, they have to delicately disconnect.
"We have designed a special mechanism that we have thought very carefully about," said Marshall.

"It's been exposed to the harsh radiation of space and highly different thermal temperatures, and after eight years this is a spring mechanism that has to then release very gently… As it releases, it actually also twists in order to start the spin of that spacecraft as well."
With two orbiters at Mercury, both packed with instruments, the BepiColombo team hopes to find answers to Mercury's mysteries.
Of course, they may uncover many more once they arrive.

articles.title: Kellie Sloane says she’s ‘pretty sure’ NSW Liberals exodus is over after Mark Speakman resigns
articles.summary:
Former NSW opposition leader warns party against being ‘One Nation lite’ as he became eighth out of 24 Liberal MPs not to recontest seat in March

  • Get our

blocks.text: The New South Wales opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, says she is “pretty sure” the exodus of Liberals before the March state election has finished, after Mark Speakman became the eighth MP to decide not to recontest their lower house seats.

In a late-night speech on Thursday, the final sitting day of NSW’s legislative assembly before the vote, Speakman said he would not run again in his south Sydney seat of Cronulla, which he has held since 2011.

A third of the 24 current Liberal MPs have announced they will not recontest their seat in March, including Jordan Lane, Mark Coure, Tanya Davies, Ray Williams, James Griffin, Alister Henskens and Mark Taylor.
In a press conference on Friday, Sloane insisted the departures were not an indictment of the party’s election prospects.

“No, that’s not the truth. What we are seeing is an impressive cross section of abilities and talent and tenure in our party,” she told reporters in the same room where, exactly a year ago, Speakman announced he would resign as Liberal leader in her favour.
“We have people who have been in government before. We have people who have been in for a medium amount of time, and we’re going to have people with fresh ideas.”
Sloane said she had tried to convince Speakman to stay and said many of the MPs leaving had been in parliament for more than 10 years, although Lane is a first-term MP.
Sloane said a significant number of Liberals had retired before the 2023 election, in which the Coalition lost government and the party dropped nine seats.

Asked if she could guarantee that further MPs would not step down ahead of the March vote, Sloane said: “Look, I certainly hope not. I certainly hope not. I’m pretty sure that’s done. I’m pretty sure that’s done.”
Warnings against becoming ‘One Nation lite’
Since last year’s leadership spill, the Coalition has gone from commanding 28% of the primary vote in NSW to 23%, Sydney Morning Herald Resolve polling suggests.
Labor has gone from 37% to 30%, while One Nation, which Resolve did not start polling separately until March, is now at 26%.

Last week, Sloane said her party would not form government with One Nation, but she did not rule out a confidence and supply arrangement. The Australian Financial Review has reported many of her MPs privately expect the Liberals to go into a coalition with One Nation.
On Friday, Sloane rejected the claims from “anonymous names in a Financial Review article”, saying the Coalition only needed to flip six Labor seats to form minority government.

In his speech in the dying minutes of the parliamentary term, Speakman, a member of the party’s moderate faction, said the Liberals faced an “existential threat” following a wipeout at the 2025 federal election and an “orange wave that seems to be coming across the country”.
He warned the Liberals against becoming “Labor lite” or “One Nation lite”, saying they should stick to the values of “Menzian Liberalism”.
after newsletter promotion
Referencing Pauline Hanson’s notion of “monoculture”, Speakman said Australia was “the most successful multicultural society on the planet” and was “so much better for it”.
“You know, we hear certain people say we want a monoculture, and that people who don’t support that monoculture somehow are enemies of Australia, hate Australia,” he said.
“I love Australia for its multiculturalism. Diversity is our strength. It is our strength, and we should build on that.”
Speakman, a barrister, served as environment minister between 2015 and 2017, and was attorney general between 2017 and the Perrottet government’s defeat in the 2023 election.
He was chosen as the Liberal and opposition leader after Dominic Perrottet’s resignation, a position he held until November last year.

On Thursday, he said being opposition leader “is often said to be the toughest job in politics” and, while it had “ultimately unravelled” for him, he had mostly led an opposition “which was competitive with, or even ahead of, the government in the polls”.

He said his record as attorney general included legislating for NSW to be the first Australian jurisdiction to criminalise coercive control, introducing affirmative consent tests in criminal sexual assault trials and reforming criminal and civil child sexual abuse cases.
Earlier on Thursday, the NSW premier, Chris Minns, announced the former Liberal councillor and parliamentary staffer Tanya Raffoul would contest the Liberal-held seat of Epping as a Labor candidate.
On Friday, Sloane said Raffoul had been talking to her about Liberal party roles “only two months ago”.
“She’s decided to chase personal ambition. She’s a very ambitious person, but she’s changed sides, and that’s a decision Chris Minns has made.”

Earlier, the NSW treasurer, Daniel Mookhey, rejected the idea that One Nation was pushing Labor to become “Liberal lite”, saying Raffoul’s candidacy reflected “a journey that I think many Liberal people are going through as well”.

articles.title: Race to be next UN secretary general exposes divisions among world powers
articles.summary:
Debate about dominance of permanent five members could reignite if major powers block Costa Rican frontrunner

The race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment…

blocks.text: The race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment on Friday when a UN security council vote is likely to reveal whether the Costa Rican frontrunner for the post would be blocked by the big powers. If so, the setback will reignite a debate about the dominance of the permanent five (P5) members at the United Nations.

Rebeca Grynspan, an economist and UN insider who is from a family of Polish-Jewish wartime refugees to Costa Rica, has been in the lead in all but one of the eight straw polls of the 15 UN security council members since the first secret ballot was held on 30 July. Each member goes down the list of candidates, casting an “encourage”, “discourage” or “no opinion” vote for each candidate.

Despite countries not being required to reveal how they voted, it is thought Grynspan’s candidature has been resisted by Russia and the US, two of the five permanent security council members that can ultimately wield a veto against a candidate. Knowledge among the security council delegations of how countries are voting is down to private intelligence, leaks and a process of elimination.

The intensive lobbying over the job has spread across the globe, but Friday is especially important since the poll is slated to differentiate the voting of the P5 from the 10 elected members (E10) of the security council. To be recommended as secretary general to the UN general assembly, a candidate needs nine votes and no vetoes. In Friday’s colour-coded secret ballot, the P5 will cast red ballots and the E10 white.
One diplomat said: “The electoral system means it is important how many votes you win, but equally how many of certain votes you don’t lose.”

blocks.caption: Polarisation has also hampered the incumbent secretary general, António Guterres. Photograph: Ted Aljibe/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: The protracted 140-day deadlock confirms the polarisation that has hampered the incumbent secretary general, António Guterres, but also belies claims the role is now an irrelevance.

Friday’s secret ballot may also reveal whether the United Arab Emirates’ campaign for its diplomat, Lana Nusseibeh, is about to blow up in its face due to the hostility to the UAE’s brand of active, commercially driven diplomacy, not just in Sudan, but also Somalia, Western Sahara, Libya and Yemen.

A late entrant, in the two straw polls in which she has contested so far, Nusseibeh secured only seven “encourage” votes, six “discourage” and two “no opinions”. This is despite prestigious big-power backing and her acknowledged personal diplomatic skills.

Nusseibeh has US and Russian backing. The French foreign ministry may have misgivings about the UAE, but Emmanuel Macron, the French president, travelled to the UAE in the midst of French riots to see the UAE president, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, and secure 100,000 metric tons of diesel a month.

blocks.caption: The UAE’s Lana Nusseibeh has US and Russian backing. Photograph: David Dee Delgado/Reuters

blocks.text: In the UK, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has kept his counsel, but he shares a Polish-Jewish refugee heritage with Grynspan and cannot be an admirer of the UAE’s human rights record or its evasion of EU sanctions on Russia. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has UAE connections from his time as mayor of Manchester, and Nusseibeh is a fellow alumnus of the University of Cambridge. At the UN she worked closely with the UK in an informal group called “Friends of the Future of the UN”.

Yet 68 British MPs, including the Labour chair of the international development select committee, Sarah Champion, last week signed a letter calling on Burnham to veto Nusseibeh, describing her as “a tainted and compromised figure”.

Some of the opposition to her from elected security council members is not wholly political. Latin American countries believe an informal rotation system means it is their turn to lead the UN. As a result Panama and Colombia, currently on the security council, will oppose her. China has also been supportive of this rotation principle.

But others deeply object to what they consider to be the UAE’s dollar diplomacy and preparedness to use its extraordinary wealth to exacerbate and exploit pre-existing divisions in a country to gain a commercial foothold. Somalia, for instance, has a seat on the Security Council, and its president, Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, this week went on TV to accuse the UAE of buying ports, establishing military bases and supporting armed forces outside Somalia’s national security framework without federal approval.

It is also possible that Finland and Latvia, the two elected members with the greatest stake in Ukraine, are unimpressed that the UAE gave Vladimir Putin red carpet treatment when he visited Abu Dhabi in December 2023, nine months after the international criminal court had issued an arrest warrant for child trafficking. Greece, less engaged in Ukraine, may be more flexible.

Since the last poll, Nusseibeh has been to Bahrain, Britain and Pakistan, a clue as to where extra votes may be harvested. She also had a “thoughtful exchange” with Zeng Jixin, the Chinese ambassador to the UAE.

The two hurdles are whether someone so deep inside the UAE inner circle would have the courage in office to show true independence, and whether her active denials of UAE involvement in arming the RSF in Sudan leave her irretrievably tainted. From a Palestinian intellectual family, she insists she would make peace in Sudan her number one priority.

In the last ballot on 5 November, Grynspan won 12 votes in favour and three negative. But on 16 October – the only colour-coded ballot so far – which distinguishes between permanent and elected members – she received two discourage votes from permanent members, the equivalent of a veto. Nusseibeh had not joined the race at that point.

blocks.caption: Russia has opposed the Argentine candidate Rafael Grossi, objecting to his interventions over the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant in Ukraine. Photograph: Matthias Schräder/AP

blocks.text: In an administration as personalised as the US, it has been hard for Grynspan to gain influence, with many sensing that Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, is the key influencer.

Grynspan has been reluctant to make the fact she is Jewish a feature of her candidacy, but the election of a Jewish person to run the UN might be seen as something the US could embrace as transformative. Her age – she is 70 – could be considered a drawback among those calling for a younger generation to renew the institution.

Although there are other Latin American candidates, Grynspan is seen as a more viable candidate than her rival, the Argentine Rafael Grossi, the head of the UN weapons inspectorate. Russia has opposed Grossi, objecting to his interventions over the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant in Ukraine.
One way or the other, the logjam has to be broken soon.

articles.title: Iraq university’s removal of male professors teaching women sparks weeks of protests
articles.summary:
Al-Qadisiyah University’s move a sign of the country’s slide into a Taliban-like gender segregation, say activists

The removal of male professors teaching female students at a university in…
articles.byline: Ali Aziz, Maria Talal and Tom Levitt

blocks.text: The removal of male professors teaching female students at a university in southern Iraq has sparked protests and been criticised by activists as a Taliban-like gender segregation policy.

As many as 400 women are estimated to have joined protests over the past two weeks calling for the return of their professors at Al-Qadisiyah University in a move that appears to have surprised its administrators.

The university said the move was necessary to “prevent the mixing” of men and women and had been requested by the families of female students. But students said their families had known since before they enrolled that there were men on the teaching staff and supported their daughters’ protest.

Students said university bosses had mocked their protests and refused to discuss their concerns about the sudden loss of their academic supervisors. On social media, commentators also accused the women of seeking to keep male professors to “establish immoral relationships with them”.

“My classmates and I went to demonstrate, and the university president, Rahi al-Yasiri, blocked our path with his bodyguards, who then began making fun of us. He ordered them to take photographs of our faces, in an attempt to intimidate us and punish us later,” said Huda, 22, one of the female students.

Huda said the students tried to explain how men and women still worked together in society in Iraq. “Aren’t there doctors who treat both men and women? Why then do you prevent male professors from teaching us, too?” In response, Huda said Al-Yasiri replied: “Even if you hit your heads against the wall, I will not bring back the professors.”

The students said a large number of them were tied to graduation projects and research supervised by the professors. They said they had grown accustomed to their professors’ teaching methods, who also knew their students’ strengths and weaknesses, which made replacing them at this stage more complicated.
Female students said they had been told by the university that if they were not happy with the change, they should drop out.

An Iraqi-British feminist researcher, Balsam Mustafa, from the University of Cardiff, said the female students were “treated as if they are minors without the right to object to decisions affecting their academic lives”.

Mustafa said the removal of the male professors was a part of a worrying trend in women’s rights in the country, with “growing discussion about women’s clothing and chastity reflected in the celebration of female students who wear the abaya”.
An Iraqi lawyer and human rights activist, Israa Salman, said the restrictions on women was a “societal catastrophe”.

“Attempts are being made to suppress women’s talents and turn Iraqi society – a society that has produced remarkable minds and expertise, with women playing pioneering roles in many fields – into something resembling Kabul under Taliban rule.
“This contradicts Iraq’s constitution and the international treaties and conventions the country has signed and ratified,” said Salman.
Produced in collaboration with Jummar, an independent Iraqi media platform

articles.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon’s explanations of body disposal ‘ring hollow’, court hears
articles.summary:
Former police officer has pleaded not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in Paddington in February 2024

  • Get our

blocks.text: Beau Lamarre-Condon knew he had murdered two men and his attempts to explain the disposal of their bodies “ring completely hollow”, a court has heard.
Lamarre-Condon is accused of fatally shooting Jesse Baird and his new partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home in Sydney on 19 February 2024.
The former officer has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.
Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC went through Lamarre-Condon’s attempts to clean up the alleged crime scene and dispose of the bodies on Friday as the trial wrapped up its ninth week.
The defence does not dispute Lamarre-Condon’s actions in the aftermath of the deaths, instead arguing he did so because he “panicked considerably”.
But Hatfield told the New South Wales supreme court his conduct was not that of a person who panicked after something unintended, but behaviour that was “deliberate, sustained and very purposeful”.

The crown prosecutor said Lamarre-Condon took extensive steps to distance himself from the deaths, manufactured evidence to make it look like Baird was alive by texting people from the dead man’s phone, and “disposed of the bodies in an utterly callous manner”.
“The lies, concealment and disposal of the bodies are not equally explained by manslaughter or accident,” Hatfield said.
“His conduct is immediate and the steps are so extreme you might think it’s only consistent with having intentionally killed both men and a planned murder.
“His explanations in his evidence … ring completely hollow.”

Lamarre-Condon claimed his initial steps came out of concern for the housemates, but by leaving the bodies in the courtyard, he risked them making a “completely terrifying discovery”, Hatfield told the court.
Hatfield said the accused had an understanding that “exactly what he’d done was murder”.
“His conduct was an exercise in avoiding accountability in what he knew he had done,” he said.

blocks.caption: Luke Davies and Jesse Baird.  Composite: Supplied/NSW Supreme Court

blocks.text: Earlier on Friday, Hatfield re-iterated the prosecution’s arguments about the day of the alleged murders, playing the audio of the two gunshots that killed Baird.
after newsletter promotion
The lawyer invited the jury to consider what they could do in the four seconds between the shots.
Making a gun gesture with his own hand, Hatfield argued there was only time to walk a few steps and fire and “not opportunity for much more than that”.
Lamarre-Condon then came up with a “pathetic moral dilemma” and claimed he feared he could be killed in jail, when he knew he would be in protective custody, the prosecution alleged.
The defence alleges Baird and Davies were killed in two separate struggles when Lamarre-Condon was acting in “self-defence”.

Going through forensic evidence, Hatfield noted Davies’ DNA was found on the gun, but says this is “entirely unremarkable evidence”, alleging Lamarre-Condon had handled his body at the scene and then touched the weapon.
“It’s just something he’s grabbed on to in order to weave this invented narrative about Mr Davies shooting himself,” the lawyer said.

Earlier evidence provided by a weapons expert indicated it would take the force equivalent to almost 3kg to pull the trigger, which would not happen without a conscious movement on behalf of the person holding the gun, the prosecution alleged.
The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

articles.title: White House replaces cyber security chief after tech outages
articles.summary: Sean Cairncross is leaving his role as national cyber director after a chaotic week of tech outages. Kirsten Davies, the Pentagon's chief information officer, will assume the position in an acting…

image.caption: Kirsten A. Davies will take over as acting national cyber directorImage: Jacquelyn Martin/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Sean Cairncross is exiting his post as White House national cyber director after a series of technology-related outages in the United Statesover the week led to disruptions in air travel, banking and national security systems.

Shortly after Axios and other US news outlets first reported Cairncross' departure, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced Department of Defense Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies as the new cyber director, congratulating her on X.
"Look forward to working together to strengthen America's cybersecurity," Rubio said.
Davies will assume the position in an acting capacity.

"Our nation stands in the crossroad of analog, digital, and quantum technologies, our American way of living increasingly interconnected," Davies wrote on X late Thursday night, as she thanked US President Donald Trump and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller for their "faith and steady confidence" in her.

"Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come …but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future."
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth referred to Davies' tenure at the Pentagon as one in which "she has proven herself to be a dedicated patriot and professional."
"We are confident she will advance President Trump's America First agenda across the cybersecurity landscape," the Pentagon chief said.
Cairncross leaves after US tech outages

The Trump administration came under scrutiny in recent days after the US witnessed a major tech meltdown as service outages affected not just travel, communications, and e-commerce, but also the National Security Agency.
Top US officials have since sought to assure people in the country that there was no evidence of a cyberattack.
In 2025, Trump nominated Cairncross to serve as his top adviser on cybersecurity and data protection policy. He was subsequently confirmed to the post by the Senate.

During Trump's first stint in the Oval Office, Cairncross took on various roles as a White House insider. He was ⁠also an executive at ​the Republican National Committee before becoming the cybersecurity chief.

articles.title: Texas death row execution takes more than an hour as inmate heard complaining of pain
articles.summary: The execution of Reinaldo Dennes in Texas took over an hour as prison staffers struggled to find a suitable vein for the two intravenous needles carrying the lethal dose of the sedative…

image.caption: This image provided by the Texas Department of Criminal Justice shows Reinaldo Dennes on April 14. He was executed Thursday in a procedure that took 63 minutes to complete. (Texas Department of Criminal Justice/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

The execution of Reinaldo Dennes in Texas took over an hour as prison staffers struggled to find a suitable vein for the two intravenous needles carrying the lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital. He was the second person put to death in the country Thursday after Florida carried out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year, of Thomas Mitchell Overton.
Reinaldo Dennes yelled out 'I don't think this is normal,' before dying 63 minutes after being strapped down

The execution of Reinaldo Dennes in Texas took over an hour as prison staffers struggled to find a suitable vein for the two intravenous needles carrying the lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital.
He was the second person put to death in the country Thursday after Florida carried out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year, of Thomas Mitchell Overton.

The executions of two men in their 70s cast a renewed spotlight on the aging of the U.S. death row population. They also follow renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the U.S. in the aftermath of Tennessee's failed execution of Christa Pike in September.

Dennes, who was found guilty of capital murder in the death of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer found shot multiple times in his Houston office in January 1996, gave a brief statement in which he said he wanted his loved ones to know he was blessed the past 30 years "knowing the love of the father."
Then he told the warden: "Go, warden!"

Almost immediately he exclaimed: "The pain! Go! Go!" He uttered an expletive and implored "the father" to "take this pain." "Let me go, father," he said again and again. "Let me go. … I'm here. I've been your son all these years."

Then he shouted: "My right leg is killing me!" and described it as a cramp. After another profanity, he grunted, then said, "I don't think this is normal. Take me, father. Don't let me suffer like this. C'mon."
Pentagon’s plan to livestream execution sparks outrage
Procedures followed appropriately, say prison officials

After three loud groans, Dennes began snoring sounds — eight of them — that progressively got quieter before a final loud snore. Then he began breathing quietly, about a dozen breaths, also getting progressively less pronounced.

The procedure was completed at 7:07 p.m., 63 minutes after he was strapped to the gurney. A minute later, after being examined by a physician, Dennes was pronounced dead at 7:08 p.m. at the penitentiary in Huntsville.

Prison officials said all procedures were followed appropriately. Spokesperson Amanda Hernandez acknowledged a number of unsuccessful attempts to find a suitable vein before the execution team managed to insert the needles in Dennes' left foot and on the left side of his neck.
She did not know how many attempts were unsuccessful but said the sites ultimately used are in accordance with the state's procedures.
This image provided by the Florida Department of Corrections shows Thomas Mitchell Overton, who was put to death in Florida Thursday. (Florida Department of Corrections/The Associated Press)

Earlier in the day, Florida carried out its execution of Thomas Mitchell Overton, 71, who was convicted of murdering a pregnant woman and her husband, Susan and Michael MacIvor, during a home invasion.

Overton was pronounced dead at 6:19 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison. In a final statement, he denied ever breaking into the couple's home and attacking them, saying, "I never killed anyone."
Florida has carried out half of all U.S. executions in 2026

Florida has now carried out more than half of the nation's 39 executions to date this year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who has made aggressive use of the death penalty like few other governors. The executions follow renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the U.S. in the aftermath of Tennessee's failed execution of Christa Pike in September.

DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said he wanted justice for families who've waited decades for death sentences to be carried out. He signed the death warrants that led to a record of 19 executions in 2025, then the most in a single year in Florida since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. After a record-setting Thursday, Florida is planning two more executions in December.
Texas set a record for executions there when 40 people were put to death in 2000.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis has taken an aggressive stance on death row executions since taking office. (Chris O'Meara/The Associated Press)
Overton case
In Florida, Overton was seen strapped to a gurney with an IV in his arm when the death chamber curtain lifted at 6 p.m.
"I've never sexually assaulted anyone. I never killed anyone," Overton said, denying ever having been in the MacIvors' home or gated community. "I didn't kill the MacIvors."

The injection began immediately afterward with Overton panting and breathing heavily before all movement ceased. A warden then shook Overton and shouted his name without answer before a medic declared the inmate dead.

The MacIvors' bodies were found in their Tavernier, Fla., home on Aug. 22, 1991, court records show. Autopsies determined they were strangled and that Susan MacIvor, eight months pregnant, had been raped. The medical examiner said her unborn male child likely survived for about half an hour after her death.

Investigators collected DNA evidence but found no match with the state's database. But when Overton, who had worked at a gas station near the MacIvors' home, was arrested on an unrelated burglary charge in 1996, his DNA sample matched one from the MacIvors' home.
Overton was subsequently convicted in 1999 of two first-degree murder counts and received a death sentence for each.
Michael MacIvor's sister, two brothers and cousin witnessed the execution. The man's sister, Sharon MacIvor, said watching Overton die gave her a sense of relief but not satisfaction.

"One of the hardest things I have ever had to hear was how my brother Michael fought to stay alive," Sharon MacIvor said. "Michael was my little brother. He was loved, he had a family, and he had a lifetime ahead of him."
Christa Pike's lawyers demand answers, transparency over botched execution
Dennes case

Dennes, a jewelry designer, had an office in the same building as Szucs, according to court documents. A cleaning woman testified at trial that Dennes arranged for her to open the building's back door after hours, allowing Dennes and his brother entry the night of the shooting. Records showed she also distracted the security guard at Dennes' request.
The guard was shot twice but recovered and identified Dennes as his assailant.

Police found the jeweller's body in his office, but his safe was empty with no sign of the diamonds or some $200,000 US in cash he supposedly kept there, court filings indicated. Authorities said the diamonds were never located.
Dennes's attorneys later argued there was insufficient evidence to prove he killed Szucs.
A year after Dennes was convicted, his brother, Jose Albert Dennes, pleaded guilty to murder in the case and was sentenced to 45 years in prison. He was released on parole in 2019.
